Q: Why do cats sometimes sleep in plant pots? My grandparent’s cats slept in their plant pot when it had nothing in, they only did it often in summer. I wonder why they would want their pelts to be dirty with …
A: Same reason they sleep in other locations - warmth and comfort.

Plant pots containing soil warm up in the daytime in summer, the soil and pot retaining that heat (especially if they're terracotta pots). It seems natural that a cat would find a plant pot an attractive place to stay.

Being round allows the feline to curl up comfortably as well.

They don't especially want dirt and grit on their coats, but that's something they can deal with afterwards (most of the time they'll probably shrug the dirt right off).

Q: Why does my cat eat plants? I have caught my cat a couple of times chewing on household plants. Most of the plants now have chewed leaves. I have seen him do it outside but I suspect he might. Why …
A: Roughage, to aid digestion, help them pass/regurgitate hairballs, and sometimes just because they like the texture or it cleans their teeth (same reasons some cats like puncturing paper).

If you want to discourage nibbling on your houseplants, consider planting a pot of cat grass (in the literal sense, not "kitty pot" aka catnip). Most pet suppliers offer seeds for one or another member of the grass family, for just this purpose.

Q: How much water should my pet drink, and how do I spot dehydration?
A: Keep fresh, clean water out at all times, in places your pet can easily reach. Cats that eat wet food often drink less, because the food is mostly water. Cats on dry food need to drink more.

Signs of dehydration:
- Dry or sticky gums
- Skin that stays "tented" when you gently lift it at the back of the neck, instead of snapping back
- Sunken eyes, weakness, low energy or poor appetite

Vomiting and diarrhea can cause dehydration fast. Call your vet today if you think your pet is dehydrated. Go now if they haven't eaten or drunk anything for 24 hours, or are very weak.

Drinking much more than usual also needs a vet visit within a day. It can be a sign of kidney disease, diabetes or other illness.

Q: How much water should I let my dog drink? My dog is a Labrador schnoodle cross and he is almost one year old. I want to know how much water I should allow him to drink because I don't want …
A: As much as he wants! There are very few instances where you should limit the amount your dog drinks. An example would be:
- Your dog is vomiting - better to offer small amounts of water several times a day instead of him engulfing large quantities at once. If vomiting persists your pet should be seen by a veterinarian as frequent vomiting can lead to dehydration.

It is important to monitor how much he drinks as an increase can be an indicator to illnesses such as diabetes and kidney disease.

Q: Can a pet legally be put to sleep in the Philippines?
A: Only for reasons the Animal Welfare Act allows. Section 6 of RA 8485 permits killing a pet when, for example:

- A licensed vet certifies it has an incurable communicable disease
- A licensed vet certifies it is needed to end the animal's suffering
- It is needed to prevent immediate danger to human life or limb

It must be done humanely, using methods approved by the Committee on Animal Welfare. Electrocution of dogs is banned under RA 9482. Talk to your vet if you're facing this decision.

Q: Is it legal to sell or eat dog meat in the Philippines?
A: No. RA 9482 bans the trade of dog meat. LGUs must enforce this ban (Section 7).

Under Section 11, anyone caught trading dog meat faces a fine of at least P5,000 per dog and 1 to 4 years in prison. The same penalty applies to using electrocution to put dogs to sleep. Foreigners who break these rules are deported after serving their sentence.

Killing dogs for food is also not among the allowed reasons for killing animals under the Animal Welfare Act (RA 8485, Section 6).

A: Assuming the problem is not the result of dehydration or a medical condition, then, to be honest, I think you're doing the right thing. Dogs need to be corrected while in the act or, ideally, just before the act and it's not physical correction that you want to do, it's the tone and display of displeasure. If he reacts correctly, show him you're pleased with his response (mildly) and if he doesn't, strengthen the tone until he does.

Q: My dog drank some beer someone left on the table during our party.
A: Alcohol is absorbed quickly and can be dangerous for pets. Call your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now and take him in.

Signs include vomiting, diarrhea, wobbling, sleepiness, trouble breathing and tremors, and in severe cases coma or death.

Before you go:
- Tell the vet what drink it was and roughly how much he had.
- Only make him vomit if a vet tells you to.
- Don't give coffee or anything else to "sober him up". Caffeine is also toxic to pets.

On the way, keep him calm and watch his breathing.

Raw bread dough with yeast can also make alcohol inside the stomach, so keep both drinks and dough out of reach.

messages.content: My dog has no chest movement for 10 seconds. Help, what do I do?

This sounds like it could be cPR. Only for a pet who is unconscious, not breathing and has no heartbeat. Get someone to drive to the vet while you work.

What to do now:
- Lay them on their right side on a firm surface. Put flat-chested breeds like Bulldogs on their back.
- Cats and small dogs: wrap one hand around the chest just behind the elbows and squeeze. Larger dogs: stack both hands on the widest part of the chest. On their back: press on the breastbone.
- Push hard and fast: a third to a half of the chest's width, 100â€“120 times a minute (the beat of "Stayin' Alive"). Let the chest come all the way back up.
- After 30 compressions, close the mouth, straighten the neck and give 2 quick breaths into the nose, watching the chest rise.
- Keep going 30 compressions to 2 breaths. Check for breathing and a heartbeat every 2 minutes, and keep going on the way to the vet.

Don't:
- CPR on a pet who is breathing or has a heartbeat. It can hurt them.

Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now.

Q: What papers do I need to bring my dog or cat to another island or province?
A: You need a local shipping permit from the Bureau of Animal Industry (BAI), applied for online at nvqsd.bai.gov.ph. Under the BAI Citizen's Charter, dogs and cats need:

- A veterinary health certificate from a licensed vet, showing rabies vaccine details (brand, batch/lot number, date given, next due date)
- A rabies vaccination certificate signed by the vet with their PRC number
- The pet should be about 3 to 4 months old or older
- The rabies shot should be at least 14 days and not more than 1 year old (annual boosters can ship right away)

The permit is free; processing takes up to 3 working days. Rules may change, so confirm with BAI before your trip.

messages.content:
Where do I get a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (health certificate) and acclimation certificate?

I have heard that I will need a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection to travel with a pet (dog) and some airlines require an acclimation certificate. Where can I obtain these certificates and is there anything I should know before attempting to get them?

Here's a link to a checklist from the American Veterinary Medical Association where they give a link to the USDA website to find an accredited veterinarian. If anything, I would say give the veterinarian that you normally visit a call, and ask if they're accredited to give those certificates. If they're not, you could ask if they know of another veterinarian who is.

Basically the goal of the inspection is to make sure is that you take your pet into a veterinarian for a health inspection before travelling. They might also require your dog to be up-to-date on heartworm pills. Similar to people travelling, it's really just to make sure the dog is is healthy and provide any needed vaccines to protect against diseases and parasites from where it's travelling. You might also be required to go through a follow-up visit when you return.

Q: Do you walk cats, or should you? I do not own pets as of now, but I'm interested. I read that dogs should be walked at best twice a day, but I was wondering where the cats get their exercise. …
A: To exercise cats, play with them. Give them something to pounce and chase like a laser-pointer dot or a string or a light ball or a feather wand. Give them climbing/jumping opportunities -- all the better if the jump is a bit challenging but is rewarded with a good resting/watching spot or a view out a window. My two, siblings, sometimes like to wrestle or chase each other around the house.

Remember that they're taking a pretty good jump for their size every time they leap onto a chair or your lap. Simply living in a human household gives them some exercise.

Q: Why is zinc oxide bad for dogs? This answer to applying sunscreen to dogs says that you shouldn't apply human sunscreen to them because it contains zinc oxide and that's bad for dogs. What about it is bad, and what …
A: The primary reason for concern would be zinc toxicosis. This is basically the formation of zinc salts in the stomach acid which are toxic and can lead to diarrhea, lethargy, seizures, and more. It's quite dangerous and can require surgical intervention to treat.

Common sources of zinc poisoning in dogs and cats include the Lincoln penny(!) and zinc-oxide creams. Dogs are more likely to get this problem because they more freely eat whats around them, but using human sunscreen on a dog or cat is very likely to result in them attempting to lick it off and, well, poison themselves.

sources.text: Q: Does a dog's pink or white skin need special care? I have noticed there's a dog with white fur and pink skin on her belly, under her fur and on her nose. Her skin is paler than most dogs I … A: This answer is only addressing one aspect relating to skin and coat color. Skin cancer and sunburn Lighter colored skin is more prone to sunburn and skin cancer. Generally there is a link with coat color and skin color. White hair, fair skin, black hair darker skin. Why does my dog howl at airplanes?

I noticed that whenever an airplane passes over our house, my dog starts howling and doesn't stop until the plane is a very far distance from our house.

Is this a normal behaviour?

If not what can I do to keep my dog from howling at planes?

In addition to John Cavan's answer, if you've ruled out any medical problems your dog most likely howls at the plane to make it go away - and it's working!

If planes pass over your house frequently enough, you'll want to desensitise your dog to the noise.

Try searching for airplane noises on YouTube and play them at a volume that your dog is comfortable with. Reward with lots of treats and praise.

Increase the volume in very small steps, as you will undo a lot of the work if you misjudge your dog's limits and he starts howling.

Have lots of patience, it'll likely take a while for your dog to get used to the noise and to associate it with good things happening(TM).

Q: How much water should my pet drink, and how do I spot dehydration?
A: Keep fresh, clean water out at all times, in places your pet can easily reach. Cats that eat wet food often drink less, because the food is mostly water. Cats on dry food need to drink more.

Signs of dehydration:
- Dry or sticky gums
- Skin that stays "tented" when you gently lift it at the back of the neck, instead of snapping back
- Sunken eyes, weakness, low energy or poor appetite

Vomiting and diarrhea can cause dehydration fast. Call your vet today if you think your pet is dehydrated. Go now if they haven't eaten or drunk anything for 24 hours, or are very weak.

Drinking much more than usual also needs a vet visit within a day. It can be a sign of kidney disease, diabetes or other illness.

sources.label: FurFriends first-aid guide: Hit by a vehicle or fall
sources.text:
Hit by a vehicle or fall. Internal bleeding and chest injuries may not show at first. Pets that fall from balconies or windows need a vet check too.
Signs: Limping, not putting weight on a leg; Fast breathing, pale gums; Swelling belly, bleeding from the nose or mouth; Seems fine but was hit or fell. Still go.
What to do now:
1. Make sure you're safe from traffic first.
2. Approach slowly and speak softly. Hurt animals bite, so use a towel or muzzle unless they're vomiting or struggling to breathe.
3. Move them as little as possible. Slide a large dog onto a board or blanket to use as a stretcher, keeping the back and neck straight. Put small pets in a box or carrier.
4. Press on any bleeding, keep them calm, and go to the vet now.
Don't: Giving any painkiller. Trying to straighten or splint a leg. Giving food or water.
Go to a vet now.

Q: My old pet has really bad breath. Is that dental disease?
A: Often, yes. Gum disease is very common in older pets, especially small dogs. Signs include:
- Bad breath that doesn't go away
- Red or swollen gums
- Trouble picking up, chewing or swallowing food

Bad breath can also point to other illness. A sweet smell may mean diabetes, and a urine-like smell may mean kidney disease.

See your vet for a mouth check. Proper cleaning below the gumline needs anesthesia. Vets check older pets carefully first, and treating mouth pain often makes them much happier.

At home, brush your pet's teeth with pet toothpaste, never human toothpaste. See a vet soon if your pet stops eating or has a lump in the mouth.

Q: What does 5-in-1 or 6-in-1 vaccine mean?
A: The number tells you how many diseases one shot protects against. Combining them means fewer injections.

Labels often use letters, for example:
- D = distemper
- A2 = adenovirus type 2 (protects against hepatitis)
- P = parvovirus
- P = parainfluenza
- L = leptospirosis

So "DA2PP" covers four diseases, and adding L gives "DA2LPP". Products differ in what they add, such as extra lepto strains or other germs, so the number alone doesn't tell you the exact mix.

For cats, the common combo is FVRCP: feline viral rhinotracheitis (herpesvirus), calicivirus and panleukopenia.

Ask your vet which diseases your pet's vaccine card covers.

Q: What danger signs indicate health issues when aquiring a new dog?

I am considering buying or adopting a new dog, and was wondering what signs I should look for to indicate health issues?
A: HEALTH ISSUES SIGNS

- The dog might have lost a lot of hair.
- The dog might also scoot a lot.
- The dog might have a dry and rough coat.

messages.content: how do I know if my dog is too fat

Vets use a 9-point body condition score (BCS) from WSAVA. You can do a quick check at home:
- Ribs: Run your hands along the sides. At a healthy weight you can feel the ribs under a thin layer of fat. If you can't feel them without pressing, there is too much fat.
- Waist: Look down from above. You should see a waist behind the ribs.
- Belly: From the side, a dog's belly should tuck up. A cat at a healthy weight has only a small fat pad on the belly.

Signs of overweight are ribs that are hard to feel, no waist, a rounded belly, and fat over the lower back (and in dogs, the base of the tail).

Ideal is 4 to 5 out of 9 for dogs and 5 out of 9 for cats. Ask your vet to score your pet and plan safe weight loss.

Q: My senior dog seems confused and paces at night. What's wrong?
A: This can be a sign of cognitive dysfunction, a condition like dementia in people. It affects about 14 to 22% of dogs over 8 years old. Signs include:
- Getting lost or stuck in corners at home
- Sleeping more in the day and restless at night
- Less interest in family members
- Toilet accidents in the house
- Pacing, anxiety or barking for no clear reason

Cats can get it too, and often meow more.

Pain, vision loss and other illnesses can cause similar changes, so see your vet for a full check. Treatment works best when started early. Gentle exercise, new toys and simple games can help keep your pet's mind active.

Q: Any internal medicine to get rid of maggots in dogs? There's a 6 month puppy in my area and he's been infected with maggots in his right rear leg. He's too scared of humans so i cant go near him …
A: No, there is not a strictly internal/oral medication that can be used to treat maggots living in a live dog. The condition is called fly strike or Myiasis it can be fatal if untreated, there has been some success orally with Ivermectin in treating cattle, but there is some indication that dying larvae excrete toxins that can be fatal so close monitoring of the animal is required.

Most remedies involve physically removing the maggots, followed by treatment for related issues.

Q: At what age is my dog considered a senior?
A: There's no single age, because dogs age at different rates depending on breed and size. Vets often call a dog senior when it is in the last quarter of its expected lifespan. As a rough guide, many dogs reach this stage at around 7 to 8 years.

From that age:
- See the vet at least twice a year
- Ask about blood and urine tests every 6 to 12 months to catch problems early
- Have blood pressure and thyroid checked yearly

Watch for changes at home, like slowing down, drinking more, weight change or confusion, and tell your vet. Old age is not a disease. Many changes can be treated.

Q: How do I safely move an injured dog or cat to the vet?
A: Call your vet first, then leave as soon as you can. To move your pet safely:

- Protect yourself. Pain can make any pet bite or scratch. Covering the head and eyes with a towel can calm them.
- A cloth muzzle can help with dogs, but don't use one on flat-faced breeds or a dog with a chest injury, and never leave a muzzled dog alone.
- Keep the head, neck and spine as still as possible. Use a board, thick cardboard or a folded blanket as a stretcher.
- Put cats and small pets in a box or carrier with air holes.
- If something is stuck in the body, don't pull it out. Keep it from moving.
- Move slowly and avoid sudden jerks.

On the way, have one person drive while another watches the pet.

Q: How often should I feed my adult dog or cat, and how much?
A: Adult dogs: most do well on 1 or 2 meals a day. The ASPCA suggests two meals, about 8 to 12 hours apart.

Adult cats (from about 1 year old): once or twice a day suits most cats. Leaving food out all day works for some cats, but makes others overeat and gain weight. Replace any food left out with fresh food daily.

How much:
- The amount on the label is based on an average pet. A less active pet may need less.
- Check your pet's body. You should be able to feel the ribs without pressing hard, and see a waist behind the ribs from above.
- If you can't feel the ribs without pressing, there is too much fat. Ask your vet how much to cut back.

Always keep fresh, clean water out.

Q: How do I trim my dog's or cat's nails safely?
A: Go slowly and keep it positive with treats and praise.

Dogs:
- Trim when the nails touch the ground or click on the floor. For many dogs this is about monthly.
- Cut small bits at a time. On light nails, stop a little short of the pink quick. On dark nails, trim just the very tip.
- Don't forget the dewclaws.

Cats:
- Gently press the toe pad so the claw comes out.
- Snip only the sharp white tip. Avoid the pink part, which has nerves and blood vessels.
- Trim every 2 to 3 weeks. At first, do just one or two claws per session.

If a nail bleeds, press styptic powder or cornstarch on the tip and make sure it stops. If your pet fights or gets upset, stop. Your vet can help.

Q: My cat is sneezing and has runny eyes. Is it cat flu?
A: It may be an upper respiratory infection, often called cat flu. Viruses like feline herpesvirus and calicivirus are common causes, and they spread easily between cats. Signs include sneezing, runny eyes or nose, mouth sores, tiredness and poor appetite.

What helps:
- Gently wipe her nose clean. A blocked nose can stop her smelling food, so she may eat less.
- Make sure she keeps eating and drinking.

See your vet within 24 hours if the sneezing doesn't stop. Go now if she:
- Has trouble breathing, or her gums look bluish
- Hasn't eaten properly for 24 hours
- Is a kitten. Young cats are more likely to get seriously ill.

Vaccines can make these infections milder.

Q: My dog ate a chocolate bar. What should I do?
A: Chocolate is poisonous to dogs, especially dark and baking chocolate. Call or go to a vet now, even if your dog seems fine, because signs can take hours to show.

While you get there:
- Note the type of chocolate, how much, and when it was eaten
- Bring the wrapper if you can
- Don't make your dog vomit unless the vet tells you to

Watch for vomiting, restlessness, fast breathing, shaking or seizures, and tell the vet straight away if you see them.

Q: My dog ate a handful of macadamia nuts from a cookie tin.
A: Macadamia nuts can make dogs sick, usually within 12 hours. Signs include weakness, vomiting, wobbling, tremors, fever and low energy. Most dogs get better within 1 to 3 days, but call your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now and take him in.

Cookies and nut mixes can also contain chocolate or raisins, which are more dangerous, so tell the vet everything that was in the tin.

Before you go:
- Bring the packaging and estimate how much he ate.
- Only make him vomit if a vet tells you to.

On the way, keep him calm and comfortable, and note any vomiting or shaking.

Q: How often should I bathe my dog or cat?
A: Dogs: The ASPCA suggests a bath at least once every three months. Dogs that spend a lot of time outdoors or have skin problems may need baths more often.

Cats: Most cats keep themselves clean. They only need a bath if they get very dirty or into something sticky or smelly.

Bath tips:
- Brush out loose hair and mats first.
- Use lukewarm water and a shampoo made for pets. Human shampoo can irritate or dry out the skin.
- Keep water out of the eyes, ears and nose. Wipe the face with a damp cloth.
- Rinse well and dry fully, including any skin folds.
- For cats, trim the claws first and use a rubber mat so they don't slip.

See your vet if you notice scabs, bald spots, redness or constant scratching.

Q: How common is cats' love for computer keyboards? One of my 'issues' is the need to move my cat's paws or head off of my keyboard. He just loves to sleep on my 'affairs!' I even had to take off …
A: Cats love warm places and they love to be the center of attention (as trond hansen already remarked). A laptop keyboard combines both characteristics and is twice as interesting for cats.

If you want to keep your cat off your keys, teach him that he's not supposed to sit on it by pushing him off. Offer him a more intetesting and comfortable alternative like a carton. Cats love cartons because they have insulating properties and feel warm to them. (This is also the reason why cats sit on books or papers.) Move the carton close to your screen but conveniently out of your way.

Q: Do dogs seek revenge on their owners? Let's say a pet owner leave his dog inside for a whole day because of a trip. The owner returns to find that the dog has peed on the furniture. Is the dog …
A: Dogs do not have a concept of "revenge". Their mental processes revolve primarily around the "pack" identity: one member of the pack is the alpha, and all have their places in a distinct pecking order. (For owners that aren't mindful of this psychology, the dog usually believes itself to be the alpha.)

Q: My dog walked through insecticide our neighbor sprayed and now he's drooling and shaking.
A: This could be insecticide poisoning, which can get serious fast. Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now.

Signs from many bug sprays, such as organophosphates and carbamates, include heavy drooling, tiny pupils, vomiting, diarrhea, peeing a lot, trembling, weakness, trouble breathing and seizures.

Before and on the way:
- If he's breathing well and it won't delay you, wear gloves and gently wash his paws and coat with mild dish soap and lots of water. Don't scrub with a brush.
- If he's struggling to breathe, skip the bath and go straight away.
- Bring the product label, or ask the neighbor what was used.
- Only make him vomit if a vet tells you to, and don't rub oil on him.

Keep pets off sprayed areas until they are dry.

Q: My pet ate something poisonous. Should I make him throw up at home?
A: Only if a vet tells you to. Making a pet vomit can do more harm than good. It's dangerous with burning chemicals like drain cleaner or bleach, with batteries, if your pet is drowsy, trembling or having seizures, or if a few hours have passed. Home remedies like salt water can also poison pets.

Instead:
- Move your pet away from the poison.
- Call your vet or the nearest 24-hour veterinary clinic now and go in.
- Bring the package, label or a photo, and note what was eaten, how much and when.
- If it's on the skin or fur, wash with mild soap and water.

On the way, keep your pet calm and watch the breathing. Some poisons cause delayed signs, so go even if your pet seems fine.

Q: A stray dog bit my dog. Should I worry about rabies?
A: Rabies spreads mainly through bites and scratches. Once signs appear, it is almost always fatal, so act quickly.

For your dog:
- Wear gloves and wash the wound with soap and water
- Call your vet today, even if your dog is vaccinated. Your vet will check the wound and advise what to do next

For people: if you or a family member is bitten or scratched, wash the wound right away with soap and water and see a doctor urgently. Treatment after exposure works very well when started early.

Worldwide, dogs cause most human rabies deaths. Keeping your pets' rabies vaccines up to date protects them and your family.

Q: My dog was bitten by a stray that might have rabies. What happens now?
A: Take your dog to a vet right away and tell them about the bite. The implementing rules of RA 9482 say:

- A previously vaccinated dog that can be identified should be revaccinated immediately and confined for at least 90 days
- A dog bitten by a suspected rabid or unknown animal should be confined under a vet's supervision for 6 months
- An unvaccinated dog bitten by a confirmed rabid animal must be put to sleep right away

Wear gloves if you need to handle wounds, and avoid contact with your dog's saliva. Your city or municipal veterinary office can guide you.

Q: How do I brush my dog's or cat's teeth?
A: Use a toothpaste made for pets. Never use human toothpaste. It isn't meant to be swallowed and can upset the stomach, and some contain xylitol, which is toxic to dogs.

Steps:
- Start slowly. Rub a finger or soft cloth along the outside of a few teeth, near the gums.
- Let your pet lick a little pet toothpaste from your finger.
- Once they accept that, put toothpaste on the cloth, then move to a finger brush or small, soft toothbrush.
- Brush the outer surfaces at the gumline. Start with the big back teeth and the long fang teeth, where plaque builds up fastest. Aim for about 30 seconds per side.

Brush daily if you can, and at least three times a week. Keep sessions short and calm, and praise your pet.

Q: My cat is sneezing and has runny eyes. Is it cat flu?
A: It may be an upper respiratory infection, often called cat flu. Viruses like feline herpesvirus and calicivirus are common causes, and they spread easily between cats. Signs include sneezing, runny eyes or nose, mouth sores, tiredness and poor appetite.

What helps:
- Gently wipe her nose clean. A blocked nose can stop her smelling food, so she may eat less.
- Make sure she keeps eating and drinking.

See your vet within 24 hours if the sneezing doesn't stop. Go now if she:
- Has trouble breathing, or her gums look bluish
- Hasn't eaten properly for 24 hours
- Is a kitten. Young cats are more likely to get seriously ill.

Vaccines can make these infections milder.

Q: My dog or cat has diarrhea. When do I need a vet?
A: Mild diarrhea in an adult pet that is still bright and eating can sometimes be watched at home for a short time.

Home care:
- Always keep fresh water out. Diarrhea can quickly cause dehydration.
- Ask your vet about a short rest for the stomach, or small meals of a bland or gut-friendly diet.
- When the stool firms up, switch back to the usual food slowly over about a week.

See your vet if it lasts more than 24 hours.

Go now if there is:
- Blood in the stool, or black, tarry stool
- Vomiting, weakness, fever, belly pain or no appetite
- Diarrhea in a puppy. It can be an early sign of parvo, which can be deadly.
- Straining with nothing coming out

Q: Is it legal to sell or eat dog meat in the Philippines?
A: No. RA 9482 bans the trade of dog meat. LGUs must enforce this ban (Section 7).

Under Section 11, anyone caught trading dog meat faces a fine of at least P5,000 per dog and 1 to 4 years in prison. The same penalty applies to using electrocution to put dogs to sleep. Foreigners who break these rules are deported after serving their sentence.

Killing dogs for food is also not among the allowed reasons for killing animals under the Animal Welfare Act (RA 8485, Section 6).

Q: My cat isn't eating. How long is too long?
A: Don't wait it out. A cat that stops eating can develop a serious liver problem called hepatic lipidosis (fatty liver). It can be fatal if not treated quickly. Overweight cats are at higher risk.

What to do:
- If your cat hasn't eaten properly for 24 hours, take her to the vet now.
- Go right away if her gums, ears, skin or the whites of her eyes look yellow, or if she is very weak.
- Tell the vet when she last ate and if anything changed at home.

Most cats with fatty liver have another illness that caused the poor appetite, so the vet will look for that too. Fatty liver needs prompt treatment, so don't wait to see if she starts eating again.

Q: Is it legal to sell or eat dog meat in the Philippines?
A: No. RA 9482 bans the trade of dog meat. LGUs must enforce this ban (Section 7).

Under Section 11, anyone caught trading dog meat faces a fine of at least P5,000 per dog and 1 to 4 years in prison. The same penalty applies to using electrocution to put dogs to sleep. Foreigners who break these rules are deported after serving their sentence.

Killing dogs for food is also not among the allowed reasons for killing animals under the Animal Welfare Act (RA 8485, Section 6).

Q: My dog or cat has bad breath. What causes it?
A: A healthy pet's breath should not smell bad. The most common cause is dental disease. Plaque and tartar build up on the teeth and inflame the gums, and the bacteria make the smell.

Bad breath can also point to other illness:
- Sweet or fruity smell: possible diabetes
- Urine-like smell: possible kidney disease
- Foul smell with vomiting, poor appetite or yellow gums: possible liver problems

What to do:
- Have your vet check bad breath that doesn't go away. A proper cleaning is done under anesthesia.
- Go sooner if you also see red or swollen gums, more drinking and peeing, weight loss, or poor appetite.
- At home, brush the teeth with pet toothpaste, ideally daily.

Dogs can be very territorial animals.

Q: How do I potty train my puppy?
A: Patience, a routine and rewards work best.

- Take your puppy out at least every two hours, and right after waking up, eating and playing.
- Feed meals at the same times each day.
- Use the same outdoor spot each time, and say a cue word like "potty" while they go.
- Praise or give a treat right after they finish.
- Watch for sniffing, circling or scratching at the door, then go out right away.
- When you can't watch, use a crate or a small gated area.
- A puppy can often hold it about one hour per month of age. A 3-month-old may need a break about every 3 hours.

Never punish accidents. Calmly take the puppy to the outdoor spot, reward them if they finish there, and clean the mess well.

Q: How long should neutered cat use shredded newspaper litter box? I neutered my cat yesterday and changed his litter box so that it's full of shredded newspaper. For how long should he stay away from his regular sand litter box? …
A: Newspaper as a substitute for litter after neutering is a short-term approach. According to PetMD:

Sometimes litter can get stuck to the incision, so veterinarians will often recommend using torn newspaper in the litter box for 24 hours after surgery to avoid this.

Other sites recommend different periods; the Toby Project suggests five days, and SNAP recommends 7-10 days, but all cite the same reason of preventing litter dust from irritating or becoming embedded in the incisions.

Once the surgical incisions have closed up sufficiently that dust and particles of litter won't get stuck to them or cause irritation leading to pain or over-grooming, you should be safe to switch back to your regular litter.

Q: When should I spay or neuter my dog or cat?
A: The best age depends on your pet, so ask your vet. General guidance:

Cats: Many groups advise spaying or neutering before about 5 months old. Some vets do it around 6 months. Healthy kittens can be fixed as young as 8 weeks.

Dogs: The traditional age is about 6 to 9 months, and some groups advise before 5 months. Giant-breed males kept as house pets are often neutered after they stop growing, at about 12 to 15 months.

Benefits include:
- No heat cycles and no unplanned litters
- Lower risk of womb infections and breast tumors in females
- No testicular cancer in males, and less roaming and urine marking

messages.content: when should I neuter my cat

The best age depends on your pet, so ask your vet. General guidance:

Cats: Many groups advise spaying or neutering before about 5 months old. Some vets do it around 6 months. Healthy kittens can be fixed as young as 8 weeks.

Dogs: The traditional age is about 6 to 9 months, and some groups advise before 5 months. Giant-breed males kept as house pets are often neutered after they stop growing, at about 12 to 15 months.

Benefits include:
- No heat cycles and no unplanned litters
- Lower risk of womb infections and breast tumors in females
- No testicular cancer in males, and less roaming and urine marking

Pets can gain weight after surgery, so watch their food portions.

Q: At what age is my dog considered a senior?
A: There's no single age, because dogs age at different rates depending on breed and size. Vets often call a dog senior when it is in the last quarter of its expected lifespan. As a rough guide, many dogs reach this stage at around 7 to 8 years.

From that age:
- See the vet at least twice a year
- Ask about blood and urine tests every 6 to 12 months to catch problems early
- Have blood pressure and thyroid checked yearly

Watch for changes at home, like slowing down, drinking more, weight change or confusion, and tell your vet. Old age is not a disease. Many changes can be treated.

Q: How do I trim my dog's or cat's nails safely?
A: Go slowly and keep it positive with treats and praise.

Dogs:
- Trim when the nails touch the ground or click on the floor. For many dogs this is about monthly.
- Cut small bits at a time. On light nails, stop a little short of the pink quick. On dark nails, trim just the very tip.
- Don't forget the dewclaws.

Cats:
- Gently press the toe pad so the claw comes out.
- Snip only the sharp white tip. Avoid the pink part, which has nerves and blood vessels.
- Trim every 2 to 3 weeks. At first, do just one or two claws per session.

If a nail bleeds, press styptic powder or cornstarch on the tip and make sure it stops. If your pet fights or gets upset, stop. Your vet can help.

Q: Is it legal to sell or eat dog meat in the Philippines?
A: No. RA 9482 bans the trade of dog meat. LGUs must enforce this ban (Section 7).

Under Section 11, anyone caught trading dog meat faces a fine of at least P5,000 per dog and 1 to 4 years in prison. The same penalty applies to using electrocution to put dogs to sleep. Foreigners who break these rules are deported after serving their sentence.

Killing dogs for food is also not among the allowed reasons for killing animals under the Animal Welfare Act (RA 8485, Section 6).

Q: My cat keeps shaking her head and scratching her ears. Ear mites?
A: It could be. Ear mites are tiny parasites that live in the ear canal and are especially common in cats. Signs include:
- Head shaking
- Scratching at the ears
- Itching that can be mild or severe
- A drooping ear

Ear mites spread easily between pets, so every animal that has contact with your cat should be treated at the same time.

Other ear problems look similar, so let your vet confirm the cause and show you how to clean the ears. See a vet soon if the ear is swollen, has pus, or your cat seems to be in pain. Ask your vet for a product that suits your cat's weight and age.

Q: My dog keeps shaking his head and scratching his ears. What's wrong?
A: This is a common sign of an ear infection. Other signs are red ears, a bad smell, dark or yellowish discharge, and pain when you touch the ear. Allergies are often behind it, and dogs with floppy or hairy ears get them more often.

See your vet within 24 hours. The vet needs to look at the ear canal and eardrum and find the cause before choosing a treatment. Some ear medicines can cause hearing loss if the eardrum is torn, so don't use leftover or store-bought drops on your own.

Go now if he is in severe pain. Go today if the ear flap suddenly swells up. Left untreated, ear infections can damage the eardrum and cause lasting hearing loss.

Q: How do I brush my dog's or cat's teeth?
A: Use a toothpaste made for pets. Never use human toothpaste. It isn't meant to be swallowed and can upset the stomach, and some contain xylitol, which is toxic to dogs.

Steps:
- Start slowly. Rub a finger or soft cloth along the outside of a few teeth, near the gums.
- Let your pet lick a little pet toothpaste from your finger.
- Once they accept that, put toothpaste on the cloth, then move to a finger brush or small, soft toothbrush.
- Brush the outer surfaces at the gumline. Start with the big back teeth and the long fang teeth, where plaque builds up fastest. Aim for about 30 seconds per side.

Brush daily if you can, and at least three times a week. Keep sessions short and calm, and praise your pet.

I am wondering what can be done for a husky who howls whenever the owner is leaving and then absent from his or her home.
A: - Look into separation anxiety. Depending on the specific temperament of the doggie and the amount of abuse it has suffered prior, it might take few months and doggie doesn't necessarily have to fully become OK with the separation.

Q: How do I brush my dog's or cat's teeth?
A: Use a toothpaste made for pets. Never use human toothpaste. It isn't meant to be swallowed and can upset the stomach, and some contain xylitol, which is toxic to dogs.

Steps:
- Start slowly. Rub a finger or soft cloth along the outside of a few teeth, near the gums.
- Let your pet lick a little pet toothpaste from your finger.
- Once they accept that, put toothpaste on the cloth, then move to a finger brush or small, soft toothbrush.
- Brush the outer surfaces at the gumline. Start with the big back teeth and the long fang teeth, where plaque builds up fastest. Aim for about 30 seconds per side.

Brush daily if you can, and at least three times a week. Keep sessions short and calm, and praise your pet.

Q: My old cat drinks a lot of water and pees a lot. Why?
A: Drinking and peeing more is a common early sign of kidney disease in older cats. Kidney disease affects up to 40% of cats over 10 and about 80% of cats over 15.

Other signs can follow:
- Weight loss
- Poor appetite
- Low energy and a messy coat

The same signs can also come from diabetes or an overactive thyroid, so blood and urine tests are needed to find the cause.

Book a vet visit soon, and don't limit her water. Go to a vet today if she stops eating, vomits repeatedly or seems very weak. Catching kidney disease early, often with a special diet, can help your cat feel better for longer.

Q: My dog or cat has bad breath. What causes it?
A: A healthy pet's breath should not smell bad. The most common cause is dental disease. Plaque and tartar build up on the teeth and inflame the gums, and the bacteria make the smell.

Bad breath can also point to other illness:
- Sweet or fruity smell: possible diabetes
- Urine-like smell: possible kidney disease
- Foul smell with vomiting, poor appetite or yellow gums: possible liver problems

What to do:
- Have your vet check bad breath that doesn't go away. A proper cleaning is done under anesthesia.
- Go sooner if you also see red or swollen gums, more drinking and peeing, weight loss, or poor appetite.
- At home, brush the teeth with pet toothpaste, ideally daily.

Q: A dog bit me (nakagat ako ng aso). What should I do?
A: Act right away, even if the dog looks healthy.

- Wash the wound with soap and running water for about 15 minutes
- Don't put garlic or other home remedies on it, and don't rely on "tandok" or "tambal" healers
- Go to the nearest Animal Bite Treatment Center (ABTC) or Animal Bite Center promptly for post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP)
- Finish the full vaccine schedule the health workers give you

Don't wait for symptoms. Once rabies symptoms appear, it is almost always fatal. If the dog has an owner, they should report the bite and have the dog observed for 14 days.

Q: A stray dog bit my dog. Should I worry about rabies?
A: Rabies spreads mainly through bites and scratches. Once signs appear, it is almost always fatal, so act quickly.

For your dog:
- Wear gloves and wash the wound with soap and water
- Call your vet today, even if your dog is vaccinated. Your vet will check the wound and advise what to do next

For people: if you or a family member is bitten or scratched, wash the wound right away with soap and water and see a doctor urgently. Treatment after exposure works very well when started early.

Worldwide, dogs cause most human rabies deaths. Keeping your pets' rabies vaccines up to date protects them and your family.

Q: My dog is vomiting. Can I treat him at home?
A: One vomit in a dog that otherwise seems well is often not serious, and many cases settle within a day. But vomiting can also be a sign of poisoning, a blockage or other illness.

Go to the vet right away if he vomits and also has:
- Blood in the vomit
- Diarrhea, belly pain or fever
- Low energy, no appetite or signs of dehydration
- A chance he swallowed something toxic or an object

See your vet today if vomiting goes on for more than 24 hours, even if he seems fine.

For a mild case, your vet may suggest resting the stomach for a short time, then small, frequent meals of a bland food. Keep fresh water available. Don't give human medicines unless your vet tells you to.

sources.text:
Q: My pet ate something poisonous. Should I make him throw up at home?
A: Only if a vet tells you to. Making a pet vomit can do more harm than good. It's dangerous with burning chemicals like drain cleaner or bleach, with batteries, if your pet is drowsy, trembling or having seizures, or if a few hours have passed. Home remedies like salt water can also poison pets.

Instead:
- Move your pet away from the poison.
- Call your vet or the nearest 24-hour veterinary clinic now and go in.
- Bring the package, label or a photo, and note what was eaten, how much and when.
- If it's on the skin or fur, wash with mild soap and water.

On the way, keep your pet calm and watch the breathing. Some poisons cause delayed signs, so go even if your pet seems fine.

Q: My dog isn't eating. When should I worry?
A: A dog that stops eating is often unwell, so take it seriously and involve your vet early.

What to check:
- Does he seem hungry but struggle to pick up, chew or swallow food? That points to pain in the mouth, teeth or jaw.
- Has anything changed lately, like a move, a new food or a new medicine?
- Are there other signs, like vomiting, diarrhea, pain or low energy?

When to go:
- Skipped meals but otherwise acting normal: see your vet today, within 24 hours.
- Go now if he hasn't eaten or drunk anything for 24 hours, or if he is also vomiting, very weak or in a lot of pain.
- If he has diabetes and refuses even one meal, call your vet right away.

Q: Should I discourage playful biting? While playing, my puppy likes to try and bite me occasionally. If she succeeds, it's not a full on bite, nor is it aggressive. But should I discourage this behavior? If I proceed to allow …
A: Consider how others will react. You know the dog is just grabbing, gently -- but if she does this to someone else, they may panic.

If you do permit this, you should clearly train her to distinguish when and where it is appropriate. That's going to take more dedicated effort than simply training not to do this to people.

Q: Can I use my dog's flea medicine on my cat?
A: No. Some flea and tick products that are safe for dogs are toxic to cats.

Stay safe:
- Only use a product labeled for cats, and check that it fits your cat's age and weight
- After treating your dog, keep your cat away from him until the product is dry
- Read the label every time
- Ask your vet before using any product on a kitten, a sick, old, pregnant or nursing pet

Go to a vet right away if your pet shows drooling, shaking or trembling, wobbly walking, seizures, vomiting or unusual tiredness after a flea product. Remove a flea collar at once if it causes a reaction. Bring the package with you.

Q: I accidentally put my dog's flea spot-on on my cat.
A: This can be life-threatening, so treat it as an emergency. Many dog flea and tick products contain permethrin, which cats can't break down well. Call your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now and take her in, even if she seems fine.

Signs include drooling, restlessness, twitching or trembling, wobbliness, vomiting and seizures.

Before you go:
- Bring the product box.
- Ask the vet on the phone whether to wash the spot first. They may tell you to use mild dish soap and plenty of water, then dry her well.
- Stop her from licking the area.

On the way, keep her calm in her carrier. Only use flea products labelled for cats, and keep cats away from newly treated dogs until the product dries.

Q: I just got a new puppy. What should I do first?
A: Book a vet visit soon. Your puppy will need a series of shots and deworming.

- Vaccines: puppies get shots every 2 to 3 weeks until they are about 4 months old. Your vet will set the exact schedule.
- Until the shots are done, keep your puppy away from dogs that may not be vaccinated.
- Deworming: worms are common in puppies. Your vet may deworm and check stool samples every 2 to 4 weeks until two tests in a row are clear.
- Feeding: puppies 6 to 12 weeks old usually eat 4 small meals a day of puppy food.
- Potty training: start early. Take the puppy out often and praise them when they go outside.
- Socializing: let them meet people and other animals gently, especially at 2 to 4 months old.

Q: Why does my dog lay down when he sees another dog? My dog (~7 year Lab mix) is mostly well-behaved on leash, though he still has a few triggers that we're working on (mostly harmless, but can seem intimidating to …
A: You're misinterpreting this. Our two Huskies show the very same behavior and it's not being aggressive or getting ready to pounce. Quite the opposite.

As Kosh mentioned, it's to show submission to some extent and signal "get over here, I want no harm".

The following "jump start" is more some kind of over-anticipation and the dog no longer wanting to wait.

Overall I wouldn't try to change this behavior as it's basically a positive one. As for the dashing portion: I usually try to hold the leash firm and tense so there's little to no room for the dog to jump forward.

Q: My pet ate something poisonous. Should I make him throw up at home?
A: Only if a vet tells you to. Making a pet vomit can do more harm than good. It's dangerous with burning chemicals like drain cleaner or bleach, with batteries, if your pet is drowsy, trembling or having seizures, or if a few hours have passed. Home remedies like salt water can also poison pets.

Instead:
- Move your pet away from the poison.
- Call your vet or the nearest 24-hour veterinary clinic now and go in.
- Bring the package, label or a photo, and note what was eaten, how much and when.
- If it's on the skin or fur, wash with mild soap and water.

On the way, keep your pet calm and watch the breathing. Some poisons cause delayed signs, so go even if your pet seems fine.

Q: My dog is vomiting. Can I treat him at home?
A: One vomit in a dog that otherwise seems well is often not serious, and many cases settle within a day. But vomiting can also be a sign of poisoning, a blockage or other illness.

Go to the vet right away if he vomits and also has:
- Blood in the vomit
- Diarrhea, belly pain or fever
- Low energy, no appetite or signs of dehydration
- A chance he swallowed something toxic or an object

See your vet today if vomiting goes on for more than 24 hours, even if he seems fine.

For a mild case, your vet may suggest resting the stomach for a short time, then small, frequent meals of a bland food. Keep fresh water available. Don't give human medicines unless your vet tells you to.

Q: What danger signs indicate health issues when aquiring a new dog?

I am considering buying or adopting a new dog, and was wondering what signs I should look for to indicate health issues?
A: "Health issues" is such a broad brush... So, a general answer would be to examine the dog and make sure everything seems correct and use some common sense.

Are they clean, well kept, groomed, skinny/fat, breathing normally?

You can also get them out on a leash and make sure they walk/run correctly (no limping or favoring). Maybe let them out in a fenced area... watch for any signs of abnormal behavior.

Check the eyes, are they clouded or abnormal?

Generally spend some time with the dog and use your common sense.

If you are looking for a more specific health issue, list that in the question.

Q: My dog eats grass. Is that normal?
A: Yes, it is very common, and most grass-eating dogs are not sick. Studies show fewer than 1 in 4 dogs vomit after eating grass. Dogs may eat grass for fiber, out of boredom or to get attention, or simply from instinct.

Things to watch:
- Grass sprayed with weed killers or pesticides can poison your dog. Keep him off treated lawns.
- Grass can carry worm eggs from other animals' poop. Ask your vet about regular deworming.
- If he seems bored or lonely, spend more time playing with him.

See your vet if he eats grass and then vomits often or seems to have stomach pain. That can point to a stomach or gut problem that needs checking.

Q: What are my legal responsibilities as a dog owner in the Philippines?
A: Section 5 of RA 9482 lists the duties of pet owners:

- Have your dog vaccinated against rabies regularly and keep a registration card with its vaccination records
- Register your dog with the LGU
- Don't let your dog roam public places without a leash
- Give your dog proper grooming, food and shelter
- Report any bite within 24 hours and have the dog observed by a vet
- Help the bite victim right away and pay for their medical costs

Breaking these rules can lead to fines under Section 11.

A: Please take her to the vet!

Q: Do I need to keep my dog's vaccination card?
A: Yes. Section 5 of RA 9482 requires owners to keep a registration card that records all of their dog's vaccinations. The implementing rules say the card should show the registration number, the dog's description, and vaccination details.

- If your dog bites someone and its rabies status is checked

Taking a photo of the card is a handy backup.

Q: How often should I deworm my puppy?
A: Puppies pick up worms easily, so they're dewormed more often than adults. A common schedule is:
- Every 2 weeks from about 2 weeks old until 12 weeks
- Then monthly until 6 months old
- Then every 3 months for adults

Your vet will choose the right product and dose for your puppy's weight, so ask them before giving anything. Keep the yard clean and treat fleas too, since fleas can spread tapeworm.

Q: How do I trim my dog's or cat's nails safely?
A: Go slowly and keep it positive with treats and praise.

Dogs:
- Trim when the nails touch the ground or click on the floor. For many dogs this is about monthly.
- Cut small bits at a time. On light nails, stop a little short of the pink quick. On dark nails, trim just the very tip.
- Don't forget the dewclaws.

Cats:
- Gently press the toe pad so the claw comes out.
- Snip only the sharp white tip. Avoid the pink part, which has nerves and blood vessels.
- Trim every 2 to 3 weeks. At first, do just one or two claws per session.

If a nail bleeds, press styptic powder or cornstarch on the tip and make sure it stops. If your pet fights or gets upset, stop. Your vet can help.

messages.content: how often should I cut my dog's nails

Go slowly and keep it positive with treats and praise.

Dogs:
- Trim when the nails touch the ground or click on the floor. For many dogs this is about monthly.
- Cut small bits at a time. On light nails, stop a little short of the pink quick. On dark nails, trim just the very tip.
- Don't forget the dewclaws.

Cats:
- Gently press the toe pad so the claw comes out.
- Snip only the sharp white tip. Avoid the pink part, which has nerves and blood vessels.
- Trim every 2 to 3 weeks. At first, do just one or two claws per session.

If a nail bleeds, press styptic powder or cornstarch on the tip and make sure it stops. If your pet fights or gets upset, stop. Your vet can help.

A: Just treat the pup normally. Jack's been through a lot in the last couple of months. Your friend left, you moved, he probably went into quarantine for a little while, and instead of going back home, he's in a new home and the friend is back. Q: How often does my dog need the anti-rabies shot by law?
A: Every year. Section 5 of RA 9482 says owners must have their dogs "regularly" vaccinated against rabies. The implementing rules make it clearer: a properly immunized dog is one vaccinated yearly, and LGUs register and vaccinate dogs annually.

The shot must be given by a licensed veterinarian, or by a trained vaccinator under a vet's direct supervision during government mass vaccination drives.

Keep the record of each shot on your dog's vaccination or registration card.

Q: My dog or cat has bad breath. What causes it?
A: A healthy pet's breath should not smell bad. The most common cause is dental disease. Plaque and tartar build up on the teeth and inflame the gums, and the bacteria make the smell.

Bad breath can also point to other illness:
- Sweet or fruity smell: possible diabetes
- Urine-like smell: possible kidney disease
- Foul smell with vomiting, poor appetite or yellow gums: possible liver problems

What to do:
- Have your vet check bad breath that doesn't go away. A proper cleaning is done under anesthesia.
- Go sooner if you also see red or swollen gums, more drinking and peeing, weight loss, or poor appetite.
- At home, brush the teeth with pet toothpaste, ideally daily.

Q: My cat is vomiting. Is it just hairballs?
A: Many cats bring up a hairball once every week or two, and that alone is usually not a worry. A hairball is a wet, tube-shaped wad of swallowed hair.

See your vet soon if she:
- Vomits more than once a week
- Seems tired or weak, or eats less
- Has blood in the vomit
- Drinks or pees more or less than usual, or also has diarrhea

Go now if she keeps retching or vomiting with nothing coming up, refuses food for more than a day, or is very weak. A hairball or a swallowed object like string can block the gut, and that can be fatal without surgery.

To help prevent hairballs, comb her coat daily, especially when she sheds. Don't give laxatives or hairball products unless your vet says so.

Q: My dog is vomiting. Can I treat him at home?
A: One vomit in a dog that otherwise seems well is often not serious, and many cases settle within a day. But vomiting can also be a sign of poisoning, a blockage or other illness.

Go to the vet right away if he vomits and also has:
- Blood in the vomit
- Diarrhea, belly pain or fever
- Low energy, no appetite or signs of dehydration
- A chance he swallowed something toxic or an object

See your vet today if vomiting goes on for more than 24 hours, even if he seems fine.

For a mild case, your vet may suggest resting the stomach for a short time, then small, frequent meals of a bland food. Keep fresh water available. Don't give human medicines unless your vet tells you to.

Q: A bee stung my dog and his face is swelling up.
A: Swelling of the face, head or neck after a sting can become serious because it can block breathing. Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now if the swelling is large or spreading, if he has any trouble breathing, or if he was stung inside the mouth or on the tongue.

While you get ready to go:

- Hold a cold pack wrapped in a cloth on the swollen spot.
- On the way, watch his breathing closely.

Q: When leaving my dog alone is it better to leave some lights on or all off? I always ask myself what is better. Leaving some lights on wouldn't prevent the dog to have a nice sleep? Leaving all lights off …
A: It depends on the individual animal, of course, but the wolf ancestors of domesticated dogs are nocturnal, and dogs have good low-light vision. Most dogs are not afraid of darkness.

For roughly the same evolutionary reasons, most dogs won't be kept awake by light; they've been domesticated to follow a roughly diurnal schedule but their wolf ancestors slept mostly during the day. And indeed many dogs seem to prefer to sleep in patches of sunlight (although it's likely the warmth rather than the light itself they're seeking...)

Which diseases can humans carry from cat to cat?

I regularly pet and feed stray cats. Some of them live together and some live apart, so sometimes I touch two different cats that normally wouldn't interact with each other.

Also, currently there is an epidemic of FIP in Turkey. There are so many fund raisers for cats suffering from FIP, most of which are short on money because the Turkish currency is too weak for FIP medication sold by USD.

So, when I pet two different cats without washing my hands, which diseases I might carry? Is FIP one of them? Are disinfectants enough to clean my hand between cats?

Thanks in advance!

FIP is caused by infection with feline coronavirus (FeCV). From the National Library of Medicine:

"The most likely route of infection of feline corona virus (FeCV) is oral; therefore, cats from catteries and multi-cat household environments, where cats are shedding the virus in feces and sharing litter boxes, are at higher risk of being infected with the virus."

FeLV is another candidate, it is often called a "friendly disease" since sniffing each others noses or mutual grooming are sufficient to start the initial infection in the upper respiratory tract. The virus is also resilient enough to survive for at least 15 minutes on human skin or clothing and as such can be transferred from cat to cat by hitchhiking on the human, without the human being a host.

- Hydrogen peroxide or alcohol in the wound. They damage tissue.
- Pulling out something stuck in the wound.

Q: My puppy bites and nips a lot. How do I stop it?
A: Mouthing is normal for puppies. The goal is to teach them to be gentle.

- When teeth press hard, give a high-pitched yelp and let your hand go limp. Praise your puppy when they stop.
- If that doesn't work, ignore them for 10 to 20 seconds or walk away, then play again calmly.
- Keep a chew toy or tug toy handy and offer it when they go for your hands or feet.
- Play fetch or tug instead of rough games with your hands.
- Don't jerk your hands away. It invites more grabbing.
- Never hit, slap or shake your puppy. It can make biting worse and cause fear.

Get help from a certified animal behaviorist or veterinary behaviorist if bites come with a stiff body, growling or pulled-back lips, or hurt much more than play bites.

"Pit bulls" should be as capable of being gentle/careful as any other dog. But a puppy is a baby; as surrogate parent, it's your job to teach him how to be a Good Dog.

Oh -- and give the pup some good chew-toys.

Is loneliness or other emotions a factor?

sources.text:
Toad poisoning. Cane toads, the large brown toads that come out after rain, release a poison when a dog or cat bites or licks them.
Signs: Sudden heavy drooling or foaming at the mouth; Pawing at the mouth, shaking the head; Bright red gums; Vomiting, wobbliness, a racing heartbeat, seizures
What to do now:
1. Rinse the mouth straight away. Point the head down and run a gentle stream of water across the gums and tongue from the side, so it flows out of the mouth. Keep going for 10 minutes.
2. Wipe the gums and tongue with a damp cloth to remove the sticky poison.
3. Go to the vet now, especially if there's anything more than drooling.
Don't: Spraying water down the throat. It can go into the lungs. Making them vomit.
Go to a vet now.

sources.text:
Q: How often should I feed my puppy?
A: Puppies do best with small meals more often while young, then fewer meals as they grow. A common schedule:
- 6 to 12 weeks old: 4 meals a day of puppy food
- 3 to 6 months: 3 meals a day
- 6 to 12 months: 2 meals a day
- Over 12 months: 1 or 2 meals a day of adult food

Use a food made for growing puppies or for all life stages. Adjust the amount based on how your puppy grows, and have your vet check weight and body condition at each visit. Large and giant breeds need careful portions to protect their bones and joints. Keep treats under 10% of daily calories.

Feeding at the same times each day also helps potty training, since puppies often need to go soon after eating.

sources.text:
Trouble breathing. Breathing problems can come from heart disease, asthma, injury or allergic reactions. They are always urgent.
Signs: Open-mouth breathing in a cat; Neck stretched out, elbows held out, belly heaving; More than 40 breaths a minute at rest; Blue, grey or pale gums; noisy breathing
What to do now:
1. Keep them calm and cool, and handle them as little as possible.
2. Loosen or remove a tight collar or harness.
3. Let them pick the position that's comfortable. Carry small pets in an open carrier.
4. Go to the vet now, with the car's air-con on.
Don't: Holding them tightly or covering their face. Offering food or water.
Go to a vet now.

Q: My cat is breathing with her mouth open and sitting hunched up. Is that normal?
A: No. In cats, open-mouth breathing is a sign of serious trouble and means she may not be getting enough oxygen. Fast or hard breathing, sitting or crouching in a stiff upright position, and bluish gums are also warning signs.

This is an emergency. Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour veterinary clinic now.

On the way:
- Keep her as calm and still as possible.
- Put her in a carrier or box with good air holes, and cover it lightly with a cloth to help her feel safe.
- Don't hold her tightly or press on her chest.

What to do now:
- Keep them calm and cool, and handle them as little as possible.
- Loosen or remove a tight collar or harness.
- Let them pick the position that's comfortable. Carry small pets in an open carrier.
- Go to the vet now, with the car's air-con on.

Don't:
- Holding them tightly or covering their face.
- Offering food or water.

Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now.

Q: Is it legal to sell or eat dog meat in the Philippines?
A: No. RA 9482 bans the trade of dog meat. LGUs must enforce this ban (Section 7).

Under Section 11, anyone caught trading dog meat faces a fine of at least P5,000 per dog and 1 to 4 years in prison. The same penalty applies to using electrocution to put dogs to sleep. Foreigners who break these rules are deported after serving their sentence.

Killing dogs for food is also not among the allowed reasons for killing animals under the Animal Welfare Act (RA 8485, Section 6).

Q: My dog is vomiting. Can I treat him at home?
A: One vomit in a dog that otherwise seems well is often not serious, and many cases settle within a day. But vomiting can also be a sign of poisoning, a blockage or other illness.

Go to the vet right away if he vomits and also has:
- Blood in the vomit
- Diarrhea, belly pain or fever
- Low energy, no appetite or signs of dehydration
- A chance he swallowed something toxic or an object

See your vet today if vomiting goes on for more than 24 hours, even if he seems fine.

For a mild case, your vet may suggest resting the stomach for a short time, then small, frequent meals of a bland food. Keep fresh water available. Don't give human medicines unless your vet tells you to.

Q: What are the signs of tick fever in dogs?
A: "Tick fever" usually means germs like Ehrlichia, Anaplasma or Babesia spread by ticks. In the Philippines, the warm climate suits the brown dog tick, which can live in homes and kennels. Ehrlichia canis was the most common tick-borne germ found in a study of dogs in Metro Manila and Laguna.

Signs may show 1 to 3 weeks after a bite:
- Fever, low energy, poor appetite
- Swollen glands, stiffness or limping
- Nosebleeds, bruises on the skin or gums, or blood in urine or poop

See a vet today if you notice bleeding, bruising, pale gums or weakness. A blood test is needed to confirm it.

Prevent it with year-round tick control your vet recommends and daily tick checks.

Q: Why is my cat peeing outside the litter box?
A: First, have your vet rule out a medical problem. Peeing outside the box can be a sign of a bladder problem.

Go to the vet now if your cat strains in the box with little or no pee coming out, cries while peeing, or is vomiting or very tired. A blocked bladder can kill, and male cats are most at risk.

If the vet finds nothing wrong, check the box:
- One box per cat, plus one extra
- Scoop daily, and change all the litter weekly
- Most cats like unscented, clumping, fine litter
- Put boxes in quiet spots, away from food bowls and busy areas

Stress, like a move or a new pet, can also cause it. Clean accidents with an enzyme cleaner for pet odors. Never punish your cat.

A: Yes. Feline guidelines call cats seniors once they are over 10 years old.

Older cats are good at hiding illness, so regular checks matter. Many vets suggest a visit every 6 months, with blood tests, a urine test and a blood pressure check at least once a year. Cats with health problems may need visits more often.

Common problems in older cats include kidney disease, an overactive thyroid, high blood pressure, diabetes, arthritis and dental disease.

Tell your vet if you notice weight loss, drinking or peeing more, changes in eating, litter box accidents, hiding, or crying at night.

Q: My dog or cat has bad breath. What causes it?
A: A healthy pet's breath should not smell bad. The most common cause is dental disease. Plaque and tartar build up on the teeth and inflame the gums, and the bacteria make the smell.

Bad breath can also point to other illness:
- Sweet or fruity smell: possible diabetes
- Urine-like smell: possible kidney disease
- Foul smell with vomiting, poor appetite or yellow gums: possible liver problems

What to do:
- Have your vet check bad breath that doesn't go away. A proper cleaning is done under anesthesia.
- Go sooner if you also see red or swollen gums, more drinking and peeing, weight loss, or poor appetite.
- At home, brush the teeth with pet toothpaste, ideally daily.

Q: My old pet has really bad breath. Is that dental disease?
A: Often, yes. Gum disease is very common in older pets, especially small dogs. Signs include:
- Bad breath that doesn't go away
- Red or swollen gums
- Trouble picking up, chewing or swallowing food

Bad breath can also point to other illness. A sweet smell may mean diabetes, and a urine-like smell may mean kidney disease.

See your vet for a mouth check. Proper cleaning below the gumline needs anesthesia. Vets check older pets carefully first, and treating mouth pain often makes them much happier.

At home, brush your pet's teeth with pet toothpaste, never human toothpaste. See a vet soon if your pet stops eating or has a lump in the mouth.

Q: How often should I feed my adult dog or cat, and how much?
A: Adult dogs: most do well on 1 or 2 meals a day. The ASPCA suggests two meals, about 8 to 12 hours apart.

Adult cats (from about 1 year old): once or twice a day suits most cats. Leaving food out all day works for some cats, but makes others overeat and gain weight. Replace any food left out with fresh food daily.

How much:
- The amount on the label is based on an average pet. A less active pet may need less.
- Check your pet's body. You should be able to feel the ribs without pressing hard, and see a waist behind the ribs from above.
- If you can't feel the ribs without pressing, there is too much fat. Ask your vet how much to cut back.

Always keep fresh, clean water out.

Q: Why do my cats twitch when they're sleeping? When both of my cats sleep they start to twitch, all over their bodies. their paws/toes, ears, whiskers, tail, even their sides will all twitch as they sleep. It's cute because it …
A: This sounds like Myoclonus these twitches are usually caused by sudden muscle contractions or from brief lapses of contraction.

They are not considered problematic unless it results in an inability to fall asleep. Or unless they are symptom of a related illness. For the most part, it is just a twitch as one is falling asleep, you have probably had them yourself.

It is not usually problematic in cats, but if you have concerns you should contact your vet.

Q: My cat always sleeps upside down

Whenever my cat goes to sleep,after a minute or so, it turns upside down (belly up)and there is some twitching in the paws legs tail and whiskers. Is it normal or some disease?
A: Entirely normal.

Some people prefer to sleep on their stomachs, others on their sides or backs; some change position depending on how warm or cold they are or for other reasons.

The same is true of cats. Upside down may look silly to us, but it really doesn't mean anything but that the cat is comfortable that way, and that it trusts you not to try to take advantage of this less-defended pose.

A bit of twitching of paws and face usually just indicates that the cat is dreaming.

Trouble breathing. Breathing problems can come from heart disease, asthma, injury or allergic reactions. They are always urgent.
Signs: Open-mouth breathing in a cat; Neck stretched out, elbows held out, belly heaving; More than 40 breaths a minute at rest; Blue, grey or pale gums; noisy breathing
What to do now:
1. Keep them calm and cool, and handle them as little as possible.
2. Loosen or remove a tight collar or harness.
3. Let them pick the position that's comfortable. Carry small pets in an open carrier.
4. Go to the vet now, with the car's air-con on.
Don't: Holding them tightly or covering their face. Offering food or water.
Go to a vet now.

How can I eliminate set-in dog urine scent from a carpet?

Our 15-year-old dog has decided she no longer wants to be house trained. As a result, we have several set-in dog urine spots in our carpet.

We have a consumer Hoover "steam" cleaner and have repeatedly gone over the affected areas on several occasions, but can't get rid of the odor. Is there any hope for getting rid of the smell? We don't want to replace the carpet yet, as it's likely she'll keep repeating the behavior.

Are there any ways to effectively remove the smell? How can I know if the smell is permanent and the carpet/padding need to be replaced?

I actually like Nature's Miracle as far as pet stain and smell removers go. You can get it in different strengths. If You're finding that it's a tough stain, you might want to try the version made for cat urine. Cat urine generally sticks around more than dog's, so the kinds made to get rid of cat urine are stronger because of that.

Something else you can try is vinegar. It's actually really good at getting rid of carpet smells. Basically the vinegar smell replaces the smell of ammonia from the urine, and then you can easily dissipate the vinegar smell with an open window and a few minutes. Just makes sure to use a shop-vac or something to get all the moisture out of the carpet so it doesn't mold underneath.

messages.content: No chest movement for 10 seconds in my cat. Is this serious?

This sounds like it could be cPR. Only for a pet who is unconscious, not breathing and has no heartbeat. Get someone to drive to the vet while you work.

What to do now:
- Lay them on their right side on a firm surface. Put flat-chested breeds like Bulldogs on their back.
- Cats and small dogs: wrap one hand around the chest just behind the elbows and squeeze. Larger dogs: stack both hands on the widest part of the chest. On their back: press on the breastbone.
- Push hard and fast: a third to a half of the chest's width, 100â€“120 times a minute (the beat of "Stayin' Alive"). Let the chest come all the way back up.
- After 30 compressions, close the mouth, straighten the neck and give 2 quick breaths into the nose, watching the chest rise.
- Keep going 30 compressions to 2 breaths. Check for breathing and a heartbeat every 2 minutes, and keep going on the way to the vet.

Don't:
- CPR on a pet who is breathing or has a heartbeat. It can hurt them.

Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now.

Q: I just got a new kitten. What should I do first?
A: Take your kitten to a vet as soon as you can. Ask where you got her about any vaccines, deworming and food she has had.

- Vet visits: kittens usually see the vet every 3 to 4 weeks until about 6 months old, for shots and parasite treatment.
- Vaccines: the core kitten shots start at about 6 to 8 weeks and are repeated every 3 to 4 weeks until 16 to 20 weeks old.
- Deworming: worms are very common in kittens, so many vets deworm them routinely.
- Testing: a kitten with an unknown history should be tested for FeLV and FIV. Keep her apart from your other cats until the vet has checked her.
- Feeding: use kitten food, given several times a day.
- Litter box: one per cat, plus one extra, kept clean.

Q: Can a pet legally be put to sleep in the Philippines?
A: Only for reasons the Animal Welfare Act allows. Section 6 of RA 8485 permits killing a pet when, for example:

- A licensed vet certifies it has an incurable communicable disease
- A licensed vet certifies it is needed to end the animal's suffering
- It is needed to prevent immediate danger to human life or limb

It must be done humanely, using methods approved by the Committee on Animal Welfare. Electrocution of dogs is banned under RA 9482. Talk to your vet if you're facing this decision.

Q: Dog DNA test from stool not swabs

Does anyone know of a dog dna test that can provide heritage details from stool samples instead of by mouth swab?
A: It sort of depends on what your intent is. You can expect dog feces to be highly contaminated with DNA not from the dog, and therefore I would guess that you probably couldn't get a truly accurate DNA profile of the dog that way. However, if you already have accurate DNA profiles of dogs from mouth swabs, you may be able to get enough DNA from the feces to guess which dog in your database produced the waste with a reasonable level of accuracy. There are businesses that provide that service, with the intent of helping communal living spaces such as apartment complexes catch residents who aren't cleaning up after their pets. Poo Prints is one such business.

Q: Why does my cat knock over her water dish? I just adopted a cute little 1 year old and one of the first things I noticed when I brought her home is that she liked to knock over her water …
A: Cats in the wild prefer running water. Still water can have leaves and scum on it, so cats learn to clear the surface with a paw. Those where this instinct is strong can make a big mess.

A good way is to replace a water dish with a recirculating fountain to create a permanent stream. This will also encourage your cat to drink, which can help fight kidney disease in later life.

Pet Travel Safety — Keeping pets safe in the car
- Bring plenty of water, food, a bowl, leash, waste bags, grooming supplies, medication and first-aid, and any travel documents including proof of rabies vaccination. Feed your pet 3 to 4 hours before leaving on your trip to prevent car sickness or vomiting. - Make frequent stops to allow dogs to go to the bathroom and stretch their legs. - Never leave your pet alone in a parked vehicle. On hot days, temperatures can rise quickly within minutes and can cause death. In cold weather, animals left in cars can freeze to death.

I see a fair number of people in my area leaving their dogs in the car while they eat at a restaurant.

This doesn't strike me as a particularly safe or healthy practice.

Is it hot enough to "fry an egg"?

Then it's also hot enough to fry a dog's brain.
- U.S. Public Service Announcement from 1987

The answer to this question is common sense; you don't leave a child unattended in a car because the interior of a car can heat up intensely within minutes. Dogs in particular cannot sweat, they can only pant; this heat can affect them even more severely than other animals.

Q: My dog got into a plate of dark chocolate brownies. How worried should I be?
A: Call your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now and take him in. Dark chocolate, baking chocolate and cocoa powder are the most dangerous types because they contain the most theobromine, a stimulant dogs clear very slowly. Rich brownies are also fatty, which can trigger pancreatitis.

Signs can start within a few hours: vomiting, diarrhea, restlessness, panting, drinking and peeing more, a racing heart, tremors and seizures.

Before you go:
- Note your dog's weight, the type of chocolate and how much he ate, and bring the wrapper or recipe.
- If the brownies were sugar-free, tell the vet, since xylitol is also dangerous.
- Only make him vomit if a vet tells you to.
- Don't wait for signs to appear.

On the way, keep him calm and watch for shaking.

Q: My dog ate a chocolate bar. What should I do?
A: Chocolate is poisonous to dogs, especially dark and baking chocolate. Call or go to a vet now, even if your dog seems fine, because signs can take hours to show.

While you get there:
- Note the type of chocolate, how much, and when it was eaten

- Don't make your dog vomit unless the vet tells you to

Is it healthy for my cat to eat rice? 1 In Australia, by snack, I do not mean a treat, … A: My vet advises feeding rice and chicken for stomach/intestine upsets, so rice and tuna should be fine. Q: How often should I bathe my dog or cat?
A: Dogs: The ASPCA suggests a bath at least once every three months. Dogs that spend a lot of time outdoors or have skin problems may need baths more often.

Cats: Most cats keep themselves clean. They only need a bath if they get very dirty or into something sticky or smelly.

Bath tips:
- Brush out loose hair and mats first.
- Use lukewarm water and a shampoo made for pets. Human shampoo can irritate or dry out the skin.
- Keep water out of the eyes, ears and nose. Wipe the face with a damp cloth.
- Rinse well and dry fully, including any skin folds.
- For cats, trim the claws first and use a rubber mat so they don't slip.

See your vet if you notice scabs, bald spots, redness or constant scratching.

If you need to use soap, be sure to use a soap that is approved to be used on dogs. There are special soaps available in most pet stores or online that don't affect the protective layers on the skin too much.
