Q: Should I put a collar on my indoor cat? I have a very strictly indoor cat, that has tried to dart outside a couple of times and sometimes succeeded, only making it to the edge of our patio before we …
A: Yes, you should put an orange collar on your strictly-indoor cat to mark him as an escaped convict. Check out The Kitty Convict Project

While having your kitty micro chipped is awesome, many lost kitties never get reported or brought in to the shelter to be scanned as outdoor cats are so common.
While this project is still catching on, the orange collar will help indicate that your kitty isn't supposed to be outside. You can even add small tags or embroidery on the collar so your neighbors can return her without having to go get his chip scanned.

If you do decide to get her a collar, please ensure it's a breakaway safety collar.

Q: My dog was panting really hard after our walk in the heat and now he collapsed. What do I do?
A: This sounds like heatstroke, which is an emergency. Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour veterinary clinic now.

Before you leave and on the way:
- Move him out of the sun into shade or an air-conditioned space.
- Wet his body with cool (not ice-cold) water or wet towels, especially the belly, and use a fan or the car aircon.
- Don't dunk him in a tub of cold water.
- Offer small sips of water only once he is alert and starting to cool.

Other heatstroke signs are hot skin, drooling, vomiting, and wobbly walking. Keep cooling him on the drive, and let the vet check him even if he seems to improve.

sources.label: FurFriends checked answer
sources.text:
Q: My dog suddenly collapsed and isn't responding to me.
A: This needs a vet immediately. Call your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic and leave right away.

Quick checks:
- Breathing: watch whether the chest rises and falls.
- Heartbeat: put your hand flat on the chest to feel for it.

If there's no breathing or heartbeat, ask the clinic on the phone to guide you through chest compressions. Keep going until your dog breathes on his own or the vet takes over.

On the way:
- Have someone else drive, especially if you're doing compressions.
- Lay him on a firm, flat surface and keep his head level and neck straight.
- Be careful when he wakes up, since a confused dog may bite.

sources.label: FurFriends first-aid guide: Hit by a vehicle or fall
sources.text:
Hit by a vehicle or fall. Internal bleeding and chest injuries may not show at first. Pets that fall from balconies or windows need a vet check too.
Signs: Limping, not putting weight on a leg; Fast breathing, pale gums; Swelling belly, bleeding from the nose or mouth; Seems fine but was hit or fell. Still go.
What to do now:
1. Make sure you're safe from traffic first.
2. Approach slowly and speak softly. Hurt animals bite, so use a towel or muzzle unless they're vomiting or struggling to breathe.
3. Move them as little as possible. Slide a large dog onto a board or blanket to use as a stretcher, keeping the back and neck straight. Put small pets in a box or carrier.
4. Press on any bleeding, keep them calm, and go to the vet now.
Don't: Giving any painkiller. Trying to straighten or splint a leg. Giving food or water.
Go to a vet now.

Trouble breathing. Breathing problems can come from heart disease, asthma, injury or allergic reactions. They are always urgent.
Signs: Open-mouth breathing in a cat; Neck stretched out, elbows held out, belly heaving; More than 40 breaths a minute at rest; Blue, grey or pale gums; noisy breathing
What to do now:
1. Keep them calm and cool, and handle them as little as possible.
2. Loosen or remove a tight collar or harness.
3. Let them pick the position that's comfortable. Carry small pets in an open carrier.
4. Go to the vet now, with the car's air-con on.
Don't: Holding them tightly or covering their face. Offering food or water.
Go to a vet now.

Q: My old pet has really bad breath. Is that dental disease?
A: Often, yes. Gum disease is very common in older pets, especially small dogs. Signs include:
- Bad breath that doesn't go away
- Red or swollen gums
- Trouble picking up, chewing or swallowing food

Bad breath can also point to other illness. A sweet smell may mean diabetes, and a urine-like smell may mean kidney disease.

See your vet for a mouth check. Proper cleaning below the gumline needs anesthesia. Vets check older pets carefully first, and treating mouth pain often makes them much happier.

At home, brush your pet's teeth with pet toothpaste, never human toothpaste. See a vet soon if your pet stops eating or has a lump in the mouth.

Q: How do I get rid of fleas in my house?
A: Most of the flea problem lives in your home, not on your pet. Eggs fall off into carpets, bedding and corners, and flea cocoons can wait there for months.

What helps:
- Treat every dog and cat in the home, not just the itchy one, using products your vet recommends
- Vacuum often
- Wash pet bedding and blankets regularly
- If you use a home spray, keep pets out of the room and follow the label
- Never put a house or yard product directly on a pet

Fleas can live indoors all year, so experts advise year-round flea prevention. It can take weeks to months of steady treatment to fully clear an infestation.

Q: My puppy bites and nips a lot. How do I stop it?
A: Mouthing is normal for puppies. The goal is to teach them to be gentle.

- When teeth press hard, give a high-pitched yelp and let your hand go limp. Praise your puppy when they stop.
- If that doesn't work, ignore them for 10 to 20 seconds or walk away, then play again calmly.
- Keep a chew toy or tug toy handy and offer it when they go for your hands or feet.
- Play fetch or tug instead of rough games with your hands.
- Don't jerk your hands away. It invites more grabbing.
- Never hit, slap or shake your puppy. It can make biting worse and cause fear.

Get help from a certified animal behaviorist or veterinary behaviorist if bites come with a stiff body, growling or pulled-back lips, or hurt much more than play bites.

Q: How do I potty train my puppy?
A: Patience, a routine and rewards work best.

- Take your puppy out at least every two hours, and right after waking up, eating and playing.
- Feed meals at the same times each day.
- Use the same outdoor spot each time, and say a cue word like "potty" while they go.
- Praise or give a treat right after they finish.
- Watch for sniffing, circling or scratching at the door, then go out right away.
- When you can't watch, use a crate or a small gated area.
- A puppy can often hold it about one hour per month of age. A 3-month-old may need a break about every 3 hours.

Never punish accidents. Calmly take the puppy to the outdoor spot, reward them if they finish there, and clean the mess well.

Q: Is it OK to feed dogs dairy products? A recent answer included feeding dairy products to a dog, in the answer is was Cream Cheese, but it does bring up the whole question of if dairy products are appropriate for …
A: It probably comes as a surprise to most people, but many adult dogs and cats are actually lactose intolerant as well. While they may enjoy the taste of dairy, it's not a normal part of either diet and can lead to:
- Flatulence
- Diarrhea
- Vomiting

It doesn't take much either, according to Blackwell, 1.5 grams per kilogram of lactose per day can cause these symptoms and, for reference, 1 cup of milk has about 11 grams of lactose in it. So, unless there's a specific need to feed them dairy (e.g. illness recovery on recommendation of a vet), I would probably avoid it.

Q: My Shih Tzu got into a fight and one eye looks like it's bulging out of the socket.
A: This is an emergency. Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now. The longer the eye stays exposed, the more it dries out and gets damaged, which lowers the chance of saving his sight. Flat-faced breeds like Shih Tzus and Pugs are more prone to this.

On the way:

- Keep it moist if you can, for example with a clean cloth dampened with saline. Ask the clinic how when you call.
- Stop him from pawing or rubbing at it.
- Keep him calm and still.

For other eye injuries, also see a vet right away. Flush chemicals out with lots of water first, and never pull out an object stuck in the eye.

Q: A dog bit me (nakagat ako ng aso). What should I do?
A: Act right away, even if the dog looks healthy.

- Wash the wound with soap and running water for about 15 minutes
- Don't put garlic or other home remedies on it, and don't rely on "tandok" or "tambal" healers
- Go to the nearest Animal Bite Treatment Center (ABTC) or Animal Bite Center promptly for post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP)
- Finish the full vaccine schedule the health workers give you

Don't wait for symptoms. Once rabies symptoms appear, it is almost always fatal. If the dog has an owner, they should report the bite and have the dog observed for 14 days.

Q: What container holds a 26-pound bag of kibble? I would like to transfer the contents of a 26-pound bag of dry dog food from the bag to a more convenient container. Any suggestions for a container to hold that amount, …
A: 7-Gallon Bucket

That 26-pound bag happens to just fit a 7-gallon bucket available from brewers supply companies with just a bit of room to spare.

Add a screw-type lid from a home building supply company and you have a nice complete kibble storage system.

Calculation

My clever friend determined this would work by weighing a cup of the kibble, and dividing that weight into the 26 pounds to determine how many cups of kibble are in a bag. The she divided the 7 gallon volume to get the number of cups would fit in the bucket. Voilà.

You could apply this strategy to your own kibble and your own container under consideration.

Q: My dog licked toilet bowl cleaner and my cat stepped in spilled bleach. What do I do?
A: Strong cleaners can burn the mouth, throat, skin and eyes. Burns from drain cleaners may not hurt at first and can show up hours later. Cats often lick chemicals off their paws. Call your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now and go in.

Before and on the way:
- Don't make your pet vomit. It can cause more burns.
- Ask the vet before giving anything to drink. They may tell you to offer water or milk.
- Rinse skin and paws with lots of water, then wash with mild shampoo.
- If it got in the eyes, flush with water or saline for a long time, ideally while someone else drives.
- Move your pet to fresh air if there are fumes.
- Bring the bottle.

Never mix bleach with ammonia cleaners, as this makes a toxic gas.

A: Burns are often worse than they look, because fur hides the damage. Large or deep burns, burns on the face, and any chemical or electrical burn need a vet right away. To be safe, go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now.

Before and on the way:
- Gently flush the area with cool water.
- Cover it loosely with a clean, non-stick dressing.
- Don't put creams or home remedies on it unless the vet says so.
- Wrap her in a towel and put her in a carrier to keep her calm.

If a chemical caused the burn, rinse with lots of water and bring the product label to the vet.

Q: What is the best way to toilet train a puppy? My friend's dog uses the restroom on his carpet a lot, and he's already tried lots of methods to get it to stop. Does anyone know an effective way to …
A: I've had a lot of success with crate training.

Dogs won't relieve themselves where they sleep or eat. Keeping them in an enclosed area and bringing them outside when they have to go to relieve themselves teaches them where it's OK to do so.

I recommend buying an expandable crate. You want to give them just enough room to stand up and turn around, but not enough that they'll start going in the corner. As they grow you can increase the size of the crate accordingly.

The Humane Society has some great info on crate training.

Q: How do I potty train my puppy?
A: Patience, a routine and rewards work best.

- Take your puppy out at least every two hours, and right after waking up, eating and playing.
- Feed meals at the same times each day.
- Use the same outdoor spot each time, and say a cue word like "potty" while they go.
- Praise or give a treat right after they finish.
- Watch for sniffing, circling or scratching at the door, then go out right away.
- When you can't watch, use a crate or a small gated area.
- A puppy can often hold it about one hour per month of age. A 3-month-old may need a break about every 3 hours.

Never punish accidents. Calmly take the puppy to the outdoor spot, reward them if they finish there, and clean the mess well.

messages.content: What do I do? My cat shows no heartbeat on the left side of the chest, just behind the elbow and no chest movement for 10 seconds.

This sounds like it could be cPR. Only for a pet who is unconscious, not breathing and has no heartbeat. Get someone to drive to the vet while you work.

What to do now:
- Lay them on their right side on a firm surface. Put flat-chested breeds like Bulldogs on their back.
- Cats and small dogs: wrap one hand around the chest just behind the elbows and squeeze. Larger dogs: stack both hands on the widest part of the chest. On their back: press on the breastbone.
- Push hard and fast: a third to a half of the chest's width, 100â€“120 times a minute (the beat of "Stayin' Alive"). Let the chest come all the way back up.
- After 30 compressions, close the mouth, straighten the neck and give 2 quick breaths into the nose, watching the chest rise.
- Keep going 30 compressions to 2 breaths. Check for breathing and a heartbeat every 2 minutes, and keep going on the way to the vet.

Don't:
- CPR on a pet who is breathing or has a heartbeat. It can hurt them.

Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now.

Why does my cat 'gently' attack my legs when I'm walking?

When I'm walking down my hallway my cat follows me as always, but she always attacks my legs with her 2 front paws. It is very gentle, no scratching, hissing or biting.

I'm just curious, why is this happening?

The attack using the front paws to catch something this way can be seen among younger cats when they play very frequently (watch cat videos on YT). It is a technique needed for hunting. You can see this when big cats as lions hunt and nearly always when kittens play.

Your legs resemble the back of a fellow cat. This is an ideal test prey. Be happy that your cat is playing this gently. Not all cats are so considerate. This means your cat knows about your fur beeing rather thin and delicate and thus keeps her claws withdrawn. With fellow cats this is not necessary the case.

My cats used to play this way, too, when they were younger. They also liked it, when I turned the table on them and chased them.

Q: My cat is sneezing and has runny eyes. Is it cat flu?
A: It may be an upper respiratory infection, often called cat flu. Viruses like feline herpesvirus and calicivirus are common causes, and they spread easily between cats. Signs include sneezing, runny eyes or nose, mouth sores, tiredness and poor appetite.

What helps:
- Gently wipe her nose clean. A blocked nose can stop her smelling food, so she may eat less.
- Make sure she keeps eating and drinking.

See your vet within 24 hours if the sneezing doesn't stop. Go now if she:
- Has trouble breathing, or her gums look bluish
- Hasn't eaten properly for 24 hours
- Is a kitten. Young cats are more likely to get seriously ill.

Vaccines can make these infections milder.

Q: How do I trim my dog's or cat's nails safely?
A: Go slowly and keep it positive with treats and praise.

Dogs:
- Trim when the nails touch the ground or click on the floor. For many dogs this is about monthly.
- Cut small bits at a time. On light nails, stop a little short of the pink quick. On dark nails, trim just the very tip.
- Don't forget the dewclaws.

Cats:
- Gently press the toe pad so the claw comes out.
- Snip only the sharp white tip. Avoid the pink part, which has nerves and blood vessels.
- Trim every 2 to 3 weeks. At first, do just one or two claws per session.

If a nail bleeds, press styptic powder or cornstarch on the tip and make sure it stops. If your pet fights or gets upset, stop. Your vet can help.

Take your cat to the veterinarian regularly to keep it healthy and prevent infectious diseases. Talk to your veterinarian about preventive treatments for fleas, heartworms, ticks, and other parasites. Contact your veterinarian if you notice any signs of illness in your pet. Q: My dog or cat has diarrhea. When do I need a vet?
A: Mild diarrhea in an adult pet that is still bright and eating can sometimes be watched at home for a short time.

Home care:
- Always keep fresh water out. Diarrhea can quickly cause dehydration.
- Ask your vet about a short rest for the stomach, or small meals of a bland or gut-friendly diet.
- When the stool firms up, switch back to the usual food slowly over about a week.

See your vet if it lasts more than 24 hours.

Go now if there is:
- Blood in the stool, or black, tarry stool
- Vomiting, weakness, fever, belly pain or no appetite
- Diarrhea in a puppy. It can be an early sign of parvo, which can be deadly.
- Straining with nothing coming out

Q: Why do cats pat the area before they lay down? I've noticed that my cats pat the area where they intend to lay down for a pretty long time, 30 seconds to up to 3 minutes. Interestingly enough, this is …
A: This is an instinct every cat has. They only do this on soft surfaces and they do this to be sure the place can carry their weight. Out in nature, a very soft area is an unsafe area and it is not only cats that react to this. Humans do it too!
If you are out walking and suddenly step into a very soft ground you stop without thinking.

If your cat is on a hard surface it doesn't pat the area before laying down, it only walks in a circle or two and lays down.

Q: Can I give moong dal (fried lentils) to dogs?

Can I give moong dal to stray dogs? Moong dal ingredients are Moong Lentis, Edible Vegetable Oil and Edible Common Salt.
A: Probably not.

Lentils on their own, properly cooked are probably fine. The fact that it's deep fried is probably not a good thing. And from my recollection, deep fried moong dahl's on the salty side, and too much salt is bad for dogs.

While Indian street dogs are hardy — it doesn't feel like the best idea, even if you have a big pile of 'em lying around. Junk food is as bad for them as it is for us.

Q: How much water should my pet drink, and how do I spot dehydration?
A: Keep fresh, clean water out at all times, in places your pet can easily reach. Cats that eat wet food often drink less, because the food is mostly water. Cats on dry food need to drink more.

Signs of dehydration:
- Dry or sticky gums
- Skin that stays "tented" when you gently lift it at the back of the neck, instead of snapping back
- Sunken eyes, weakness, low energy or poor appetite

Vomiting and diarrhea can cause dehydration fast. Call your vet today if you think your pet is dehydrated. Go now if they haven't eaten or drunk anything for 24 hours, or are very weak.

Drinking much more than usual also needs a vet visit within a day. It can be a sign of kidney disease, diabetes or other illness.

Q: Why did our dog hum / moan when hugged or when burying itself under the bed clothes? We had a dachshund many years ago, now sadly deceased. When she was picked up and hugged or squeezed a little bit more, …
A: It is indeed a moan and is part of the natural range of vocalizations a dog uses.

It can mean pretty much exactly what a human moan means. Some examples:
- Content at stretching after waking up
- Content at having that annoying itch scratched
- Content at laying down in a comfortable position
- Annoyance at being woken up
- Annoyance at being hugged too tightly

As with most expressions of dogs, this moaning must always be interpreted in the context of the situation. It's seldom only positive or negative.

Some dogs are more vocal than others, moaning just to say something. Others are more reserved and seldom moan at all.

Q: My dog eats grass. Is that normal?
A: Yes, it is very common, and most grass-eating dogs are not sick. Studies show fewer than 1 in 4 dogs vomit after eating grass. Dogs may eat grass for fiber, out of boredom or to get attention, or simply from instinct.

Things to watch:
- Grass sprayed with weed killers or pesticides can poison your dog. Keep him off treated lawns.
- Grass can carry worm eggs from other animals' poop. Ask your vet about regular deworming.
- If he seems bored or lonely, spend more time playing with him.

See your vet if he eats grass and then vomits often or seems to have stomach pain. That can point to a stomach or gut problem that needs checking.

Q: I just got a new kitten. What should I do first?
A: Take your kitten to a vet as soon as you can. Ask where you got her about any vaccines, deworming and food she has had.

- Vet visits: kittens usually see the vet every 3 to 4 weeks until about 6 months old, for shots and parasite treatment.
- Vaccines: the core kitten shots start at about 6 to 8 weeks and are repeated every 3 to 4 weeks until 16 to 20 weeks old.
- Deworming: worms are very common in kittens, so many vets deworm them routinely.
- Testing: a kitten with an unknown history should be tested for FeLV and FIV. Keep her apart from your other cats until the vet has checked her.
- Feeding: use kitten food, given several times a day.
- Litter box: one per cat, plus one extra, kept clean.

Q: Is it legal to sell or eat dog meat in the Philippines?
A: No. RA 9482 bans the trade of dog meat. LGUs must enforce this ban (Section 7).

Under Section 11, anyone caught trading dog meat faces a fine of at least P5,000 per dog and 1 to 4 years in prison. The same penalty applies to using electrocution to put dogs to sleep. Foreigners who break these rules are deported after serving their sentence.

Killing dogs for food is also not among the allowed reasons for killing animals under the Animal Welfare Act (RA 8485, Section 6).

Q: Should I change my senior pet's food?
A: Maybe. Older dogs and cats have different needs:

Senior dogs:
- Usually need fewer calories, and gain weight easily
- May benefit from more fiber and good-quality protein to protect muscle

Senior cats:
- Often digest food less well, and may lose weight and muscle
- May need tasty, easy-to-digest, higher-protein food in smaller, more frequent meals

For both, aim for a healthy body shape, not too thin and not too heavy. Extra weight strains joints, while weight loss can be a sign of illness such as kidney disease.

Change foods slowly over several days. Ask your vet to check your pet's weight and muscle and suggest a diet that suits its health.

Q: How can I tell if my cat has arthritis?
A: Cats hide pain well, but arthritis is very common in older cats. Studies show more than 60% have it in at least one joint. Signs are often subtle:
- Not jumping up as high, or hesitating before jumping
- Avoiding stairs
- Trouble getting in and out of the litter box, or going outside it
- Grooming less, so the coat looks messy
- Sleeping more and being less active

Ways to help at home:
- Use a litter box with a low side
- Add steps or ramps to favorite spots
- Keep her at a healthy weight

Ask your vet for a check. Never give your cat human pain medicine unless your vet says so.

Q: How do I know if my old dog has arthritis?
A: Arthritis (joint wear and pain) is common in older dogs. Look for:
- Stiffness, especially after resting
- Limping or a changed way of walking
- Trouble with stairs, jumping into the car or onto the sofa, or getting up
- Less interest in walks or play
- Thinner leg muscles
- Grumpiness or snapping when touched

What helps:
- Keep your dog at a healthy weight
- Gentle, regular exercise like leash walks
- Non-slip rugs and ramps at home

See your vet for a proper diagnosis and pain plan. Don't give any pain medicine, including human medicine, without your vet's advice.

Q: Why is my cat peeing outside the litter box?
A: First, have your vet rule out a medical problem. Peeing outside the box can be a sign of a bladder problem.

Go to the vet now if your cat strains in the box with little or no pee coming out, cries while peeing, or is vomiting or very tired. A blocked bladder can kill, and male cats are most at risk.

If the vet finds nothing wrong, check the box:
- One box per cat, plus one extra
- Scoop daily, and change all the litter weekly
- Most cats like unscented, clumping, fine litter
- Put boxes in quiet spots, away from food bowls and busy areas

Stress, like a move or a new pet, can also cause it. Clean accidents with an enzyme cleaner for pet odors. Never punish your cat.

Q: My dog or cat has diarrhea. When do I need a vet?
A: Mild diarrhea in an adult pet that is still bright and eating can sometimes be watched at home for a short time.

Home care:
- Always keep fresh water out. Diarrhea can quickly cause dehydration.
- Ask your vet about a short rest for the stomach, or small meals of a bland or gut-friendly diet.
- When the stool firms up, switch back to the usual food slowly over about a week.

See your vet if it lasts more than 24 hours.

Go now if there is:
- Blood in the stool, or black, tarry stool
- Vomiting, weakness, fever, belly pain or no appetite
- Diarrhea in a puppy. It can be an early sign of parvo, which can be deadly.
- Straining with nothing coming out

sources.text:
Snake bite. Venom spreads faster when your pet moves. Keep them still and get to a vet. Signs can be delayed.
Signs: A sudden yelp, swelling, puncture marks; Bleeding that won't stop; Drooling, wide pupils, trembling; Weakness, wobbliness, trouble breathing, collapse
What to do now:
1. Keep yourself safe. Don't try to catch or kill the snake. Take a photo from a distance if it's easy.
2. Keep your pet calm and still, and carry them if you can.
3. Take off the collar if the bite is on the head or neck, because it may swell.
4. Go to the vet now. Call ahead so they can check for antivenom.
Don't: Cutting the wound, sucking out venom, tourniquets or ice. Waiting for signs to appear.
Go to a vet now.

Q: How often should adult dogs and cats be dewormed?
A: Parasite experts (CAPC) recommend year-round protection for adult pets. Many monthly preventives cover worms together with heartworm, fleas or ticks.

If your pet isn't on a year-round preventive:
- Deworm about four times a year
- Have a stool (fecal) test 2 to 4 times a year

Even on prevention, healthy adults should have their poop checked at least twice a year. Pets that hunt, roam, travel or mix with many animals may need it more often.

Ask your vet for a product that suits your pet's weight and age, and which worms are common where you live.

Q: A dog bit me (nakagat ako ng aso). What should I do?
A: Act right away, even if the dog looks healthy.

- Wash the wound with soap and running water for about 15 minutes
- Don't put garlic or other home remedies on it, and don't rely on "tandok" or "tambal" healers
- Go to the nearest Animal Bite Treatment Center (ABTC) or Animal Bite Center promptly for post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP)
- Finish the full vaccine schedule the health workers give you

Don't wait for symptoms. Once rabies symptoms appear, it is almost always fatal. If the dog has an owner, they should report the bite and have the dog observed for 14 days.

Q: How often should I bathe my dog or cat?
A: Dogs: The ASPCA suggests a bath at least once every three months. Dogs that spend a lot of time outdoors or have skin problems may need baths more often.

Cats: Most cats keep themselves clean. They only need a bath if they get very dirty or into something sticky or smelly.

Bath tips:
- Brush out loose hair and mats first.
- Use lukewarm water and a shampoo made for pets. Human shampoo can irritate or dry out the skin.
- Keep water out of the eyes, ears and nose. Wipe the face with a damp cloth.
- Rinse well and dry fully, including any skin folds.
- For cats, trim the claws first and use a rubber mat so they don't slip.

See your vet if you notice scabs, bald spots, redness or constant scratching.

sources.label: CDC Healthy Pets, Ways to Stay Healthy Around Animals
sources.text:
Ways to Stay Healthy Around Animals — Overview
There are many health benefits of owning a pet. They can increase opportunities to exercise, get outside, and socialize. Regular walking or playing with pets can decrease blood pressure, cholesterol levels, and triglyceride levels. Pets can help manage loneliness and depression by providing companionship. Studies have shown that the bond between people and their pets is linked to several health benefits, including: - Decreased blood pressure, cholesterol and triglyceride (fat) levels, feelings of loneliness, anxiety, and symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder. - Increased opportunities for exercise and outdoor activities, better cognitive function in older adults, and more opportunities to socialize. However, pets can sometimes carry harmful germs that can make us sick even when the pet appears healthy. The diseases people get from animals are called zoonotic diseases. Below are some tips to help you and your family stay healthy while enjoying pets.

messages.content: body condition score for dogs and cats

Vets use a 9-point body condition score (BCS) from WSAVA. You can do a quick check at home:
- Ribs: Run your hands along the sides. At a healthy weight you can feel the ribs under a thin layer of fat. If you can't feel them without pressing, there is too much fat.
- Waist: Look down from above. You should see a waist behind the ribs.
- Belly: From the side, a dog's belly should tuck up. A cat at a healthy weight has only a small fat pad on the belly.

Signs of overweight are ribs that are hard to feel, no waist, a rounded belly, and fat over the lower back (and in dogs, the base of the tail).

Ideal is 4 to 5 out of 9 for dogs and 5 out of 9 for cats. Ask your vet to score your pet and plan safe weight loss.

Q: I just got a new kitten. What should I do first?
A: Take your kitten to a vet as soon as you can. Ask where you got her about any vaccines, deworming and food she has had.

- Vet visits: kittens usually see the vet every 3 to 4 weeks until about 6 months old, for shots and parasite treatment.
- Vaccines: the core kitten shots start at about 6 to 8 weeks and are repeated every 3 to 4 weeks until 16 to 20 weeks old.

- Feeding: use kitten food, given several times a day.
- Litter box: one per cat, plus one extra, kept clean.

Q: Do spayed cats still spray?

If I get my indoor female cats spayed, will they no longer spray? Or will they just spray for territorial reasons only?
A: Any cat can spray if sufficiently motivated to. It is a natural response.

Spaying does, however, remove a very strong trigger for a female cat. Biology demands that she broadcast to tomcats that she is ready for breeding, so come and get it. After spaying, that motivation goes away entirely.

But spaying may also be a signal for other cats to stay away, a claiming of ownership. If this is the driving force, then spraying could persist until whatever causes this distress is handled in some way.

Q: My dog isn't eating. When should I worry?
A: A dog that stops eating is often unwell, so take it seriously and involve your vet early.

What to check:
- Does he seem hungry but struggle to pick up, chew or swallow food? That points to pain in the mouth, teeth or jaw.
- Has anything changed lately, like a move, a new food or a new medicine?
- Are there other signs, like vomiting, diarrhea, pain or low energy?

When to go:
- Skipped meals but otherwise acting normal: see your vet today, within 24 hours.
- Go now if he hasn't eaten or drunk anything for 24 hours, or if he is also vomiting, very weak or in a lot of pain.
- If he has diabetes and refuses even one meal, call your vet right away.

Does talking to your pet help build trust?

I talk to my dog a fair amount more than the other people I live with, and my dog seems to listen and trust me/do what I say more than for the others and their dogs.

So I was wondering, if talking to your pets builds some sort of relationship, whether it's trust, or the whole 'leader' thing, or something else entirely.

Does anyone else have any ideas from their experiences, or proof of one way or another?

Talking to your dog is a common practice in dog training to teach a dog to pay attention to you and your commands at any time. With the correct mix of normal talking and code words like his name and occasional commands, as well as showing him affection/giving treats when he pays attention and keeps focus on you. From what you're describing you naturally found the right way to communicate, since your dog seems to listen better than others.

However there's a fine line between training your dog to listen versus becoming a babbling background noice your dog tends to ignore. Besides training attention and focus, talking to your dog often helps to calm your dog down when facing stressful situations, since your voice became a well known, positively associated sound.

In terms of bonding, imitating the noises of your dog (works with cats too) is more recommended.

Q: How often should I bathe my dog or cat?
A: Dogs: The ASPCA suggests a bath at least once every three months. Dogs that spend a lot of time outdoors or have skin problems may need baths more often.

Cats: Most cats keep themselves clean. They only need a bath if they get very dirty or into something sticky or smelly.

Bath tips:
- Brush out loose hair and mats first.
- Use lukewarm water and a shampoo made for pets. Human shampoo can irritate or dry out the skin.
- Keep water out of the eyes, ears and nose. Wipe the face with a damp cloth.
- Rinse well and dry fully, including any skin folds.
- For cats, trim the claws first and use a rubber mat so they don't slip.

See your vet if you notice scabs, bald spots, redness or constant scratching.

messages.content:
Can you bottle feed a kitten?

I have an orphaned baby kitten and it is to young for solid food, how do I nurse them?

The related question Kitten Food in an Emergency talks about what foods to use, but how do I get them to drink it?

Yes, you can bottle-feed a kitten. There are kits designed for this purpose, available at many pet stores, but you don't necessarily need them if you have baby bottles at home. Basically, the key is to have the liquid be able to drip from the opening of the bottle slowly, without needing to squeeze it, so that the kitten can easily get the fluid without the need for significant suction. If you have a bottle that isn't doing that, you can widen the hole of the nipple using a heated needle.

As for milk, it's not cow's milk that you should be looking at. There are kitten milk replacements that you should get from the pet store or your vet. Warm this according to directions (about 100 °F / 37 °C) to avoid upset tummies.

Q: Is there free anti-rabies vaccine for dogs from the government?
A: Often, yes. Section 6 of RA 9482 tells the Department of Agriculture to lead free anti-rabies vaccination of dogs, with priority for high-risk, low-income areas. LGUs must fund vaccines and run registration and vaccination (Section 7).

Executive Order No. 84 (1999) also calls for mass dog vaccination with free vaccines every March, Rabies Awareness Month.

Schedules differ by place, so watch for announcements from your barangay or ask your city or municipal veterinary office about the next free vaccination drive.

Q: How often does my dog need the anti-rabies shot by law?
A: Every year. Section 5 of RA 9482 says owners must have their dogs "regularly" vaccinated against rabies. The implementing rules make it clearer: a properly immunized dog is one vaccinated yearly, and LGUs register and vaccinate dogs annually.

Q: How often should I deworm my puppy?
A: Puppies pick up worms easily, so they're dewormed more often than adults. A common schedule is:
- Every 2 weeks from about 2 weeks old until 12 weeks
- Then monthly until 6 months old
- Then every 3 months for adults

Your vet will choose the right product and dose for your puppy's weight, so ask them before giving anything. Keep the yard clean and treat fleas too, since fleas can spread tapeworm.

Q: How often should adult dogs and cats be dewormed?
A: Parasite experts (CAPC) recommend year-round protection for adult pets. Many monthly preventives cover worms together with heartworm, fleas or ticks.

If your pet isn't on a year-round preventive:
- Deworm about four times a year
- Have a stool (fecal) test 2 to 4 times a year

Even on prevention, healthy adults should have their poop checked at least twice a year. Pets that hunt, roam, travel or mix with many animals may need it more often.

Ask your vet for a product that suits your pet's weight and age, and which worms are common where you live.

Q: What's the penalty for animal cruelty in the Philippines?
A: Section 9 of the Animal Welfare Act, as amended by RA 10631, sets penalties after conviction:

- Animal dies: 1 year, 6 months and 1 day to 2 years in prison, and/or a fine up to P100,000
- Animal survives but is severely injured and can't survive without human help: 1 year and 1 day to 1 year and 6 months, and/or up to P50,000
- Other cruelty or neglect: 6 months to 1 year, and/or up to P30,000

Penalties go up to 2 years and 1 day to 3 years and/or up to P250,000 if the offense involves a syndicate, a business, a public officer, or 3 or more animals.

Q: My dog or cat has diarrhea. When do I need a vet?
A: Mild diarrhea in an adult pet that is still bright and eating can sometimes be watched at home for a short time.

Home care:
- Always keep fresh water out. Diarrhea can quickly cause dehydration.
- Ask your vet about a short rest for the stomach, or small meals of a bland or gut-friendly diet.
- When the stool firms up, switch back to the usual food slowly over about a week.

See your vet if it lasts more than 24 hours.

Go now if there is:
- Blood in the stool, or black, tarry stool
- Vomiting, weakness, fever, belly pain or no appetite
- Diarrhea in a puppy. It can be an early sign of parvo, which can be deadly.
- Straining with nothing coming out

messages.content: My dog: vomiting or diarrhea. What should I do?

This sounds like it could be heatstroke. Overheating can damage organs within minutes. Flat-faced and thick-coated breeds are most at risk.

What to do now:
- Move them out of the sun right away, into shade or an air-conditioned room.
- Wet the coat with cool tap water, especially the belly, armpits, groin and paws, then fan them so the water evaporates.
- Offer small sips of cool water if they're alert. Don't force them to drink.
- Keep cooling for 10â€“15 minutes, then go to the vet with the car's air-con on, even if they seem better. Damage can show up hours later.
- If you have a rectal thermometer, stop active cooling at about 39.5 Â°C so they don't get too cold.

Don't:
- Ice or ice-cold water. It narrows blood vessels and slows cooling.
- Leaving a wet towel draped over them. It traps heat. Wet the coat and keep air moving instead.
- Waiting to see if they recover on their own.

Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now.

Q: Why is my cat peeing outside the litter box?
A: First, have your vet rule out a medical problem. Peeing outside the box can be a sign of a bladder problem.

Go to the vet now if your cat strains in the box with little or no pee coming out, cries while peeing, or is vomiting or very tired. A blocked bladder can kill, and male cats are most at risk.

If the vet finds nothing wrong, check the box:
- One box per cat, plus one extra
- Scoop daily, and change all the litter weekly
- Most cats like unscented, clumping, fine litter
- Put boxes in quiet spots, away from food bowls and busy areas

Stress, like a move or a new pet, can also cause it. Clean accidents with an enzyme cleaner for pet odors. Never punish your cat.

Q: Are rawhide bones or natural raw bones potentially dangerous for a dog? Chewing can be a very rewarding activity for dogs and it also provides mental stimulation and helps clean their teeth. So I'm planning to give a bone to …
A: The biggest danger I'm aware of (aside from possible chewing off a piece bigger than they can chew and choking) is that the rawhide can expand when it gets wet. So when a dog ingests rawhide, it expands either in their stomach, or in their intestines, blocking their normal bodily functions and causing them harm.

Another is a manufacturing issue. Rawhide is made from separated animal skins, a process that is usually done with chemicals that can be harmful to dogs. As long as you make sure to buy trusted brands, you shouldn't have to worry about it though.

Q: Are chicken bones dangerous for dogs?

I often heard that chicken bones are dangerous for dogs as they may break, splinter and damage the internal organs.

Is there any truth to this claim?
A: Cooked bones can be dangerous for dogs or cats. The cooking dries them out and makes them more likely to splinter.

I've been advised by vets to give dogs and cats raw bones, never cooked. The size of the dog would make a difference, too - a large dog is much more likely to gulp down a chicken bone whole and have it lodge somewhere it shouldn't, where a small dog wouldn't have that issue.

Q: My cat is breathing with her mouth open and sitting hunched up. Is that normal?
A: No. In cats, open-mouth breathing is a sign of serious trouble and means she may not be getting enough oxygen. Fast or hard breathing, sitting or crouching in a stiff upright position, and bluish gums are also warning signs.

This is an emergency. Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour veterinary clinic now.

On the way:
- Keep her as calm and still as possible.
- Put her in a carrier or box with good air holes, and cover it lightly with a cloth to help her feel safe.
- Don't hold her tightly or press on her chest.
- Call the clinic ahead so the team can get ready for her.

Q: Is some blood during cat delivery normal?

My cat is delivering and I see some blood, seemingly originating from the vaginal canal, not very much. Is this normal?
A: Some fluid isn't abnormal, there will be a small amount at the start as she discharges the vaginal plug prior to birthing the first kitten. During the process, she will chew off the umbilical cords of each kitten. Finally, as her uterus contracts there will be some additional fluid discharged.

Observation, post delivery, is important though. If you continue to see a bright, red, bloody discharge continue or she shows signs of disinterest or lethargy, unwillingness to eat, then it may be wise to contact a vet for advice. Don't stress though, cats have been doing this for thousands of years without our help. :)

sources.text:
Toad poisoning. Cane toads, the large brown toads that come out after rain, release a poison when a dog or cat bites or licks them.
Signs: Sudden heavy drooling or foaming at the mouth; Pawing at the mouth, shaking the head; Bright red gums; Vomiting, wobbliness, a racing heartbeat, seizures
What to do now:
1. Rinse the mouth straight away. Point the head down and run a gentle stream of water across the gums and tongue from the side, so it flows out of the mouth. Keep going for 10 minutes.
2. Wipe the gums and tongue with a damp cloth to remove the sticky poison.
3. Go to the vet now, especially if there's anything more than drooling.
Don't: Spraying water down the throat. It can go into the lungs. Making them vomit.
Go to a vet now.

Q: My old pet has really bad breath. Is that dental disease?
A: Often, yes. Gum disease is very common in older pets, especially small dogs. Signs include:
- Bad breath that doesn't go away
- Red or swollen gums
- Trouble picking up, chewing or swallowing food

Bad breath can also point to other illness. A sweet smell may mean diabetes, and a urine-like smell may mean kidney disease.

See your vet for a mouth check. Proper cleaning below the gumline needs anesthesia. Vets check older pets carefully first, and treating mouth pain often makes them much happier.

At home, brush your pet's teeth with pet toothpaste, never human toothpaste. See a vet soon if your pet stops eating or has a lump in the mouth.

Q: How often should I feed my puppy?
A: Puppies do best with small meals more often while young, then fewer meals as they grow. A common schedule:
- 6 to 12 weeks old: 4 meals a day of puppy food
- 3 to 6 months: 3 meals a day
- 6 to 12 months: 2 meals a day
- Over 12 months: 1 or 2 meals a day of adult food

Use a food made for growing puppies or for all life stages. Adjust the amount based on how your puppy grows, and have your vet check weight and body condition at each visit. Large and giant breeds need careful portions to protect their bones and joints. Keep treats under 10% of daily calories.

Feeding at the same times each day also helps potty training, since puppies often need to go soon after eating.

Q: My German Shepherd ate a big meal and then ran around. Now he's restless and drooling. Can bloat wait until morning?
A: No. Bloat (GDV), where the stomach fills with gas and can twist, is a life-threatening emergency. Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour veterinary clinic now. Quick treatment greatly improves the chance of survival.

Signs to watch for:
- Restlessness and seeming uncomfortable
- Retching again and again with nothing coming up
- Lots of drooling
- A swollen, painful belly
- Fast breathing, pale gums, weakness

Large, deep-chested breeds like German Shepherds, Great Danes and Dobermans are at higher risk, especially when a big meal is followed by exercise.

On the way, keep him calm, don't give food or a lot of water, and call the clinic ahead so they can prepare.

sources.text:
Bloat (twisted stomach). The stomach fills with gas and can twist. It can kill within hours and usually needs surgery. Most common in large, deep-chested dogs.
Signs: Swollen, tight belly; Retching or trying to vomit with nothing coming up; Restless, pacing, can't get comfortable; Drooling, pale gums, collapse
What to do now:
1. Go to the vet immediately. Call ahead so they can prepare.
2. Keep your dog as calm and still as you can on the way.
Don't: Waiting to see if it passes. Giving food, water or home remedies. Trying to make them vomit.
Go to a vet now.

Q: My dog eats grass. Is that normal?
A: Yes, it is very common, and most grass-eating dogs are not sick. Studies show fewer than 1 in 4 dogs vomit after eating grass. Dogs may eat grass for fiber, out of boredom or to get attention, or simply from instinct.

Things to watch:
- Grass sprayed with weed killers or pesticides can poison your dog. Keep him off treated lawns.
- Grass can carry worm eggs from other animals' poop. Ask your vet about regular deworming.
- If he seems bored or lonely, spend more time playing with him.

See your vet if he eats grass and then vomits often or seems to have stomach pain. That can point to a stomach or gut problem that needs checking.

Q: Why do dogs eat grass? I have always been told that dogs eat grass because they have upset stomachs. My dogs, however, eat grass every single time they go outside. I constantly need to remind them that grass is not …
A: Well, first, you don't need to stop them from eating the grass unless you've been chemically treating it. Dogs are not pure carnivores, unlike cats, and so they do want and need some other dietary sources in their food, such as plants. As hunter/scavengers, canines will get a lot of other food sources from their prey, which are usually herbivores, but domesticated canines are likely looking for alternate sources beyond their regular food and your grass is an easy one for them to get to.

Q: My cat is vomiting. Is it just hairballs?
A: Many cats bring up a hairball once every week or two, and that alone is usually not a worry. A hairball is a wet, tube-shaped wad of swallowed hair.

See your vet soon if she:
- Vomits more than once a week
- Seems tired or weak, or eats less
- Has blood in the vomit
- Drinks or pees more or less than usual, or also has diarrhea

Go now if she keeps retching or vomiting with nothing coming up, refuses food for more than a day, or is very weak. A hairball or a swallowed object like string can block the gut, and that can be fatal without surgery.

To help prevent hairballs, comb her coat daily, especially when she sheds. Don't give laxatives or hairball products unless your vet says so.

Q: Why is my cat so interested in me making the bed? I've noticed over many years of cat ownership, a lot of my cats have a very excited interest in bedmaking. My current cat will come from any corner of …
A: View yourself from the cat's perspective. Cats aren't used to changing their environments. I've never seen a cat move bedding around, they just sleep wherever they feel comfortable. Q: Which vaccines are core for dogs?
A: Core vaccines are the ones every dog should get, wherever it lives. For dogs these protect against:
- Distemper
- Parvovirus
- Adenovirus (infectious hepatitis)

Rabies vaccine is also core anywhere the disease is present or the law requires it.

Global guidelines now say leptospirosis vaccine should be given to all dogs in places where the disease occurs, so in those areas it is treated as core too.

Other vaccines, like kennel cough (Bordetella and parainfluenza), are "non-core". Your vet suggests them based on your dog's lifestyle, such as boarding or contact with many dogs. Ask your vet which vaccines suit your dog.

sources.text:
Q: Does my dog really need the lepto vaccine?
A: Leptospirosis is a serious bacterial disease that can also infect people. Dogs and rats can carry it and pass it out in their urine. The germs can survive for weeks to months in water and soil, and the risk goes up after floods and heavy rain.

The 2024 WSAVA guidelines say all dogs should be vaccinated where leptospirosis occurs and suitable vaccines are available.

In general:
- The first course is two doses given 2 to 4 weeks apart
- After that, a booster is usually needed every year

Keep your dog out of floodwater and puddles when you can. Your vet will tell you if lepto vaccine is right for your dog and when to give it.

A: Patience, a routine and rewards work best.

- Feed meals at the same times each day.
- Use the same outdoor spot each time, and say a cue word like "potty" while they go.
- Praise or give a treat right after they finish.
- Watch for sniffing, circling or scratching at the door, then go out right away.
- When you can't watch, use a crate or a small gated area.
- A puppy can often hold it about one hour per month of age. A 3-month-old may need a break about every 3 hours.

Never punish accidents. Calmly take the puppy to the outdoor spot, reward them if they finish there, and clean the mess well.

Q: My dog got into the trash and ate mouldy food. Now he's trembling.
A: Mouldy food, garbage and compost can contain mould toxins that cause tremors and seizures. Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now.

Signs often start within 1 to 2 hours but can take several hours. They include vomiting, shaking, wobbliness, a fast heartbeat, overreacting to touch or noise, and seizures.

Before and on the way:
- Don't make him vomit, especially now that he's trembling, because he could inhale it or have a seizure.
- Keep him in a quiet, safe spot away from stairs and edges.
- Tell the vet what he got into, such as old bread, dairy or compost.

With hospital care, tremors usually settle in 1 to 3 days. Use bins with secure lids and keep compost fenced off.

Q: Is it legal to sell or eat dog meat in the Philippines?
A: No. RA 9482 bans the trade of dog meat. LGUs must enforce this ban (Section 7).

Under Section 11, anyone caught trading dog meat faces a fine of at least P5,000 per dog and 1 to 4 years in prison. The same penalty applies to using electrocution to put dogs to sleep. Foreigners who break these rules are deported after serving their sentence.

Killing dogs for food is also not among the allowed reasons for killing animals under the Animal Welfare Act (RA 8485, Section 6).

Q: When should I spay or neuter my dog or cat?
A: The best age depends on your pet, so ask your vet. General guidance:

Cats: Many groups advise spaying or neutering before about 5 months old. Some vets do it around 6 months. Healthy kittens can be fixed as young as 8 weeks.

Dogs: The traditional age is about 6 to 9 months, and some groups advise before 5 months. Giant-breed males kept as house pets are often neutered after they stop growing, at about 12 to 15 months.

Benefits include:
- No heat cycles and no unplanned litters
- Lower risk of womb infections and breast tumors in females
- No testicular cancer in males, and less roaming and urine marking

Pets can gain weight after surgery, so watch their food portions.

Q: My dog or cat has bad breath. What causes it?
A: A healthy pet's breath should not smell bad. The most common cause is dental disease. Plaque and tartar build up on the teeth and inflame the gums, and the bacteria make the smell.

Bad breath can also point to other illness:
- Sweet or fruity smell: possible diabetes
- Urine-like smell: possible kidney disease
- Foul smell with vomiting, poor appetite or yellow gums: possible liver problems

What to do:
- Have your vet check bad breath that doesn't go away. A proper cleaning is done under anesthesia.
- Go sooner if you also see red or swollen gums, more drinking and peeing, weight loss, or poor appetite.
- At home, brush the teeth with pet toothpaste, ideally daily.

Q: My dog keeps shaking his head and scratching his ears. What's wrong?
A: This is a common sign of an ear infection. Other signs are red ears, a bad smell, dark or yellowish discharge, and pain when you touch the ear. Allergies are often behind it, and dogs with floppy or hairy ears get them more often.

See your vet within 24 hours. The vet needs to look at the ear canal and eardrum and find the cause before choosing a treatment. Some ear medicines can cause hearing loss if the eardrum is torn, so don't use leftover or store-bought drops on your own.

Go now if he is in severe pain. Go today if the ear flap suddenly swells up. Left untreated, ear infections can damage the eardrum and cause lasting hearing loss.

Q: What are the signs of tick fever in dogs?
A: "Tick fever" usually means germs like Ehrlichia, Anaplasma or Babesia spread by ticks. In the Philippines, the warm climate suits the brown dog tick, which can live in homes and kennels. Ehrlichia canis was the most common tick-borne germ found in a study of dogs in Metro Manila and Laguna.

Signs may show 1 to 3 weeks after a bite:
- Fever, low energy, poor appetite
- Swollen glands, stiffness or limping
- Nosebleeds, bruises on the skin or gums, or blood in urine or poop

See a vet today if you notice bleeding, bruising, pale gums or weakness. A blood test is needed to confirm it.

Prevent it with year-round tick control your vet recommends and daily tick checks.

Pets in Evacuation Centers — Bites and scratches
Animal bites and scratches can cause not only pain, injury, and nerve damage, but also infections. Serious bite wounds require medical attention and sometimes surgery. If a bite leads to an infection, the person may need to be treated with antibiotics, a tetanus booster, or receive other medical care. Dogs, cats, and ferrets can become infected with rabies—a deadly disease that affects the nervous system—and spread it to people or other animals through bites. If you are bitten by a dog, cat, or ferret in an evacuation center, see a doctor immediately to determine if you need a rabies vaccination.

Q: My cat isn't eating. How long is too long?
A: Don't wait it out. A cat that stops eating can develop a serious liver problem called hepatic lipidosis (fatty liver). It can be fatal if not treated quickly. Overweight cats are at higher risk.

What to do:
- If your cat hasn't eaten properly for 24 hours, take her to the vet now.
- Go right away if her gums, ears, skin or the whites of her eyes look yellow, or if she is very weak.
- Tell the vet when she last ate and if anything changed at home.

Most cats with fatty liver have another illness that caused the poor appetite, so the vet will look for that too. Fatty liver needs prompt treatment, so don't wait to see if she starts eating again.

Q: Can cats get heartworm?
A: Yes. Cats get heartworm the same way dogs do, from mosquito bites, and indoor cats can be bitten too.

Signs can be mild or sudden:
- Coughing or asthma-like breathing attacks
- Vomiting, poor appetite, weight loss
- Trouble walking, fainting or seizures

Sometimes the first sign is sudden collapse. See a vet now if your cat has trouble breathing or collapses.

There is no approved medicine to cure heartworm in cats, and the dog treatment is not safe for them. That makes prevention the only real protection. Ask your vet for a heartworm preventive made for cats that suits your cat's weight and age.

Q: What is heartworm and how does my dog get it?
A: Heartworms are long worms that live in the heart and lung blood vessels. Dogs get them from mosquito bites, which pass on tiny larvae that grow into adult worms over about 6 months. Indoor pets are at risk too, because mosquitoes come inside.

Q: Where can I report animal abuse or neglect?
A: Under the Animal Welfare Act as amended by RA 10631 (Section 10):

- The Philippine National Police (PNP), the NBI and other law enforcement agencies have animal welfare enforcement officers
- The Secretary of Agriculture can deputize trained volunteers and members of NGOs and community groups as enforcement officers
- These officers can rescue maltreated animals and arrest violators

Q: What's the penalty for animal cruelty in the Philippines?
A: Section 9 of the Animal Welfare Act, as amended by RA 10631, sets penalties after conviction:

- Animal dies: 1 year, 6 months and 1 day to 2 years in prison, and/or a fine up to P100,000
- Animal survives but is severely injured and can't survive without human help: 1 year and 1 day to 1 year and 6 months, and/or up to P50,000
- Other cruelty or neglect: 6 months to 1 year, and/or up to P30,000

Penalties go up to 2 years and 1 day to 3 years and/or up to P250,000 if the offense involves a syndicate, a business, a public officer, or 3 or more animals.

Q: How do I trim my dog's or cat's nails safely?
A: Go slowly and keep it positive with treats and praise.

Dogs:
- Trim when the nails touch the ground or click on the floor. For many dogs this is about monthly.
- Cut small bits at a time. On light nails, stop a little short of the pink quick. On dark nails, trim just the very tip.
- Don't forget the dewclaws.

Cats:
- Gently press the toe pad so the claw comes out.
- Snip only the sharp white tip. Avoid the pink part, which has nerves and blood vessels.
- Trim every 2 to 3 weeks. At first, do just one or two claws per session.

If a nail bleeds, press styptic powder or cornstarch on the tip and make sure it stops. If your pet fights or gets upset, stop. Your vet can help.

Q: A stray dog bit my dog. Should I worry about rabies?
A: Rabies spreads mainly through bites and scratches. Once signs appear, it is almost always fatal, so act quickly.

- Call your vet today, even if your dog is vaccinated. Your vet will check the wound and advise what to do next

For people: if you or a family member is bitten or scratched, wash the wound right away with soap and water and see a doctor urgently. Treatment after exposure works very well when started early.

Worldwide, dogs cause most human rabies deaths. Keeping your pets' rabies vaccines up to date protects them and your family.

While trying to feed a stray puppy in my neighbourhood, I got a needle point pierce from his tooth on my thumb, with some blood also.

Immediately I rushed to the doctor and got myself anti-rabies vaccination.

Doctor asked me to watch out for the puppy for at least 1 week to see if he dies or not.

My concerning queries are:
- What is the connection of getting rabies from a dog and his death?
- Should I be worried if he dies within a week?
- Does bite from a 2 months old puppy can risk humans being infected from rabies?

Also, this puppy has been ill for past 2 days. (No obvious symptoms and he just seems to be ill because he is neither eating nor drinking anything.)

1) Rabies is rapidly, and very unpleasantly, fatal. If the dog has rabies it is unlikely to survive a week and probably, at that age, unlikely to survive more than a few days.

2) Only if the puppy was itself infected. You probably got bitten just because it was either scared or overenthusiastic.

Q: Why does my female cat stomach area hang so low? When she's walking around I can see her belly hanging low. She has never gotten pregnant before. Does she just need to lose weight? She is also spayed and is …
A: The loose, hanging skin on a cat's belly is simply a natural part of a cat's anatomy, sometimes called the apron, or as in the following article, the primordial pouch. This is more prominent on some cats than others, and can become more obvious in cats as they age or gain or lose weight. Getting spayed or neutered does not cause your cat to gain an apron, but it may make it more obvious due to related changes in weight.

Q: A bee stung my dog and his face is swelling up.
A: Swelling of the face, head or neck after a sting can become serious because it can block breathing. Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now if the swelling is large or spreading, if he has any trouble breathing, or if he was stung inside the mouth or on the tongue.

While you get ready to go:
- If you can see the stinger, scrape it out sideways with a flat card. Don't squeeze it with tweezers.
- Hold a cold pack wrapped in a cloth on the swollen spot.
- On the way, watch his breathing closely.

Don't give him any human allergy medicine unless your vet tells you to. Even if the swelling seems mild, call your vet for advice.

Q: I adopted an adult cat with no vaccine records. What should I do?
A: If you don't know a cat's vaccine history, vets treat the cat as unvaccinated. That usually means starting a fresh set of core vaccines, much like a kitten's first series.

For kittens, the series begins at 6 to 8 weeks and is repeated every 2 to 4 weeks until about 16 weeks. Your vet will decide how many doses your adult cat needs.

When you visit, ask about:
- Core vaccines (FVRCP and rabies)
- Testing for feline leukemia (FeLV) and FIV, especially if the cat lived outdoors
- Deworming and flea control

Book a vet visit within the first week after adoption.

Q: How to keep a teething puppy from biting me and other people? I have a 9 week old pit bull puppy. He is teething for the first time. I have given him chew toys but if someone goes to pet …
A: When he nips, shout "ow! no!" a bit louder and sooner than necessary, and if necessary stop playing and walk away. That's how dogs teach each other not to nip, after all -- they growl or bark and don't play with the annoying one until he learns not to be so rough.

"Pit bulls" should be as capable of being gentle/careful as any other dog. But a puppy is a baby; as surrogate parent, it's your job to teach him how to be a Good Dog.

Oh -- and give the pup some good chew-toys.

Q: I just got a new puppy. What should I do first?
A: Book a vet visit soon. Your puppy will need a series of shots and deworming.

- Vaccines: puppies get shots every 2 to 3 weeks until they are about 4 months old. Your vet will set the exact schedule.
- Until the shots are done, keep your puppy away from dogs that may not be vaccinated.
- Deworming: worms are common in puppies. Your vet may deworm and check stool samples every 2 to 4 weeks until two tests in a row are clear.
- Feeding: puppies 6 to 12 weeks old usually eat 4 small meals a day of puppy food.
- Potty training: start early. Take the puppy out often and praise them when they go outside.
- Socializing: let them meet people and other animals gently, especially at 2 to 4 months old.

sources.label: FurFriends first-aid guide: Hit by a vehicle or fall
sources.text:
Hit by a vehicle or fall. Internal bleeding and chest injuries may not show at first. Pets that fall from balconies or windows need a vet check too.
Signs: Limping, not putting weight on a leg; Fast breathing, pale gums; Swelling belly, bleeding from the nose or mouth; Seems fine but was hit or fell. Still go.
What to do now:
1. Make sure you're safe from traffic first.
2. Approach slowly and speak softly. Hurt animals bite, so use a towel or muzzle unless they're vomiting or struggling to breathe.
3. Move them as little as possible. Slide a large dog onto a board or blanket to use as a stretcher, keeping the back and neck straight. Put small pets in a box or carrier.
4. Press on any bleeding, keep them calm, and go to the vet now.
Don't: Giving any painkiller. Trying to straighten or splint a leg. Giving food or water.
Go to a vet now.

Q: My dog isn't eating. When should I worry?
A: A dog that stops eating is often unwell, so take it seriously and involve your vet early.

What to check:
- Does he seem hungry but struggle to pick up, chew or swallow food? That points to pain in the mouth, teeth or jaw.
- Has anything changed lately, like a move, a new food or a new medicine?
- Are there other signs, like vomiting, diarrhea, pain or low energy?

When to go:
- Skipped meals but otherwise acting normal: see your vet today, within 24 hours.
- Go now if he hasn't eaten or drunk anything for 24 hours, or if he is also vomiting, very weak or in a lot of pain.
- If he has diabetes and refuses even one meal, call your vet right away.

Q: Is it legal to sell or eat dog meat in the Philippines?
A: No. RA 9482 bans the trade of dog meat. LGUs must enforce this ban (Section 7).

Under Section 11, anyone caught trading dog meat faces a fine of at least P5,000 per dog and 1 to 4 years in prison. The same penalty applies to using electrocution to put dogs to sleep. Foreigners who break these rules are deported after serving their sentence.

Killing dogs for food is also not among the allowed reasons for killing animals under the Animal Welfare Act (RA 8485, Section 6).

How often do you feed your cats?

I finally bought one of these automatic cat feeders and I’m in the process of programming it.

How often during the day should I feed the cats? They’re both older cats.

It depends on the cats and the style of feeder.

Some feeders let you pick how much food to dispense at each feeding. In that case, I would do half of their daily food budget in the morning and half in the evening, to match when cats are most active (and thus most hungry).

Other feeders can only deliver a fixed amount of food. In that case, you must set it to deliver that amount enough times per day to equal their daily food budget. I would still put one serving in the morning and one in the evening, and spread any extras needed in between during the day.

For completeness: the ideal of two feedings per day is for adult cats. Kittens need smaller meals every 4-6 hours, or just free feed them since kittens rarely need portion control.

messages.content:
Post-Injury Tricks

My small, 15-pound dog recently had a coyote attack her when she escaped into the front yard. While the coyote was scared off before it did serious damage, a small bite was taken and treated by the vet.
However, before she was fully recovered, I gave her the play dead command, where she lay down then yelped in pain as her shoulder hit the ground.
She now runs away every time I give her the play dead command.
Though it has been several weeks since the attack, she won't evade me anymore, but still ignores me when I do the play dead command.

How can I re-train this command after her injury? (Command is finger gun and saying "bang!")

She knows what I want her to do, just refuses to obey. Other commands are fine.

Take it slow and start from square one to regain her trust and confidence. Get her to associate finger and "bang" with good feelings by playing with her affectionately (petting, calm approval voice, gentle and slow) and presenting that stimulus until it is no longer associated with the physical pain.

Q: My dog suddenly collapsed and isn't responding to me.
A: This needs a vet immediately. Call your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic and leave right away.

Quick checks:
- Breathing: watch whether the chest rises and falls.
- Heartbeat: put your hand flat on the chest to feel for it.

If there's no breathing or heartbeat, ask the clinic on the phone to guide you through chest compressions. Keep going until your dog breathes on his own or the vet takes over.

On the way:
- Have someone else drive, especially if you're doing compressions.
- Lay him on a firm, flat surface and keep his head level and neck straight.
- Be careful when he wakes up, since a confused dog may bite.

Q: Is a one-eyed cat a less effective hunter? Our neighbour's cat comes into our garden quite often. Unfortunately she suffered an injury to one eye leaving her blind in that eye. I have no problem with her coming into the …
A: Not having binocular vision will make judging distance more difficult. But just like humans, cats will try to find ways to work around that limitation, using size cues to estimate distances. Q: My dog ate a handful of macadamia nuts from a cookie tin.
A: Macadamia nuts can make dogs sick, usually within 12 hours. Signs include weakness, vomiting, wobbling, tremors, fever and low energy. Most dogs get better within 1 to 3 days, but call your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now and take him in.

Cookies and nut mixes can also contain chocolate or raisins, which are more dangerous, so tell the vet everything that was in the tin.

Before you go:
- Bring the packaging and estimate how much he ate.
- Only make him vomit if a vet tells you to.

On the way, keep him calm and comfortable, and note any vomiting or shaking.

Q: My dog ate a few slices of raisin bread but he seems totally fine.
A: Please don't wait for signs. Raisins and grapes can cause kidney failure in dogs, so treat any amount seriously. Call your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now and take him in.

Vomiting or diarrhea often starts within 6 to 12 hours. Later signs include low energy, not eating, belly pain, weakness and drinking a lot. Kidney failure can develop within 1 to 3 days, and it is often fatal.

Before you go:
- Bring the bread or packaging so the vet can estimate how many raisins he ate.
- Only make him vomit if a vet tells you to.

On the way, keep him calm and note any vomiting or diarrhea to tell the vet.

Q: My cat swallowed one of my paracetamol (Biogesic) tablets that fell on the floor.
A: This is an emergency. Paracetamol (acetaminophen) can kill cats, and cats are far more sensitive to it than dogs. Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now. Don't wait for signs.

Signs can start within a few hours:
- Brown or muddy-coloured gums
- Fast or deep breathing, weakness
- Swelling of the face or paws
- Vomiting, or yellow eyes and gums

Before you go:
- Bring the medicine pack and note when it happened and how many tablets may be missing.
- Only make her vomit if a vet tells you to, and don't give milk, food or any other medicine.

On the way, keep her calm in a carrier with good airflow. Keep all medicines where pets can't reach them.

sources.text: Q: My cat is losing hair. Is it normal shedding? A: Normal shedding thins the coat evenly, with no bald patches. Hair loss is different: bald or thin patches, or hair missing from both sides of the body. Hair loss is a sign of another problem, not a disease on its own. Common causes in cats are fleas and flea allergy (the most common cause of hair loss on both sides), other parasites, fungal or bacterial skin infections, allergies, and overgrooming from stress or pain. Q: My cat has round bald patches. Is it ringworm?
A: It might be. Despite its name, ringworm is not a worm. It is a fungal skin infection. Signs include:
- Round patches of hair loss
- Broken or stubbly hair
- Scaly, crusty or red skin
- Dandruff or extra grooming

Ringworm spreads to people and other pets, and children are at higher risk. Its spores can stay in a home for many months.

What to do:
- See your vet, since flea allergy and other problems can look similar
- Keep the cat in one easy-to-clean room during treatment
- Wash hands after handling her
- Clean and disinfect the home well

Treatment often takes six weeks or more.

Q: How to keep a teething puppy from biting me and other people? I have a 9 week old pit bull puppy. He is teething for the first time. I have given him chew toys but if someone goes to pet …
A: When he nips, shout "ow! no!" a bit louder and sooner than necessary, and if necessary stop playing and walk away. That's how dogs teach each other not to nip, after all -- they growl or bark and don't play with the annoying one until he learns not to be so rough.

"Pit bulls" should be as capable of being gentle/careful as any other dog. But a puppy is a baby; as surrogate parent, it's your job to teach him how to be a Good Dog.

Oh -- and give the pup some good chew-toys.

Q: My puppy bites and nips a lot. How do I stop it?
A: Mouthing is normal for puppies. The goal is to teach them to be gentle.

- When teeth press hard, give a high-pitched yelp and let your hand go limp. Praise your puppy when they stop.
- If that doesn't work, ignore them for 10 to 20 seconds or walk away, then play again calmly.
- Keep a chew toy or tug toy handy and offer it when they go for your hands or feet.
- Play fetch or tug instead of rough games with your hands.
- Don't jerk your hands away. It invites more grabbing.
- Never hit, slap or shake your puppy. It can make biting worse and cause fear.

Get help from a certified animal behaviorist or veterinary behaviorist if bites come with a stiff body, growling or pulled-back lips, or hurt much more than play bites.

Q: Is it illegal to abandon my pet?
A: Yes. RA 10631, which amended the Animal Welfare Act, added a rule against abandoning animals.

- Leaving your pet, for good or even for a while, without a good reason and without arranging for its care counts as maltreatment
- If abandonment leads to the animal suffering or dying, the owner faces the maximum penalty

If you can no longer care for your pet, look for a new home or ask a rescue group or shelter for help instead of leaving it on the street.

Q: How often should I feed my adult dog or cat, and how much?
A: Adult dogs: most do well on 1 or 2 meals a day. The ASPCA suggests two meals, about 8 to 12 hours apart.

Adult cats (from about 1 year old): once or twice a day suits most cats. Leaving food out all day works for some cats, but makes others overeat and gain weight. Replace any food left out with fresh food daily.

How much:
- The amount on the label is based on an average pet. A less active pet may need less.
- Check your pet's body. You should be able to feel the ribs without pressing hard, and see a waist behind the ribs from above.
- If you can't feel the ribs without pressing, there is too much fat. Ask your vet how much to cut back.

Always keep fresh, clean water out.

Q: Is it legal to sell or eat dog meat in the Philippines?
A: No. RA 9482 bans the trade of dog meat. LGUs must enforce this ban (Section 7).

Under Section 11, anyone caught trading dog meat faces a fine of at least P5,000 per dog and 1 to 4 years in prison. The same penalty applies to using electrocution to put dogs to sleep. Foreigners who break these rules are deported after serving their sentence.

Killing dogs for food is also not among the allowed reasons for killing animals under the Animal Welfare Act (RA 8485, Section 6).

Q: Am I causing two cats to fight? We recently started feeding two stray cats in my apartment complex and initially they all behaved. However for the past two days one cat is trying to pick a fight and chase the …
A: First of all, you are not the reason they fight. The cats are already competitors. By feeding them, they both have to be too close to each other and this causes stress for both cats. The amount of food is not an issue.

Both cats' lives have been dependent on their ability to keep other cats out of their territory to survive. This means you need to feed them in two places as far away from each other as possible, or at least out of sight of each other.

Q: How do I know if my old dog has arthritis?
A: Arthritis (joint wear and pain) is common in older dogs. Look for:
- Stiffness, especially after resting
- Limping or a changed way of walking
- Trouble with stairs, jumping into the car or onto the sofa, or getting up
- Less interest in walks or play
- Thinner leg muscles
- Grumpiness or snapping when touched

What helps:
- Keep your dog at a healthy weight
- Gentle, regular exercise like leash walks
- Non-slip rugs and ramps at home

See your vet for a proper diagnosis and pain plan. Don't give any pain medicine, including human medicine, without your vet's advice.

Q: How can I tell if my cat has arthritis?
A: Cats hide pain well, but arthritis is very common in older cats. Studies show more than 60% have it in at least one joint. Signs are often subtle:
- Not jumping up as high, or hesitating before jumping
- Avoiding stairs
- Trouble getting in and out of the litter box, or going outside it
- Grooming less, so the coat looks messy
- Sleeping more and being less active

Ways to help at home:
- Use a litter box with a low side
- Add steps or ramps to favorite spots
- Keep her at a healthy weight

Ask your vet for a check. Never give your cat human pain medicine unless your vet says so.

Q: My dog walked through insecticide our neighbor sprayed and now he's drooling and shaking.
A: This could be insecticide poisoning, which can get serious fast. Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now.

Signs from many bug sprays, such as organophosphates and carbamates, include heavy drooling, tiny pupils, vomiting, diarrhea, peeing a lot, trembling, weakness, trouble breathing and seizures.

Before and on the way:
- If he's breathing well and it won't delay you, wear gloves and gently wash his paws and coat with mild dish soap and lots of water. Don't scrub with a brush.
- If he's struggling to breathe, skip the bath and go straight away.
- Bring the product label, or ask the neighbor what was used.
- Only make him vomit if a vet tells you to, and don't rub oil on him.

Keep pets off sprayed areas until they are dry.

Snake bite. Venom spreads faster when your pet moves. Keep them still and get to a vet. Signs can be delayed.
Signs: A sudden yelp, swelling, puncture marks; Bleeding that won't stop; Drooling, wide pupils, trembling; Weakness, wobbliness, trouble breathing, collapse

4. Go to the vet now. Call ahead so they can check for antivenom.
Don't: Cutting the wound, sucking out venom, tourniquets or ice. Waiting for signs to appear.
Go to a vet now.

Q: Why should there be one more litter box than the total number of cats? I've seen it recommended in many places that you should own a litter box for each cat in your home plus an extra. What are the …
A: According to this article on Pet Health Network, there is not really some special reason behind having an extra litter box - it is just for precautionary reasons. A dirty litter box could cause:
- Inappropriate urinating or defecating in the house (outside the litter box)
- Medical problems such as feline urethral obstruction or feline lower urinary tract disease.
