Q: In a multiple cat home, how many litter boxes should you have? I have seen a few suggestions in answers to other questions about it. But when I look I can never find it. If I have multiple cats in …
A: Rule of thumb is n + 1 litter boxes for n cats where n is greater than 1, this ensures a plentiful supply of this particular resource - with cats behaving more as individuals than a co-operative unit (such as a pack) they are more likely to accept sharing territory with another cat if there is no competition for key resources (toilet area, food, water etc)

It's by no means a hard and fast rule - my two get on just fine with two boxes between them but particularly during the introduction phase ensuring no or minimal resource competition is highly recommended.

Q: How often does my dog need the anti-rabies shot by law?
A: Every year. Section 5 of RA 9482 says owners must have their dogs "regularly" vaccinated against rabies. The implementing rules make it clearer: a properly immunized dog is one vaccinated yearly, and LGUs register and vaccinate dogs annually.

How can I train my cat not to scratch furniture?

Your best option is to work with your cat's instincts, rather than against them. Cats have an instinct to scratch so you need to provide suitable objects for them to scratch on that are more attractive than your furniture. Buy (or make) several scratching posts, bait them with catnip, and place them around the house. Cats like to scratch when they wake up, so put scratching posts near favourite sleeping spots. Another good place is right next to any place your cat has a tendency to scratch (like the arm of a sofa).

Reward your kitten (with treats or praise) for using the scratching posts, and she will build good associations with sratching there. She will learn to prefer scratching on the surfaces you provide instead of your furniture.

Q: I just got a new puppy. What should I do first?
A: Book a vet visit soon. Your puppy will need a series of shots and deworming.

- Vaccines: puppies get shots every 2 to 3 weeks until they are about 4 months old. Your vet will set the exact schedule.
- Until the shots are done, keep your puppy away from dogs that may not be vaccinated.
- Deworming: worms are common in puppies. Your vet may deworm and check stool samples every 2 to 4 weeks until two tests in a row are clear.
- Feeding: puppies 6 to 12 weeks old usually eat 4 small meals a day of puppy food.
- Potty training: start early. Take the puppy out often and praise them when they go outside.
- Socializing: let them meet people and other animals gently, especially at 2 to 4 months old.

sources.label: FurFriends checked answer
sources.text:
Q: When does my puppy start his shots, and why so many?
A: Puppies usually get their first core vaccine at 6 to 8 weeks old. Shots are then repeated every 2 to 4 weeks until the puppy is at least 16 weeks old.

Why a series? Antibodies from the mother's milk protect a young puppy, but they also block vaccines from working. These antibodies fade at a different age in each puppy, so repeat shots make sure one of them "takes". The dose given at 16 weeks or later is the most important.

Global guidelines also advise another core dose at around 6 months old instead of waiting until 1 year, to catch puppies that did not respond earlier.

Your vet will set the exact schedule for your puppy.

A: Well, not your specific case, but since you asked about common causes...

A very common cause is postpartum low blood calcium, otherwise known as milk fever. messages.content: Thick drool, bright red or very pale gums in my cat. Is this serious?

This sounds like it could be heatstroke. Overheating can damage organs within minutes. Flat-faced and thick-coated breeds are most at risk.

What to do now:
- Move them out of the sun right away, into shade or an air-conditioned room.
- Wet the coat with cool tap water, especially the belly, armpits, groin and paws, then fan them so the water evaporates.
- Offer small sips of cool water if they're alert. Don't force them to drink.

Don't:

Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now.

Q: My dog eats grass. Is that normal?
A: Yes, it is very common, and most grass-eating dogs are not sick. Studies show fewer than 1 in 4 dogs vomit after eating grass. Dogs may eat grass for fiber, out of boredom or to get attention, or simply from instinct.

Things to watch:
- Grass sprayed with weed killers or pesticides can poison your dog. Keep him off treated lawns.
- Grass can carry worm eggs from other animals' poop. Ask your vet about regular deworming.
- If he seems bored or lonely, spend more time playing with him.

See your vet if he eats grass and then vomits often or seems to have stomach pain. That can point to a stomach or gut problem that needs checking.

Q: I just got a new puppy. What should I do first?
A: Book a vet visit soon. Your puppy will need a series of shots and deworming.

- Vaccines: puppies get shots every 2 to 3 weeks until they are about 4 months old. Your vet will set the exact schedule.
- Until the shots are done, keep your puppy away from dogs that may not be vaccinated.
- Deworming: worms are common in puppies. Your vet may deworm and check stool samples every 2 to 4 weeks until two tests in a row are clear.
- Feeding: puppies 6 to 12 weeks old usually eat 4 small meals a day of puppy food.
- Potty training: start early. Take the puppy out often and praise them when they go outside.
- Socializing: let them meet people and other animals gently, especially at 2 to 4 months old.

Q: Minimize litter box smell: upstairs or downstairs? I have 3 cats and we are moving into a two story house. We are considering two main locations for one or two large uncovered litterboxes: upstairs or downstairs. Which location would minimize …
A: Smells diffuse throughout the air, moving outward in all directions. So from that point of view, upstairs or downstairs doesn't matter.

Q: When should I spay or neuter my dog or cat?
A: The best age depends on your pet, so ask your vet. General guidance:

Cats: Many groups advise spaying or neutering before about 5 months old. Some vets do it around 6 months. Healthy kittens can be fixed as young as 8 weeks.

Dogs: The traditional age is about 6 to 9 months, and some groups advise before 5 months. Giant-breed males kept as house pets are often neutered after they stop growing, at about 12 to 15 months.

Benefits include:
- No heat cycles and no unplanned litters
- Lower risk of womb infections and breast tumors in females
- No testicular cancer in males, and less roaming and urine marking

Pets can gain weight after surgery, so watch their food portions.

Q: What's the penalty for animal cruelty in the Philippines?
A: Section 9 of the Animal Welfare Act, as amended by RA 10631, sets penalties after conviction:

- Animal dies: 1 year, 6 months and 1 day to 2 years in prison, and/or a fine up to P100,000
- Animal survives but is severely injured and can't survive without human help: 1 year and 1 day to 1 year and 6 months, and/or up to P50,000
- Other cruelty or neglect: 6 months to 1 year, and/or up to P30,000

Penalties go up to 2 years and 1 day to 3 years and/or up to P250,000 if the offense involves a syndicate, a business, a public officer, or 3 or more animals.

Q: Which vaccines are core for dogs?
A: Core vaccines are the ones every dog should get, wherever it lives. For dogs these protect against:
- Distemper
- Parvovirus
- Adenovirus (infectious hepatitis)

Rabies vaccine is also core anywhere the disease is present or the law requires it.

Global guidelines now say leptospirosis vaccine should be given to all dogs in places where the disease occurs, so in those areas it is treated as core too.

Other vaccines, like kennel cough (Bordetella and parainfluenza), are "non-core". Your vet suggests them based on your dog's lifestyle, such as boarding or contact with many dogs. Ask your vet which vaccines suit your dog.

Q: Why does my dog starts drinking water when he sees people dancing? My dog starts drinking water continously when he sees anybody dancing, even though he may have just drank enough water. No matter how much water he drank before …
A: My guess is that your dog is drinking water as a nervous response to not being able to comprehend why the humans are moving around like that (they don't normally move like that)! Dogs with anxiety lick obsessively, tear things up, or develop other nervous 'ticks' (such as drinking water while under anxiety).

Look for other signs that your dog could be uncomfortable, and verify that this behavior is only triggered by certain circumstances (like the dancing).

If it's possible your dog is repeating this behavior more frequently (but maybe it was only first noticed during the dancing), consider a vet checkup, as it's possible there could be a more serious problem.

My cat buries his food. Why?

Being a cat owner for many decades and knowing much about these enigmatic creatures, my new rescue kitten (about a year old), has the strangest behavior: After eating, he scratches the floor, multiple times, from different directions; exactly like he’s covering waste in his litter box. Any ideas why?

Some cats have a stronger burying instinct than others, and will scratch to bury at surfaces that are completely unsuitable to burying, sometimes even to only cover up a smell, as there is no physical object to bury.

My cat, for instance, is a enthusiastic bury-er that scratches at his litter, the sides of the box, around the outside of the box, and any nearby objects will end up in the box. He will do this sometimes even if he's not just used the box, but because he's so fastidious about burying. I've also seen him attempting to bury nowhere near his box, at nothing. Apparently a rogue smell is enough to make him want to bury.

Therefore, I have the impression that your cat still smells the food after it has eaten it, and is trying to cover up the smell by burying.

Q: What is the life expectancy of a yorkie?

I know that various dog breeds have different life expectancies. Has there been research done on specifically the Yorkshire Terrier breed?
A: The average life expectancy for standard size Yorkies is 13-16 years; 14.5 is the median age. The average life expectancy for females is a little longer than it is for male's (1.5 years longer).

It's important to note though that teacup Yorkie's (those under 4lbs) have a shorter lifespan - just 7-9 years on average. This is largely due to the fact that they're at increased risk for traumatic injury due to their small size.

The Yorkie Info Center offers more information on the research that's been conducted, specific to this breed.

The average life expectancy for standard size Yorkies is 13-16 years; 14.5 is the median age. The average life expectancy for females is a little longer than it is for male's (1.5 years longer).

It's important to note though that teacup Yorkie's (those under 4lbs) have a shorter lifespan - just 7-9 years on average. This is largely due to the fact that they're at increased risk for traumatic injury due to their small size.

The Yorkie Info Center offers more information on the research that's been conducted, specific to this breed.

Vets use a 9-point body condition score (BCS) from WSAVA. You can do a quick check at home:
- Ribs: Run your hands along the sides. At a healthy weight you can feel the ribs under a thin layer of fat. If you can't feel them without pressing, there is too much fat.

A: Split his daily portions. Cats are designed to have smaller, frequent meals.

Q: How much exercise does my old dog need?
A: Older dogs still need daily activity to keep their muscles, joints, weight and mind healthy. The type matters more than the amount:
- Choose gentle, low-impact exercise like shorter, more frequent leash walks or swimming
- Avoid lots of hard jumping and rough play

- Ramps for the bed, sofa or car
- Block stairs or pools if eyesight or hearing is poor

Q: My pet ate something poisonous. Should I make him throw up at home?
A: Only if a vet tells you to. Making a pet vomit can do more harm than good. It's dangerous with burning chemicals like drain cleaner or bleach, with batteries, if your pet is drowsy, trembling or having seizures, or if a few hours have passed. Home remedies like salt water can also poison pets.

- If it's on the skin or fur, wash with mild soap and water.

On the way, keep your pet calm and watch the breathing. Some poisons cause delayed signs, so go even if your pet seems fine.

Q: My dog eats grass. Is that normal?
A: Yes, it is very common, and most grass-eating dogs are not sick. Studies show fewer than 1 in 4 dogs vomit after eating grass. Dogs may eat grass for fiber, out of boredom or to get attention, or simply from instinct.

Things to watch:
- Grass sprayed with weed killers or pesticides can poison your dog. Keep him off treated lawns.
- Grass can carry worm eggs from other animals' poop. Ask your vet about regular deworming.
- If he seems bored or lonely, spend more time playing with him.

See your vet if he eats grass and then vomits often or seems to have stomach pain. That can point to a stomach or gut problem that needs checking.

Q: How often should I deworm my puppy?
A: Puppies pick up worms easily, so they're dewormed more often than adults. A common schedule is:
- Every 2 weeks from about 2 weeks old until 12 weeks
- Then monthly until 6 months old
- Then every 3 months for adults

Your vet will choose the right product and dose for your puppy's weight, so ask them before giving anything. Keep the yard clean and treat fleas too, since fleas can spread tapeworm.

Q: How often should adult dogs and cats be dewormed?
A: Parasite experts (CAPC) recommend year-round protection for adult pets. Many monthly preventives cover worms together with heartworm, fleas or ticks.

If your pet isn't on a year-round preventive:
- Deworm about four times a year
- Have a stool (fecal) test 2 to 4 times a year

Even on prevention, healthy adults should have their poop checked at least twice a year. Pets that hunt, roam, travel or mix with many animals may need it more often.

Ask your vet for a product that suits your pet's weight and age, and which worms are common where you live.

Q: My dog or cat has diarrhea. When do I need a vet?
A: Mild diarrhea in an adult pet that is still bright and eating can sometimes be watched at home for a short time.

Home care:
- Always keep fresh water out. Diarrhea can quickly cause dehydration.
- Ask your vet about a short rest for the stomach, or small meals of a bland or gut-friendly diet.
- When the stool firms up, switch back to the usual food slowly over about a week.

See your vet if it lasts more than 24 hours.

Go now if there is:
- Blood in the stool, or black, tarry stool
- Vomiting, weakness, fever, belly pain or no appetite
- Diarrhea in a puppy. It can be an early sign of parvo, which can be deadly.
- Straining with nothing coming out

Q: My cat is sneezing and has runny eyes. Is it cat flu?
A: It may be an upper respiratory infection, often called cat flu. Viruses like feline herpesvirus and calicivirus are common causes, and they spread easily between cats. Signs include sneezing, runny eyes or nose, mouth sores, tiredness and poor appetite.

What helps:
- Gently wipe her nose clean. A blocked nose can stop her smelling food, so she may eat less.
- Make sure she keeps eating and drinking.

See your vet within 24 hours if the sneezing doesn't stop. Go now if she:
- Has trouble breathing, or her gums look bluish
- Hasn't eaten properly for 24 hours
- Is a kitten. Young cats are more likely to get seriously ill.

Vaccines can make these infections milder.

Q: A stray dog bit my dog. Should I worry about rabies?
A: Rabies spreads mainly through bites and scratches. Once signs appear, it is almost always fatal, so act quickly.

For your dog:
- Wear gloves and wash the wound with soap and water
- Call your vet today, even if your dog is vaccinated. Your vet will check the wound and advise what to do next

For people: if you or a family member is bitten or scratched, wash the wound right away with soap and water and see a doctor urgently. Treatment after exposure works very well when started early.

Worldwide, dogs cause most human rabies deaths. Keeping your pets' rabies vaccines up to date protects them and your family.

Q: Is it legal to sell or eat dog meat in the Philippines?
A: No. RA 9482 bans the trade of dog meat. LGUs must enforce this ban (Section 7).

Under Section 11, anyone caught trading dog meat faces a fine of at least P5,000 per dog and 1 to 4 years in prison. The same penalty applies to using electrocution to put dogs to sleep. Foreigners who break these rules are deported after serving their sentence.

Killing dogs for food is also not among the allowed reasons for killing animals under the Animal Welfare Act (RA 8485, Section 6).

Q: My puppy bites and nips a lot. How do I stop it?
A: Mouthing is normal for puppies. The goal is to teach them to be gentle.

- When teeth press hard, give a high-pitched yelp and let your hand go limp. Praise your puppy when they stop.
- If that doesn't work, ignore them for 10 to 20 seconds or walk away, then play again calmly.
- Keep a chew toy or tug toy handy and offer it when they go for your hands or feet.
- Play fetch or tug instead of rough games with your hands.
- Don't jerk your hands away. It invites more grabbing.
- Never hit, slap or shake your puppy. It can make biting worse and cause fear.

Get help from a certified animal behaviorist or veterinary behaviorist if bites come with a stiff body, growling or pulled-back lips, or hurt much more than play bites.

Q: Can a pet legally be put to sleep in the Philippines?
A: Only for reasons the Animal Welfare Act allows. Section 6 of RA 8485 permits killing a pet when, for example:

- A licensed vet certifies it has an incurable communicable disease
- A licensed vet certifies it is needed to end the animal's suffering
- It is needed to prevent immediate danger to human life or limb

It must be done humanely, using methods approved by the Committee on Animal Welfare. Electrocution of dogs is banned under RA 9482. Talk to your vet if you're facing this decision.

Q: Do old cats chase moving objects?

I know kittens usually like to chase moving objects, how about the old one? Do they also enjoy that?
A: Yes, older cats still love to play! The moving object simulates prey. A cat's natural instinct to hunt, chase, and pounce should never go away. They will slow down a little as they get older, but they should never lose the thrill of "the hunt."

Sometimes, it's up to us to make sure they don't slow down too much. We do this by providing different types of stimulation - all types of toys, things to scratch, and places to climb. Dragging string-type toys or feather wands are a great way to keep your older kitty's body and mind healthy.

Q: Can cats get rabies too, or only dogs?
A: Cats can get rabies and pass it to people through bites and scratches. Rabies can infect all mammals.

The Anti-Rabies Act (RA 9482) mainly talks about dogs, but DOH offices urge owners to vaccinate both dogs and cats against rabies regularly and not let them roam freely. The national campaign theme is "Rabies-free na pusa't aso, kaligtasan ng pamilyang Pilipino."

Ask your vet about your cat's yearly anti-rabies shot, and treat any cat bite or scratch seriously.

Q: Do all Siberian Huskies have blue eyes?

I want to buy a Siberian Husky, and I'm interested in knowing if they all have blue eyes or if they have different eye colors.
A: Siberian Huskies may have any of several different eye colors:
- pale blue
- dark blue
- amber
- green
- brown

In some individual dogs, one eye may be brown and the other blue (complete heterochromia), or one or both eyes may be "parti-colored," that is, half brown and half blue (partial heterochromia). All of these eye-color combinations are considered acceptable by the American Kennel Club1

Q: My dog isn't eating. When should I worry?
A: A dog that stops eating is often unwell, so take it seriously and involve your vet early.

What to check:
- Does he seem hungry but struggle to pick up, chew or swallow food? That points to pain in the mouth, teeth or jaw.
- Has anything changed lately, like a move, a new food or a new medicine?
- Are there other signs, like vomiting, diarrhea, pain or low energy?

When to go:
- Skipped meals but otherwise acting normal: see your vet today, within 24 hours.
- Go now if he hasn't eaten or drunk anything for 24 hours, or if he is also vomiting, very weak or in a lot of pain.
- If he has diabetes and refuses even one meal, call your vet right away.

Q: How is rabies spread?
A: Rabies spreads through the saliva of an infected animal, mostly through:

- Bites
- Scratches
- Saliva getting into open wounds, eyes, nose or mouth

Dogs cause up to 99% of human rabies cases worldwide, according to the WHO. In the Philippines, the DOH said 45% of rabies cases in 2024 came from the saliva of household pets.

Touching or feeding an animal, or a lick on unbroken skin, is not considered an exposure. Still, wash the area with soap and water.

Rabies is a virus that affects the nervous system in both animals and people. Rabies is transmitted through bites from rabid animals or through contact with their saliva. Dogs — Report dog bites
Anyone who is bitten by a dog is at risk of getting rabies. Consider contacting your local animal control agency or police department to report the incident. Q: A stray dog bit my dog. Should I worry about rabies?
A: Rabies spreads mainly through bites and scratches. Once signs appear, it is almost always fatal, so act quickly.

For your dog:
- Wear gloves and wash the wound with soap and water
- Call your vet today, even if your dog is vaccinated. Your vet will check the wound and advise what to do next

For people: if you or a family member is bitten or scratched, wash the wound right away with soap and water and see a doctor urgently. Treatment after exposure works very well when started early.

Worldwide, dogs cause most human rabies deaths. Keeping your pets' rabies vaccines up to date protects them and your family.

Q: Where can I report animal abuse or neglect?
A: Under the Animal Welfare Act as amended by RA 10631 (Section 10):

- The Philippine National Police (PNP), the NBI and other law enforcement agencies have animal welfare enforcement officers
- The Secretary of Agriculture can deputize trained volunteers and members of NGOs and community groups as enforcement officers
- These officers can rescue maltreated animals and arrest violators

LGUs are also required to enforce the anti-cruelty rules of RA 8485 (RA 9482, Section 7). You can report to the police, your LGU, or an animal welfare group. Take photos or videos and note the date and place to help your report.

Q: My dog or cat has diarrhea. When do I need a vet?
A: Mild diarrhea in an adult pet that is still bright and eating can sometimes be watched at home for a short time.

Home care:
- Always keep fresh water out. Diarrhea can quickly cause dehydration.
- Ask your vet about a short rest for the stomach, or small meals of a bland or gut-friendly diet.
- When the stool firms up, switch back to the usual food slowly over about a week.

See your vet if it lasts more than 24 hours.

Go now if there is:
- Blood in the stool, or black, tarry stool
- Vomiting, weakness, fever, belly pain or no appetite
- Diarrhea in a puppy. It can be an early sign of parvo, which can be deadly.
- Straining with nothing coming out

messages.content: My dog: panic, struggling to breathe. What should I do?

This sounds like it could be choking. Something stuck in the mouth or throat. If your pet is still breathing and coughing, go to the vet. Only step in if they can't breathe.

What to do now:
- Stay calm and hold them gently but firmly. A choking pet may bite.
- Open the mouth and look. If you can see the object and get a grip on it, remove it carefully with fingers or tweezers.
- If you can't remove it and they can't breathe: hold a cat or small dog with their back against your chest and give 5 firm thrusts inward and upward just below the ribs.
- For a large dog, put your arms around the belly from behind, make a fist just below the ribs and push firmly up and forward 5 times. If they're lying down, push from behind the ribs toward the head.
- Check the mouth again and repeat. If they collapse and stop breathing, start CPR.
- Go to the vet even if the object comes out. The throat may be injured.

Don't:
- Sweeping your fingers blindly. It can push the object deeper.
- Pulling on string, thread or tinsel hanging from the mouth or bottom. It can cut the intestines.

Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now.

Q: Socializing a puppy without all of the vaccinations I have a 10 week old puppy, but since she is too young she doesn't have all her shots. Should I wait till she's 16 weeks old to introduce her to new …
A: No, no, don't wait!!!! There are critical periods of brain development for a puppy that end around 12 weeks for socialization, so it is very important to have your puppy meet many other dogs. That being said, you want to be careful where you do this: Avoid dog parks, for example, where you do not know all of the dog owners. A great place to meet multiple dogs is a puppy kindergarten training class. If you have friends with dogs and know that they are vaccinated, then by all means introduce your puppy to them. Just be careful to introduce them slowly, as some dogs might be less tolerant of a puppy's energy and bad manners.

Q: I just got a new puppy. What should I do first?
A: Book a vet visit soon. Your puppy will need a series of shots and deworming.

- Vaccines: puppies get shots every 2 to 3 weeks until they are about 4 months old. Your vet will set the exact schedule.
- Until the shots are done, keep your puppy away from dogs that may not be vaccinated.
- Deworming: worms are common in puppies. Your vet may deworm and check stool samples every 2 to 4 weeks until two tests in a row are clear.
- Feeding: puppies 6 to 12 weeks old usually eat 4 small meals a day of puppy food.
- Potty training: start early. Take the puppy out often and praise them when they go outside.
- Socializing: let them meet people and other animals gently, especially at 2 to 4 months old.

Q: How often should I feed a pregnant cat? A stray cat adopted us a few months back. Initially, we thought it was a boy but then discovered that it's a girl and expecting kittens. I have never had a cat …
A: I always let pregnant queens eat as much as they like. You want a healthy well fed queen and fat little kittens.

Some cats will overeat and start to become obese but this is less of a risk with outdoor cats as they they get more exercise and typically have intestinal parasites. Also it is much better to have a slightly overweight queen Vs. a malnourished one.

The chance of complications and birth defects increase dramatically with malnourished queens.

Q: My old cat drinks a lot of water and pees a lot. Why?
A: Drinking and peeing more is a common early sign of kidney disease in older cats. Kidney disease affects up to 40% of cats over 10 and about 80% of cats over 15.

Other signs can follow:
- Weight loss
- Poor appetite
- Low energy and a messy coat

The same signs can also come from diabetes or an overactive thyroid, so blood and urine tests are needed to find the cause.

Book a vet visit soon, and don't limit her water. Go to a vet today if she stops eating, vomits repeatedly or seems very weak. Catching kidney disease early, often with a special diet, can help your cat feel better for longer.

Bloat (twisted stomach). The stomach fills with gas and can twist. It can kill within hours and usually needs surgery. Most common in large, deep-chested dogs.
Signs: Swollen, tight belly; Retching or trying to vomit with nothing coming up; Restless, pacing, can't get comfortable; Drooling, pale gums, collapse
What to do now:
1. Go to the vet immediately. Call ahead so they can prepare.
2. Keep your dog as calm and still as you can on the way.
Don't: Waiting to see if it passes. Giving food, water or home remedies. Trying to make them vomit.
Go to a vet now.

Q: My dog chewed up a whole pack of sugar-free gum.
A: Take him to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now, even if he looks fine. Many sugar-free gums contain xylitol (also called birch sugar), which can make a dog's blood sugar crash within 10 to 60 minutes. It can also harm the liver a day or two later, so he may need to stay for monitoring.

Watch for vomiting, weakness, wobbling, collapse and seizures.

Before you go:
- Bring the pack so the vet can check the ingredients.
- Only make him vomit if a vet tells you to.

On the way, keep him close, watch for weakness or shaking, and call the clinic ahead.

Xylitol is also in some peanut butters, toothpastes, mouthwashes and vitamins, so check labels and use only pet toothpaste.

What is the appeal of the bath tub to a cat?

My 5 month old DSH spends several minutes, two or three times per day, playing in my bath tub. He'll be running around playing, then heads to the bathroom, jumps in, rolls around on the floor, paws at the drain and the fixtures, then moves on to something else.

Q: I just got a new kitten. What should I do first?
A: Take your kitten to a vet as soon as you can. Ask where you got her about any vaccines, deworming and food she has had.

- Vet visits: kittens usually see the vet every 3 to 4 weeks until about 6 months old, for shots and parasite treatment.
- Vaccines: the core kitten shots start at about 6 to 8 weeks and are repeated every 3 to 4 weeks until 16 to 20 weeks old.
- Deworming: worms are very common in kittens, so many vets deworm them routinely.
- Testing: a kitten with an unknown history should be tested for FeLV and FIV. Keep her apart from your other cats until the vet has checked her.
- Feeding: use kitten food, given several times a day.
- Litter box: one per cat, plus one extra, kept clean.

What to do now:

2. Carry them gently in a carrier.
Don't: Pressing on the belly or bladder. Waiting until the next day.
Go to a vet now.

- Keep him calm and quiet.

A: As fun an idea as this is cats aren't really in to music, at least not human music although some early research suggests that music more tailored to cat senses is appealing to them.

Human music is generally too loud and bass-y for cats to enjoy, and part of what appeals to humans in music is the tempo being similar to human heart beats. Cat hearing operates in different ranges to ours, and is much more sensitive.

A: First, have your vet rule out a medical problem. Peeing outside the box can be a sign of a bladder problem.

Q: How much is the fine if my dog is not registered or vaccinated?
A: Section 11 of RA 9482 sets these fines for pet owners:

- Not registering or not vaccinating your dog: P2,000
- Not leashing your dog outside the house: P500 per incident
- Claiming your dog from the pound: P500 to P1,000
- Refusing to have a biting dog observed: P10,000
- Refusing observation and not paying the bite victim's medical costs: P25,000

An owner who refuses to have the dog vaccinated must also pay for the vaccination of the dog and of anyone it bites. The LGU collects most of these fines.

These amounts are as written in the 2007 law. Your city or municipality may have its own ordinance, so check with your city or municipal veterinary office.

messages.content:
Is it safe to put lavender oil on my dog's skin? If so, how should I dilute it?

Is it safe to put lavender oil on my dog's skin? If so, please tell me the best way to dilute it to help fight fleas. I use advantage plus and want something extra and heard it repels fleas.

Lavender oil is safe for dogs, cats and humans and does indeed repel fleas and ticks. Since it's the smell that repels fleas, you don't have to spread the oil over the whole body.

A very easy way to apply the oil is to rub a few drops onto the collar or bandana of your dog. The advantage is that the fur won't get oily and collect dirt.

Otherwise, rub the undiluted oil directly into the fur, one drop at a time. For small dogs one drop in the neck should suffice. For bigger dogs, add one drop to the top of their hips or the back of their hind legs, where they cannot lick it off. If your dog has very long fur, use more drops.

Repeat the treatment every few days when the oil has evaporated and your dog no longer smells like lavender.

Q: What's the penalty for animal cruelty in the Philippines?
A: Section 9 of the Animal Welfare Act, as amended by RA 10631, sets penalties after conviction:

- Animal dies: 1 year, 6 months and 1 day to 2 years in prison, and/or a fine up to P100,000
- Animal survives but is severely injured and can't survive without human help: 1 year and 1 day to 1 year and 6 months, and/or up to P50,000
- Other cruelty or neglect: 6 months to 1 year, and/or up to P30,000

Penalties go up to 2 years and 1 day to 3 years and/or up to P250,000 if the offense involves a syndicate, a business, a public officer, or 3 or more animals.

Q: My dog keeps shaking his head and scratching his ears. What's wrong?
A: This is a common sign of an ear infection. Other signs are red ears, a bad smell, dark or yellowish discharge, and pain when you touch the ear. Allergies are often behind it, and dogs with floppy or hairy ears get them more often.

See your vet within 24 hours. The vet needs to look at the ear canal and eardrum and find the cause before choosing a treatment. Some ear medicines can cause hearing loss if the eardrum is torn, so don't use leftover or store-bought drops on your own.

Go now if he is in severe pain. Go today if the ear flap suddenly swells up. Left untreated, ear infections can damage the eardrum and cause lasting hearing loss.

messages.content: My dog has collapse. Help, what do I do?

This sounds like it could be choking. Something stuck in the mouth or throat. If your pet is still breathing and coughing, go to the vet. Only step in if they can't breathe.

What to do now:
- Stay calm and hold them gently but firmly. A choking pet may bite.
- Open the mouth and look. If you can see the object and get a grip on it, remove it carefully with fingers or tweezers.
- If you can't remove it and they can't breathe: hold a cat or small dog with their back against your chest and give 5 firm thrusts inward and upward just below the ribs.
- For a large dog, put your arms around the belly from behind, make a fist just below the ribs and push firmly up and forward 5 times. If they're lying down, push from behind the ribs toward the head.
- Check the mouth again and repeat. If they collapse and stop breathing, start CPR.
- Go to the vet even if the object comes out. The throat may be injured.

Don't:
- Sweeping your fingers blindly. It can push the object deeper.
- Pulling on string, thread or tinsel hanging from the mouth or bottom. It can cut the intestines.

Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now.

Q: How often should I deworm my puppy?
A: Puppies pick up worms easily, so they're dewormed more often than adults. A common schedule is:
- Every 2 weeks from about 2 weeks old until 12 weeks
- Then monthly until 6 months old
- Then every 3 months for adults

Your vet will choose the right product and dose for your puppy's weight, so ask them before giving anything. Keep the yard clean and treat fleas too, since fleas can spread tapeworm.

Q: How often should I deworm my kitten?
A: Kittens often get roundworms from their mother's milk, so deworming starts early.

Parasite experts (CAPC) advise:
- Start at 2 weeks old
- Repeat every 2 weeks until your kitten starts a monthly year-round parasite preventive
- If a monthly preventive isn't used: every 2 weeks until 2 months old, then monthly until 6 months, then every 3 months
- Have the kitten's poop checked by the vet several times in the first year

Ask your vet for a product that suits your kitten's weight and age, and use only products made for cats.

The only way I've found to get him to give up the ball is to throw a 2nd ball for him!

Any suggestions?

First you train the dog to come when called (there are many resources on the web that can teach you how to do that). Train that to the point where the dog will come very reliably. Next I would go with the "2nd ball" approach mentioned above. If the dog doesn't bring the ball to you, then call him to come and immediately throw the second ball when s/he comes to you. The dog will likely drop the ball right away as soon as you throw the ball. Once that is established the dog will likely start dropping the first ball at your feet in anticipation of the second ball being thrown. If not, then delay throwing the second ball until the first is dropped.

Q: What age do cats stop growing on average?

I've heard humans stop growing around age 18-24. What about cats? When do they stop growing in height?
A: There are a couple of growth periods for cats. The first takes about 4 months and takes them into the kitten stage. The second growth period of a kitten takes them from about 4 months to somewhere between 8 and 12 months to adult size depending on the size of the breed. Larger breeds will take longer to reach their adult size versus smaller breeds, but despite having adult size, they're still junior cats, they don't really become adult cats until their 3rd year.

I only mention the two growth stages (which are effectively continuous) because the dietary requirements change.

A: This sounds like Myoclonus these twitches are usually caused by sudden muscle contractions or from brief lapses of contraction.

They are not considered problematic unless it results in an inability to fall asleep. Or unless they are symptom of a related illness. For the most part, it is just a twitch as one is falling asleep, you have probably had them yourself.

Why do animals try to stay awake when they need sleep?

I found a video on YouTube of animals drifting off and trying to stay awake (by jerking their heads etc. like humans do). Why do they do this instead of just letting themselves fall asleep?

Cats prefer to sleep in locations they consider secure; if for some reason they are in a location where they feel threatened or can see possible prey, they wish to stay awake but if they need sleep they display this behavior. Q: How much water should I let my dog drink? My dog is a Labrador schnoodle cross and he is almost one year old. I want to know how much water I should allow him to drink because I don't want …
A: As much as he wants! There are very few instances where you should limit the amount your dog drinks. An example would be:
- Your dog is vomiting - better to offer small amounts of water several times a day instead of him engulfing large quantities at once. If vomiting persists your pet should be seen by a veterinarian as frequent vomiting can lead to dehydration.

It is important to monitor how much he drinks as an increase can be an indicator to illnesses such as diabetes and kidney disease.

Q: How much water should my pet drink, and how do I spot dehydration?
A: Keep fresh, clean water out at all times, in places your pet can easily reach. Cats that eat wet food often drink less, because the food is mostly water. Cats on dry food need to drink more.

Signs of dehydration:
- Dry or sticky gums
- Skin that stays "tented" when you gently lift it at the back of the neck, instead of snapping back
- Sunken eyes, weakness, low energy or poor appetite

Vomiting and diarrhea can cause dehydration fast. Call your vet today if you think your pet is dehydrated. Go now if they haven't eaten or drunk anything for 24 hours, or are very weak.

Drinking much more than usual also needs a vet visit within a day. It can be a sign of kidney disease, diabetes or other illness.

Q: Socializing a puppy without all of the vaccinations I have a 10 week old puppy, but since she is too young she doesn't have all her shots. Should I wait till she's 16 weeks old to introduce her to new …
A: No, no, don't wait!!!! There are critical periods of brain development for a puppy that end around 12 weeks for socialization, so it is very important to have your puppy meet many other dogs. That being said, you want to be careful where you do this: Avoid dog parks, for example, where you do not know all of the dog owners. A great place to meet multiple dogs is a puppy kindergarten training class. If you have friends with dogs and know that they are vaccinated, then by all means introduce your puppy to them. Just be careful to introduce them slowly, as some dogs might be less tolerant of a puppy's energy and bad manners.

Q: My cat isn't eating. How long is too long?
A: Don't wait it out. A cat that stops eating can develop a serious liver problem called hepatic lipidosis (fatty liver). It can be fatal if not treated quickly. Overweight cats are at higher risk.

What to do:
- If your cat hasn't eaten properly for 24 hours, take her to the vet now.
- Go right away if her gums, ears, skin or the whites of her eyes look yellow, or if she is very weak.
- Tell the vet when she last ate and if anything changed at home.

Most cats with fatty liver have another illness that caused the poor appetite, so the vet will look for that too. Fatty liver needs prompt treatment, so don't wait to see if she starts eating again.

Q: Where can I report animal abuse or neglect?
A: Under the Animal Welfare Act as amended by RA 10631 (Section 10):

- The Philippine National Police (PNP), the NBI and other law enforcement agencies have animal welfare enforcement officers
- The Secretary of Agriculture can deputize trained volunteers and members of NGOs and community groups as enforcement officers
- These officers can rescue maltreated animals and arrest violators

LGUs are also required to enforce the anti-cruelty rules of RA 8485 (RA 9482, Section 7). You can report to the police, your LGU, or an animal welfare group. Take photos or videos and note the date and place to help your report.

messages.content: What do I do? My cat shows not responding to you and jaw chomping, drooling, losing control of pee or poo.

This sounds like it could be seizures. Most seizures stop within 2 minutes. Keep your pet safe, time it, and call your vet.

What to do now:
- Stay calm and note the time it starts.
- Move furniture and objects away, keep them away from stairs and water, and put a towel under the head. Keep your hands away from the mouth.
- Dim the lights and keep things quiet. Film it if you can, since it helps the vet.
- Afterwards, keep them somewhere quiet and cool, and speak softly while they recover.
- Call your vet after any first seizure. Go now if it lasts over 5 minutes, they have another one, they don't wake up between seizures, or they may have eaten a poison.

Don't:
- Putting fingers or anything else in their mouth. Pets can't swallow their tongue.
- Holding them down.
- Giving food, water or medicine until they're fully alert.

Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now.

Q: My pet ate something poisonous. Should I make him throw up at home?
A: Only if a vet tells you to. Making a pet vomit can do more harm than good. It's dangerous with burning chemicals like drain cleaner or bleach, with batteries, if your pet is drowsy, trembling or having seizures, or if a few hours have passed. Home remedies like salt water can also poison pets.

Instead:
- Move your pet away from the poison.

Q: My dog got bitten by a snake in the yard. What should I do?
A: Treat any snake bite as an emergency and go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now, even if the bite looks small. Some venoms, like cobra venom, cause little swelling but can affect breathing. Treatment works best when started early.

On the way:
- Keep your dog calm and limit his movement. Carry him if you can.
- Don't cut the bite, try to suck out the venom, or tie a tourniquet.
- Don't put ice, cold packs, heat or sprays on it.
- Don't wait to see if signs appear.

If the snake is already dead, you can bring it without damaging the head, which helps the vet identify it. Never try to catch a live snake. Call the clinic ahead so they can prepare.

Q: Are there rules on how my pet should be transported, like by van or boat?
A: Yes. Section 4 of the Animal Welfare Act (RA 8485) sets rules for transporting animals:

- Carriers must provide clean, sanitary facilities for animals
- Animals must get food and water on trips longer than 12 hours, or when needed
- Overcrowding, cruel confinement and putting animals in vehicle trunks count as cruelty

A BAI permit is required to transport animals. For pets, apply for a BAI local shipping permit before your trip, and prepare a vet health certificate and rabies vaccination certificate.

A: Chocolate is poisonous to dogs, especially dark and baking chocolate. Call or go to a vet now, even if your dog seems fine, because signs can take hours to show.

Q: My dog got into a plate of dark chocolate brownies. How worried should I be?
A: Call your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now and take him in. Dark chocolate, baking chocolate and cocoa powder are the most dangerous types because they contain the most theobromine, a stimulant dogs clear very slowly. Rich brownies are also fatty, which can trigger pancreatitis.

Signs can start within a few hours: vomiting, diarrhea, restlessness, panting, drinking and peeing more, a racing heart, tremors and seizures.

Before you go:
- Note your dog's weight, the type of chocolate and how much he ate, and bring the wrapper or recipe.
- If the brownies were sugar-free, tell the vet, since xylitol is also dangerous.
- Only make him vomit if a vet tells you to.
- Don't wait for signs to appear.

On the way, keep him calm and watch for shaking.

Q: My pet ate something poisonous. Should I make him throw up at home?
A: Only if a vet tells you to. Making a pet vomit can do more harm than good. It's dangerous with burning chemicals like drain cleaner or bleach, with batteries, if your pet is drowsy, trembling or having seizures, or if a few hours have passed. Home remedies like salt water can also poison pets.

- If it's on the skin or fur, wash with mild soap and water.

Q: My dog is vomiting. Can I treat him at home?
A: One vomit in a dog that otherwise seems well is often not serious, and many cases settle within a day. But vomiting can also be a sign of poisoning, a blockage or other illness.

Go to the vet right away if he vomits and also has:
- Blood in the vomit
- Diarrhea, belly pain or fever
- Low energy, no appetite or signs of dehydration
- A chance he swallowed something toxic or an object

See your vet today if vomiting goes on for more than 24 hours, even if he seems fine.

For a mild case, your vet may suggest resting the stomach for a short time, then small, frequent meals of a bland food. Keep fresh water available. Don't give human medicines unless your vet tells you to.

sources.label: FurFriends first-aid guide: Toad poisoning
sources.text:
Toad poisoning. Cane toads, the large brown toads that come out after rain, release a poison when a dog or cat bites or licks them.
Signs: Sudden heavy drooling or foaming at the mouth; Pawing at the mouth, shaking the head; Bright red gums; Vomiting, wobbliness, a racing heartbeat, seizures
What to do now:
1. Rinse the mouth straight away. Point the head down and run a gentle stream of water across the gums and tongue from the side, so it flows out of the mouth. Keep going for 10 minutes.
2. Wipe the gums and tongue with a damp cloth to remove the sticky poison.
3. Go to the vet now, especially if there's anything more than drooling.
Don't: Spraying water down the throat. It can go into the lungs. Making them vomit.
Go to a vet now.

You should show him that nothing bad happens when he's close to the cat. One approach that worked well for me was to sit down with the scared animal (in your case the dog) and pet it. Then call the second animal to you and pet both at the same time.

Make sure you have each animal on either side of you. You are the safety wall that makes your dog feel protected while that cat is near.

Q: My dog or cat has bad breath. What causes it?
A: A healthy pet's breath should not smell bad. The most common cause is dental disease. Plaque and tartar build up on the teeth and inflame the gums, and the bacteria make the smell.

Bad breath can also point to other illness:
- Sweet or fruity smell: possible diabetes
- Urine-like smell: possible kidney disease
- Foul smell with vomiting, poor appetite or yellow gums: possible liver problems

What to do:
- Have your vet check bad breath that doesn't go away. A proper cleaning is done under anesthesia.
- Go sooner if you also see red or swollen gums, more drinking and peeing, weight loss, or poor appetite.
- At home, brush the teeth with pet toothpaste, ideally daily.

Q: What are the causes of a cat jumping off a roof?

Currently my cat is in serious condition and I was wondering: what happens if a cat fell from a high height, aka a roof?
A: Lots of things can make a cat fall/jump of a roof.
- Getting scared.
- Hunting attempts, for example trying to catch a bird.
- Overestimating his/her abilities.
- Getting distracted.

Cats can get hurt if the fall is too short, because they haven't enough time to righten themselves.

A cat can get hurt if it is overweight and it falls from great height.

Wanting to get down but landing wrong can cause injuries, this is most common in kittens and very young cats.

Additional information: often cats that fall from tall buildings have a greater survival rate and less injuries than cats falling from lower buildings.

Q: Is it legal to sell or eat dog meat in the Philippines?
A: No. RA 9482 bans the trade of dog meat. LGUs must enforce this ban (Section 7).

Q: What are the signs of tick fever in dogs?
A: "Tick fever" usually means germs like Ehrlichia, Anaplasma or Babesia spread by ticks. In the Philippines, the warm climate suits the brown dog tick, which can live in homes and kennels. Ehrlichia canis was the most common tick-borne germ found in a study of dogs in Metro Manila and Laguna.

Signs may show 1 to 3 weeks after a bite:
- Fever, low energy, poor appetite
- Swollen glands, stiffness or limping
- Nosebleeds, bruises on the skin or gums, or blood in urine or poop

See a vet today if you notice bleeding, bruising, pale gums or weakness. A blood test is needed to confirm it.

Prevent it with year-round tick control your vet recommends and daily tick checks.

What to do now:
- Stay calm and note the time it starts.
- Move furniture and objects away, keep them away from stairs and water, and put a towel under the head. Keep your hands away from the mouth.
- Dim the lights and keep things quiet. Film it if you can, since it helps the vet.
- Afterwards, keep them somewhere quiet and cool, and speak softly while they recover.
- Call your vet after any first seizure. Go now if it lasts over 5 minutes, they have another one, they don't wake up between seizures, or they may have eaten a poison.

Don't:
- Putting fingers or anything else in their mouth. Pets can't swallow their tongue.
- Holding them down.
- Giving food, water or medicine until they're fully alert.

Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now.

I've only been around to see three kittens acclimate, but I've always been surprised at how quickly all of them start using a litter box, especially compared to the toilet training time for puppies.

What makes cats so quick to recognize and choose a litter box to defecate into?

They feel that when they have to go, they have to go to a soft soily area and that's what the litter box replicates (remember that cats like to cover the area with dirt after they finish??). In the house, there is no other area like that so the litter box is the first place that they will go to.

Q: What is parvo and why is it an emergency?
A: Parvovirus is a very contagious virus that attacks a dog's gut. Puppies and unvaccinated dogs are most at risk. It spreads through infected poop and anything it touches, and it can survive in the environment for months or longer.

Signs usually start 5 to 7 days after exposure:
- Dullness, fever and not eating
- Then vomiting and diarrhea, often bloody

Dogs lose fluids fast and can go into shock. Some die within hours, but most dogs that get hospital care survive. See a vet now if your puppy has vomiting or bloody diarrhea. Call ahead so the clinic can protect other patients.

Keep sick dogs away from others. Ask your vet how to disinfect your home, because many cleaners don't kill parvo.

Q: Why do some dogs try to hump all the dogs at the dog park? I've noticed when we go to the dog park, there are certain dogs that try to hump most of the other dogs, including our much larger …
A: The dogs just "show them who's the boss".

Unfortunately many interpret this as being gay or aggressively offensive, which simply isn't true. Of course there could be more behind the whole thing in a male/female combination, but usually it's really just to mark dominance and part of playing/socializing.

Same is true for dogs trying to hump human legs. If one does, just shove it away (just like other dogs do), unless you want to drop in rank.

So if other dogs try to hump your lab, just let it solve this "issue" on its own, unless the dog can't or they're not properly socialized (i.e. they don't know when to stop or are somehow hindered).

Q: Is it legal to sell or eat dog meat in the Philippines?
A: No. RA 9482 bans the trade of dog meat. LGUs must enforce this ban (Section 7).

Under Section 11, anyone caught trading dog meat faces a fine of at least P5,000 per dog and 1 to 4 years in prison. The same penalty applies to using electrocution to put dogs to sleep. Foreigners who break these rules are deported after serving their sentence.

Killing dogs for food is also not among the allowed reasons for killing animals under the Animal Welfare Act (RA 8485, Section 6).

Q: What are the signs of tick fever in dogs?
A: "Tick fever" usually means germs like Ehrlichia, Anaplasma or Babesia spread by ticks. In the Philippines, the warm climate suits the brown dog tick, which can live in homes and kennels. Ehrlichia canis was the most common tick-borne germ found in a study of dogs in Metro Manila and Laguna.

Signs may show 1 to 3 weeks after a bite:
- Fever, low energy, poor appetite
- Swollen glands, stiffness or limping
- Nosebleeds, bruises on the skin or gums, or blood in urine or poop

See a vet today if you notice bleeding, bruising, pale gums or weakness. A blood test is needed to confirm it.

Prevent it with year-round tick control your vet recommends and daily tick checks.

Q: Do cats need clothes?

Do cats need dressing clothes when weather is cold?

If so, what is the temperature in which cats start to need clothes?
A: Cats generally have sense enough not to go outside/stay outside when it's dangerously cold unless they must. So unless you are forcing the cat outside, or your house is colder than most and you have a furless breed or much colder than most, this shouldn't be a problem.

Basically, most cats never need to wear clothes other than their fur. Remember, feral cats manage to survive in a wide range of climates.

Q: How often does my dog need the anti-rabies shot by law?
A: Every year. Section 5 of RA 9482 says owners must have their dogs "regularly" vaccinated against rabies. The implementing rules make it clearer: a properly immunized dog is one vaccinated yearly, and LGUs register and vaccinate dogs annually.

Q: When should I spay or neuter my dog or cat?
A: The best age depends on your pet, so ask your vet. General guidance:

Cats: Many groups advise spaying or neutering before about 5 months old. Some vets do it around 6 months. Healthy kittens can be fixed as young as 8 weeks.

Dogs: The traditional age is about 6 to 9 months, and some groups advise before 5 months. Giant-breed males kept as house pets are often neutered after they stop growing, at about 12 to 15 months.

Benefits include:
- No heat cycles and no unplanned litters
- Lower risk of womb infections and breast tumors in females
- No testicular cancer in males, and less roaming and urine marking

Pets can gain weight after surgery, so watch their food portions.

Q: Is it legal to sell or eat dog meat in the Philippines?
A: No. RA 9482 bans the trade of dog meat. LGUs must enforce this ban (Section 7).

Under Section 11, anyone caught trading dog meat faces a fine of at least P5,000 per dog and 1 to 4 years in prison. The same penalty applies to using electrocution to put dogs to sleep. Foreigners who break these rules are deported after serving their sentence.

Killing dogs for food is also not among the allowed reasons for killing animals under the Animal Welfare Act (RA 8485, Section 6).

Q: How often should I feed my puppy?
A: Puppies do best with small meals more often while young, then fewer meals as they grow. A common schedule:
- 6 to 12 weeks old: 4 meals a day of puppy food
- 3 to 6 months: 3 meals a day
- 6 to 12 months: 2 meals a day
- Over 12 months: 1 or 2 meals a day of adult food

Use a food made for growing puppies or for all life stages. Adjust the amount based on how your puppy grows, and have your vet check weight and body condition at each visit. Large and giant breeds need careful portions to protect their bones and joints. Keep treats under 10% of daily calories.

Feeding at the same times each day also helps potty training, since puppies often need to go soon after eating.

Q: My dog isn't eating. When should I worry?
A: A dog that stops eating is often unwell, so take it seriously and involve your vet early.

What to check:
- Does he seem hungry but struggle to pick up, chew or swallow food? That points to pain in the mouth, teeth or jaw.
- Has anything changed lately, like a move, a new food or a new medicine?
- Are there other signs, like vomiting, diarrhea, pain or low energy?

When to go:
- Skipped meals but otherwise acting normal: see your vet today, within 24 hours.
- Go now if he hasn't eaten or drunk anything for 24 hours, or if he is also vomiting, very weak or in a lot of pain.
- If he has diabetes and refuses even one meal, call your vet right away.

Q: How often should I bathe my dog or cat?
A: Dogs: The ASPCA suggests a bath at least once every three months. Dogs that spend a lot of time outdoors or have skin problems may need baths more often.

Cats: Most cats keep themselves clean. They only need a bath if they get very dirty or into something sticky or smelly.

Bath tips:
- Brush out loose hair and mats first.
- Use lukewarm water and a shampoo made for pets. Human shampoo can irritate or dry out the skin.
- Keep water out of the eyes, ears and nose. Wipe the face with a damp cloth.
- Rinse well and dry fully, including any skin folds.
- For cats, trim the claws first and use a rubber mat so they don't slip.

See your vet if you notice scabs, bald spots, redness or constant scratching.

Q: At what age is my dog considered a senior?
A: There's no single age, because dogs age at different rates depending on breed and size. Vets often call a dog senior when it is in the last quarter of its expected lifespan. As a rough guide, many dogs reach this stage at around 7 to 8 years.

From that age:
- See the vet at least twice a year
- Ask about blood and urine tests every 6 to 12 months to catch problems early
- Have blood pressure and thyroid checked yearly

Watch for changes at home, like slowing down, drinking more, weight change or confusion, and tell your vet. Old age is not a disease. Many changes can be treated.

Q: A stray dog bit my dog. Should I worry about rabies?
A: Rabies spreads mainly through bites and scratches. Once signs appear, it is almost always fatal, so act quickly.

For your dog:
- Wear gloves and wash the wound with soap and water
- Call your vet today, even if your dog is vaccinated. Your vet will check the wound and advise what to do next

Q: My dog or cat has diarrhea. When do I need a vet?
A: Mild diarrhea in an adult pet that is still bright and eating can sometimes be watched at home for a short time.

Home care:
- Always keep fresh water out. Diarrhea can quickly cause dehydration.
- Ask your vet about a short rest for the stomach, or small meals of a bland or gut-friendly diet.
- When the stool firms up, switch back to the usual food slowly over about a week.

See your vet if it lasts more than 24 hours.

Go now if there is:
- Blood in the stool, or black, tarry stool
- Vomiting, weakness, fever, belly pain or no appetite
- Diarrhea in a puppy. It can be an early sign of parvo, which can be deadly.
- Straining with nothing coming out

Stings & allergic reactions. Bee, wasp, ant and centipede stings usually cause swelling that settles. A spreading reaction or trouble breathing is an emergency.
Signs: Mild: swelling and pain where they were stung, licking the spot; Go now: the face swells and keeps spreading, or hives all over the body; Go now: vomiting, diarrhea, pale gums, weakness or collapse; Go now: trouble breathing, a sting inside the mouth or throat, or many stings
What to do now:
1. Move away from the insects.
2. If you see a bee stinger, scrape it out sideways with a card. Don't squeeze it.
3. Hold a cold pack wrapped in cloth on the spot for 10 minutes.
4. Watch closely for the next 1â€“2 hours and call your vet for advice.
Don't: Giving human allergy or cold tablets without a vet's dose. Some contain decongestants that are toxic to pets.
Call your vet for advice.

Q: A bee stung my dog and his face is swelling up.
A: Swelling of the face, head or neck after a sting can become serious because it can block breathing. Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now if the swelling is large or spreading, if he has any trouble breathing, or if he was stung inside the mouth or on the tongue.

While you get ready to go:
- If you can see the stinger, scrape it out sideways with a flat card. Don't squeeze it with tweezers.
- Hold a cold pack wrapped in a cloth on the swollen spot.
- On the way, watch his breathing closely.

Don't give him any human allergy medicine unless your vet tells you to. Even if the swelling seems mild, call your vet for advice.

Q: my dog is having a seizure right now what do i do
A: Stay calm and focus on keeping him safe.

While it's happening:
- Move furniture and hard objects away. Only move him if he's near stairs, water or another danger.
- Keep your hands away from his mouth. He can't control his jaws and may bite without meaning to.
- Don't try to hold him down.
- Time the seizure, and take a short video for the vet if you can.

Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now if the seizure lasts more than about 3 minutes, if he has more than one in a row, or if he might have eaten something poisonous. Otherwise, call your vet soon after.

Afterward he may pace or seem confused. On the way to the vet, keep him calm, quiet and away from edges.

Q: Which vaccines are core for dogs?
A: Core vaccines are the ones every dog should get, wherever it lives. For dogs these protect against:
- Distemper
- Parvovirus
- Adenovirus (infectious hepatitis)

Rabies vaccine is also core anywhere the disease is present or the law requires it.

Global guidelines now say leptospirosis vaccine should be given to all dogs in places where the disease occurs, so in those areas it is treated as core too.

Other vaccines, like kennel cough (Bordetella and parainfluenza), are "non-core". Your vet suggests them based on your dog's lifestyle, such as boarding or contact with many dogs. Ask your vet which vaccines suit your dog.

Be Prepared: Pet Safety in Emergencies — Rabies
Rabies is a virus that affects the nervous system in both animals and people. Rabies is transmitted through bites from rabid animals or through contact with their saliva. To protect you and your pet: - Report any bite wounds to medical personnel immediately. - Practice safe handling of pets in a stressful situation. - Keep your pet in a carrier or on a leash. - Do not allow your pet to interact with other animals.

Q: Can rabies be cured?
A: Once symptoms show, rabies is almost always fatal, in both people and animals. That's why acting before symptoms appear is so important.

Rabies is fully preventable:
- After a bite or scratch, wash the wound well and get post-exposure prophylaxis at an Animal Bite Treatment Center right away
- Vaccinate your dogs and cats every year

In people, symptoms can appear about one week to one year after exposure, usually after 2 to 3 months. So don't wait to see if you feel sick.

A: She may be choking, so treat this as an emergency and call or go to a vet right away.

What to do now:
- Move your pet away from the source and remove anything left in their mouth, if it's safe to do so.
- Note what they ate, about how much, and when. Bring the packaging, label or a piece of the plant.
- Call your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now and tell them you're on your way.

Q: How often should I bathe my dog or cat?
A: Dogs: The ASPCA suggests a bath at least once every three months. Dogs that spend a lot of time outdoors or have skin problems may need baths more often.

Cats: Most cats keep themselves clean. They only need a bath if they get very dirty or into something sticky or smelly.

Bath tips:
- Brush out loose hair and mats first.
- Use lukewarm water and a shampoo made for pets. Human shampoo can irritate or dry out the skin.
- Keep water out of the eyes, ears and nose. Wipe the face with a damp cloth.
- Rinse well and dry fully, including any skin folds.
- For cats, trim the claws first and use a rubber mat so they don't slip.

See your vet if you notice scabs, bald spots, redness or constant scratching.

Q: My puppy bites and nips a lot. How do I stop it?
A: Mouthing is normal for puppies. The goal is to teach them to be gentle.

- When teeth press hard, give a high-pitched yelp and let your hand go limp. Praise your puppy when they stop.
- If that doesn't work, ignore them for 10 to 20 seconds or walk away, then play again calmly.
- Keep a chew toy or tug toy handy and offer it when they go for your hands or feet.
- Play fetch or tug instead of rough games with your hands.
- Don't jerk your hands away. It invites more grabbing.
- Never hit, slap or shake your puppy. It can make biting worse and cause fear.

Get help from a certified animal behaviorist or veterinary behaviorist if bites come with a stiff body, growling or pulled-back lips, or hurt much more than play bites.

Q: What's the penalty for animal cruelty in the Philippines?
A: Section 9 of the Animal Welfare Act, as amended by RA 10631, sets penalties after conviction:

- Animal dies: 1 year, 6 months and 1 day to 2 years in prison, and/or a fine up to P100,000
- Animal survives but is severely injured and can't survive without human help: 1 year and 1 day to 1 year and 6 months, and/or up to P50,000
- Other cruelty or neglect: 6 months to 1 year, and/or up to P30,000

Penalties go up to 2 years and 1 day to 3 years and/or up to P250,000 if the offense involves a syndicate, a business, a public officer, or 3 or more animals.

Q: How often should I feed my adult dog or cat, and how much?
A: Adult dogs: most do well on 1 or 2 meals a day. The ASPCA suggests two meals, about 8 to 12 hours apart.

Adult cats (from about 1 year old): once or twice a day suits most cats. Leaving food out all day works for some cats, but makes others overeat and gain weight. Replace any food left out with fresh food daily.

How much:
- The amount on the label is based on an average pet. A less active pet may need less.
- Check your pet's body. You should be able to feel the ribs without pressing hard, and see a waist behind the ribs from above.
- If you can't feel the ribs without pressing, there is too much fat. Ask your vet how much to cut back.

Always keep fresh, clean water out.

Q: My dog drank some beer someone left on the table during our party.
A: Alcohol is absorbed quickly and can be dangerous for pets. Call your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now and take him in.

Signs include vomiting, diarrhea, wobbling, sleepiness, trouble breathing and tremors, and in severe cases coma or death.

Before you go:
- Tell the vet what drink it was and roughly how much he had.
- Only make him vomit if a vet tells you to.
- Don't give coffee or anything else to "sober him up". Caffeine is also toxic to pets.

On the way, keep him calm and watch his breathing.

Raw bread dough with yeast can also make alcohol inside the stomach, so keep both drinks and dough out of reach.

Q: My cat isn't eating. How long is too long?
A: Don't wait it out. A cat that stops eating can develop a serious liver problem called hepatic lipidosis (fatty liver). It can be fatal if not treated quickly. Overweight cats are at higher risk.

What to do:
- If your cat hasn't eaten properly for 24 hours, take her to the vet now.
- Go right away if her gums, ears, skin or the whites of her eyes look yellow, or if she is very weak.
- Tell the vet when she last ate and if anything changed at home.

Most cats with fatty liver have another illness that caused the poor appetite, so the vet will look for that too. Fatty liver needs prompt treatment, so don't wait to see if she starts eating again.

Q: How do I get rid of fleas in my house?
A: Most of the flea problem lives in your home, not on your pet. Eggs fall off into carpets, bedding and corners, and flea cocoons can wait there for months.

What helps:
- Treat every dog and cat in the home, not just the itchy one, using products your vet recommends
- Vacuum often
- Wash pet bedding and blankets regularly
- If you use a home spray, keep pets out of the room and follow the label
- Never put a house or yard product directly on a pet

Fleas can live indoors all year, so experts advise year-round flea prevention. It can take weeks to months of steady treatment to fully clear an infestation.

Q: What is heartworm and how does my dog get it?
A: Heartworms are long worms that live in the heart and lung blood vessels. Dogs get them from mosquito bites, which pass on tiny larvae that grow into adult worms over about 6 months. Indoor pets are at risk too, because mosquitoes come inside.

Many dogs show no signs at first. Later signs include:
- A mild cough that won't go away
- Tiring easily or not wanting to exercise
- Weight loss and poor appetite
- A swollen belly

Sudden trouble breathing, collapse or dark brown urine is an emergency. See a vet now.

Experts advise prevention every month of the year and a heartworm test every year. Ask your vet for a preventive that suits your dog's weight and age.

Q: How important is it to get your dog vaccinated for heartworm in India?

Is heartworm common among dogs in India, and is it necessary to get dogs vaccinated against it?
A: The only way dogs get heartworm is through an infected mosquito and India has a lot of mosquitos and you cannot tell if a mosquito is an infected carrier, same problem with mosquitos and dengue fever. Q: How often does my adult dog need booster shots?
A: It depends on the vaccine:
- Distemper, parvovirus and adenovirus: after the puppy series and an early booster (at about 6 months or 1 year old), modern vaccines protect for years. Global guidelines advise boosting no more often than every 3 years.
- Leptospirosis: protection is shorter, so it is usually given every year.
- Rabies: some vaccines last 1 year and some 3 years, but in the Philippines the rules of the Anti-Rabies Act (RA 9482) require a yearly anti-rabies shot.

Your vet will make a booster plan based on your dog's age, health, lifestyle and the products used.

Q: How often does my dog need the anti-rabies shot by law?
A: Every year. Section 5 of RA 9482 says owners must have their dogs "regularly" vaccinated against rabies. The implementing rules make it clearer: a properly immunized dog is one vaccinated yearly, and LGUs register and vaccinate dogs annually.

The shot must be given by a licensed veterinarian, or by a trained vaccinator under a vet's direct supervision during government mass vaccination drives.

Keep the record of each shot on your dog's vaccination or registration card.

Q: My cat is vomiting. Is it just hairballs?
A: Many cats bring up a hairball once every week or two, and that alone is usually not a worry. A hairball is a wet, tube-shaped wad of swallowed hair.

See your vet soon if she:
- Vomits more than once a week
- Seems tired or weak, or eats less
- Has blood in the vomit
- Drinks or pees more or less than usual, or also has diarrhea

Go now if she keeps retching or vomiting with nothing coming up, refuses food for more than a day, or is very weak. A hairball or a swallowed object like string can block the gut, and that can be fatal without surgery.

To help prevent hairballs, comb her coat daily, especially when she sheds. Don't give laxatives or hairball products unless your vet says so.

sources.text:
Snake bite. Venom spreads faster when your pet moves. Keep them still and get to a vet. Signs can be delayed.
Signs: A sudden yelp, swelling, puncture marks; Bleeding that won't stop; Drooling, wide pupils, trembling; Weakness, wobbliness, trouble breathing, collapse
What to do now:
1. Keep yourself safe. Don't try to catch or kill the snake. Take a photo from a distance if it's easy.
2. Keep your pet calm and still, and carry them if you can.
3. Take off the collar if the bite is on the head or neck, because it may swell.
4. Go to the vet now. Call ahead so they can check for antivenom.
Don't: Cutting the wound, sucking out venom, tourniquets or ice. Waiting for signs to appear.
Go to a vet now.

Q: Are chicken bones dangerous for dogs?

I often heard that chicken bones are dangerous for dogs as they may break, splinter and damage the internal organs.

Is there any truth to this claim?
A: Cooked bones can be dangerous for dogs or cats. The cooking dries them out and makes them more likely to splinter.

I've been advised by vets to give dogs and cats raw bones, never cooked. The size of the dog would make a difference, too - a large dog is much more likely to gulp down a chicken bone whole and have it lodge somewhere it shouldn't, where a small dog wouldn't have that issue.

sources.label: Pets Stack Exchange answer
sources.text:
Q: Are rawhide bones or natural raw bones potentially dangerous for a dog? Chewing can be a very rewarding activity for dogs and it also provides mental stimulation and helps clean their teeth. So I'm planning to give a bone to …
A: The biggest danger I'm aware of (aside from possible chewing off a piece bigger than they can chew and choking) is that the rawhide can expand when it gets wet. So when a dog ingests rawhide, it expands either in their stomach, or in their intestines, blocking their normal bodily functions and causing them harm.

Another is a manufacturing issue. Rawhide is made from separated animal skins, a process that is usually done with chemicals that can be harmful to dogs. As long as you make sure to buy trusted brands, you shouldn't have to worry about it though.

Q: What age do cats stop growing on average?

I've heard humans stop growing around age 18-24. What about cats? When do they stop growing in height?
A: There are a couple of growth periods for cats. The first takes about 4 months and takes them into the kitten stage. The second growth period of a kitten takes them from about 4 months to somewhere between 8 and 12 months to adult size depending on the size of the breed. Larger breeds will take longer to reach their adult size versus smaller breeds, but despite having adult size, they're still junior cats, they don't really become adult cats until their 3rd year.

I only mention the two growth stages (which are effectively continuous) because the dietary requirements change.

About Cleaning and Disinfecting Pet Supplies — Using bleach solution
- Clean and scrub with soapy water first to remove dirt. - Rinse with water to remove any remaining dirt and soapy water. - Prepare a diluted household bleach solution by mixing 2 oz (1/4 cup) bleach and 1 gallon water. - Disinfect the item by soaking it in the bleach solution for at least 10 minutes. If the item is too big to soak, wipe it with the bleach solution and leave the solution on for at least 10 minutes. - Rinse with water to remove any remaining bleach solution. - Let the item dry completely (air dry or wipe dry with a clean towel) before letting your pet use it.

A: Strong cleaners can burn the mouth, throat, skin and eyes. Burns from drain cleaners may not hurt at first and can show up hours later. Cats often lick chemicals off their paws. Call your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now and go in.

Before and on the way:
- Don't make your pet vomit. It can cause more burns.
- Ask the vet before giving anything to drink. They may tell you to offer water or milk.
- Rinse skin and paws with lots of water, then wash with mild shampoo.
- If it got in the eyes, flush with water or saline for a long time, ideally while someone else drives.
- Move your pet to fresh air if there are fumes.
- Bring the bottle.

Never mix bleach with ammonia cleaners, as this makes a toxic gas.

New puppy devours food impossibly quick

I rescued a puppy from a local rescue organization recently. The puppy is about 5-8 months old and is a German sheppard doberman mix. I feed him roughly 3 cups of dog food a day broken into 3 meals (breakfast, lunch, and dinner). Breakfast and lunch is a rounded scoop with dinner being a level scoop.

As soon as I put the food down my puppy devours it within <8 seconds. This seems absurdly fast to me but he also does not appear to get sick or have a problem holding it down. He seems to always be hungry but I'm told that is normal.

Yes, this can be normal, especially if the pup is used to having to compete with littermates for access to the food bowl. And dogs tend to eat quickly anyway, as recognized by the idiom "to wolf down a meal".

This may decrease over time as he realizes that nobody is trying to take the food away before he's done eating.

Q: How often should I feed my puppy?
A: Puppies do best with small meals more often while young, then fewer meals as they grow. A common schedule:
- 6 to 12 weeks old: 4 meals a day of puppy food
- 3 to 6 months: 3 meals a day
- 6 to 12 months: 2 meals a day
- Over 12 months: 1 or 2 meals a day of adult food

Use a food made for growing puppies or for all life stages. Adjust the amount based on how your puppy grows, and have your vet check weight and body condition at each visit. Large and giant breeds need careful portions to protect their bones and joints. Keep treats under 10% of daily calories.

Feeding at the same times each day also helps potty training, since puppies often need to go soon after eating.

Q: How do I brush my dog's or cat's teeth?
A: Use a toothpaste made for pets. Never use human toothpaste. It isn't meant to be swallowed and can upset the stomach, and some contain xylitol, which is toxic to dogs.

Steps:
- Start slowly. Rub a finger or soft cloth along the outside of a few teeth, near the gums.
- Let your pet lick a little pet toothpaste from your finger.
- Once they accept that, put toothpaste on the cloth, then move to a finger brush or small, soft toothbrush.
- Brush the outer surfaces at the gumline. Start with the big back teeth and the long fang teeth, where plaque builds up fastest. Aim for about 30 seconds per side.

Brush daily if you can, and at least three times a week. Keep sessions short and calm, and praise your pet.
