sources.text:
Can't pee (blocked bladder). A blocked bladder, most common in male cats, can be fatal within a day or two. It's often mistaken for constipation.
Signs: Straining in the litter box with little or no pee; Going back to the box again and again; Crying while trying to pee, or peeing outside the box; Licking the genitals; vomiting, hiding, low energy
What to do now:
1. Go to the vet now. Tell them when you last saw your pet pee normally.
2. Carry them gently in a carrier.
Don't: Pressing on the belly or bladder. Waiting until the next day.
Go to a vet now.

Q: How often should I feed my adult dog or cat, and how much?
A: Adult dogs: most do well on 1 or 2 meals a day. The ASPCA suggests two meals, about 8 to 12 hours apart.

Adult cats (from about 1 year old): once or twice a day suits most cats. Leaving food out all day works for some cats, but makes others overeat and gain weight. Replace any food left out with fresh food daily.

How much:
- The amount on the label is based on an average pet. A less active pet may need less.
- Check your pet's body. You should be able to feel the ribs without pressing hard, and see a waist behind the ribs from above.
- If you can't feel the ribs without pressing, there is too much fat. Ask your vet how much to cut back.

Always keep fresh, clean water out.

Q: My cat swallowed one of my paracetamol (Biogesic) tablets that fell on the floor.
A: This is an emergency. Paracetamol (acetaminophen) can kill cats, and cats are far more sensitive to it than dogs. Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now. Don't wait for signs.

Signs can start within a few hours:
- Brown or muddy-coloured gums
- Fast or deep breathing, weakness
- Swelling of the face or paws
- Vomiting, or yellow eyes and gums

Before you go:
- Bring the medicine pack and note when it happened and how many tablets may be missing.
- Only make her vomit if a vet tells you to, and don't give milk, food or any other medicine.

On the way, keep her calm in a carrier with good airflow. Keep all medicines where pets can't reach them.

messages.content:
Should I carry my elderly cocker spaniel out of the car?

I own a 13 year old cocker spaniel. I like to drive him around in my 2002 Toyota highlander. I'm worried though, because he has to jump about 2-3 feet down whenever we get out. I think this may damage his joints. He doesn't like being picked up, but he tolerates it. Should I carry him out of the car?

We kept large dogs (GSDs and Labs) for many years. All of them became arthritic in their old age, and getting in and out of vehicles could be a problem. Some of the dogs didn't mind being lifted in and out, but others found that to be painful, especially if you caught a hip joint awkwardly. The solution was simple enough: a ramp made out of a piece of plywood with some carpet glued on for traction. This allowed the dog to get in an out of a vehicle in its own time, and without the risk of being inexpertly handled. You can buy pet ramps if you do not want to make your own, although a box large enough to act as a step may be all that is needed.

messages.content: Blue or pale gums in my cat. Is this serious?

This sounds like it could be choking. Something stuck in the mouth or throat. If your pet is still breathing and coughing, go to the vet. Only step in if they can't breathe.

What to do now:
- Stay calm and hold them gently but firmly. A choking pet may bite.
- Open the mouth and look. If you can see the object and get a grip on it, remove it carefully with fingers or tweezers.
- If you can't remove it and they can't breathe: hold a cat or small dog with their back against your chest and give 5 firm thrusts inward and upward just below the ribs.
- For a large dog, put your arms around the belly from behind, make a fist just below the ribs and push firmly up and forward 5 times. If they're lying down, push from behind the ribs toward the head.
- Check the mouth again and repeat. If they collapse and stop breathing, start CPR.
- Go to the vet even if the object comes out. The throat may be injured.

Don't:
- Sweeping your fingers blindly. It can push the object deeper.
- Pulling on string, thread or tinsel hanging from the mouth or bottom. It can cut the intestines.

Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now.

sources.label: FurFriends first-aid guide: Bloat (twisted stomach)
sources.text:
Bloat (twisted stomach). The stomach fills with gas and can twist. It can kill within hours and usually needs surgery. Most common in large, deep-chested dogs.
Signs: Swollen, tight belly; Retching or trying to vomit with nothing coming up; Restless, pacing, can't get comfortable; Drooling, pale gums, collapse
What to do now:
1. Go to the vet immediately. Call ahead so they can prepare.
2. Keep your dog as calm and still as you can on the way.
Don't: Waiting to see if it passes. Giving food, water or home remedies. Trying to make them vomit.
Go to a vet now.

Q: My dog is vomiting. Can I treat him at home?
A: One vomit in a dog that otherwise seems well is often not serious, and many cases settle within a day. But vomiting can also be a sign of poisoning, a blockage or other illness.

Go to the vet right away if he vomits and also has:
- Blood in the vomit
- Diarrhea, belly pain or fever
- Low energy, no appetite or signs of dehydration
- A chance he swallowed something toxic or an object

See your vet today if vomiting goes on for more than 24 hours, even if he seems fine.

For a mild case, your vet may suggest resting the stomach for a short time, then small, frequent meals of a bland food. Keep fresh water available. Don't give human medicines unless your vet tells you to.

sources.label: FurFriends first-aid guide: Hit by a vehicle or fall
sources.text:
Hit by a vehicle or fall. Internal bleeding and chest injuries may not show at first. Pets that fall from balconies or windows need a vet check too.
Signs: Limping, not putting weight on a leg; Fast breathing, pale gums; Swelling belly, bleeding from the nose or mouth; Seems fine but was hit or fell. Still go.
What to do now:
1. Make sure you're safe from traffic first.
2. Approach slowly and speak softly. Hurt animals bite, so use a towel or muzzle unless they're vomiting or struggling to breathe.
3. Move them as little as possible. Slide a large dog onto a board or blanket to use as a stretcher, keeping the back and neck straight. Put small pets in a box or carrier.
4. Press on any bleeding, keep them calm, and go to the vet now.
Don't: Giving any painkiller. Trying to straighten or splint a leg. Giving food or water.
Go to a vet now.

sources.label: FurFriends first-aid guide: Toad poisoning
sources.text:
Toad poisoning. Cane toads, the large brown toads that come out after rain, release a poison when a dog or cat bites or licks them.
Signs: Sudden heavy drooling or foaming at the mouth; Pawing at the mouth, shaking the head; Bright red gums; Vomiting, wobbliness, a racing heartbeat, seizures
What to do now:
1. Rinse the mouth straight away. Point the head down and run a gentle stream of water across the gums and tongue from the side, so it flows out of the mouth. Keep going for 10 minutes.
2. Wipe the gums and tongue with a damp cloth to remove the sticky poison.
3. Go to the vet now, especially if there's anything more than drooling.
Don't: Spraying water down the throat. It can go into the lungs. Making them vomit.
Go to a vet now.

Q: What are the signs of rabies in a dog or cat?
A: The DOH lists these signs of rabies in animals:

- Change in behavior
- Aggressive behavior
- Excessive drooling
- Paralysis
- Fear of water

You can't confirm rabies just by looking at an animal; only a lab test can. If your pet shows these signs, keep away from its saliva, keep it confined, and call your vet or city or municipal veterinary office right away. If it bit or scratched anyone, they should go to an Animal Bite Treatment Center.

Q: A stray dog bit my dog. Should I worry about rabies?
A: Rabies spreads mainly through bites and scratches. Once signs appear, it is almost always fatal, so act quickly.

For your dog:
- Wear gloves and wash the wound with soap and water
- Call your vet today, even if your dog is vaccinated. Your vet will check the wound and advise what to do next

For people: if you or a family member is bitten or scratched, wash the wound right away with soap and water and see a doctor urgently. Treatment after exposure works very well when started early.

Worldwide, dogs cause most human rabies deaths. Keeping your pets' rabies vaccines up to date protects them and your family.

sources.text:
Stings & allergic reactions. Bee, wasp, ant and centipede stings usually cause swelling that settles. A spreading reaction or trouble breathing is an emergency.
Signs: Mild: swelling and pain where they were stung, licking the spot; Go now: the face swells and keeps spreading, or hives all over the body; Go now: vomiting, diarrhea, pale gums, weakness or collapse; Go now: trouble breathing, a sting inside the mouth or throat, or many stings
What to do now:
1. Move away from the insects.
2. If you see a bee stinger, scrape it out sideways with a card. Don't squeeze it.
3. Hold a cold pack wrapped in cloth on the spot for 10 minutes.
4. Watch closely for the next 1â€“2 hours and call your vet for advice.
Don't: Giving human allergy or cold tablets without a vet's dose. Some contain decongestants that are toxic to pets.
Call your vet for advice.

Q: How do I brush my dog's or cat's teeth?
A: Use a toothpaste made for pets. Never use human toothpaste. It isn't meant to be swallowed and can upset the stomach, and some contain xylitol, which is toxic to dogs.

Steps:
- Start slowly. Rub a finger or soft cloth along the outside of a few teeth, near the gums.
- Let your pet lick a little pet toothpaste from your finger.
- Once they accept that, put toothpaste on the cloth, then move to a finger brush or small, soft toothbrush.
- Brush the outer surfaces at the gumline. Start with the big back teeth and the long fang teeth, where plaque builds up fastest. Aim for about 30 seconds per side.

Brush daily if you can, and at least three times a week. Keep sessions short and calm, and praise your pet.

Q: How much water should my pet drink, and how do I spot dehydration?
A: Keep fresh, clean water out at all times, in places your pet can easily reach. Cats that eat wet food often drink less, because the food is mostly water. Cats on dry food need to drink more.

Signs of dehydration:
- Dry or sticky gums
- Skin that stays "tented" when you gently lift it at the back of the neck, instead of snapping back
- Sunken eyes, weakness, low energy or poor appetite

Vomiting and diarrhea can cause dehydration fast. Call your vet today if you think your pet is dehydrated. Go now if they haven't eaten or drunk anything for 24 hours, or are very weak.

Drinking much more than usual also needs a vet visit within a day. It can be a sign of kidney disease, diabetes or other illness.

Q: My cat is sneezing and has runny eyes. Is it cat flu?
A: It may be an upper respiratory infection, often called cat flu. Viruses like feline herpesvirus and calicivirus are common causes, and they spread easily between cats. Signs include sneezing, runny eyes or nose, mouth sores, tiredness and poor appetite.

What helps:
- Gently wipe her nose clean. A blocked nose can stop her smelling food, so she may eat less.
- Make sure she keeps eating and drinking.

See your vet within 24 hours if the sneezing doesn't stop. Go now if she:
- Has trouble breathing, or her gums look bluish
- Hasn't eaten properly for 24 hours
- Is a kitten. Young cats are more likely to get seriously ill.

Vaccines can make these infections milder.

Q: What's the penalty for animal cruelty in the Philippines?
A: Section 9 of the Animal Welfare Act, as amended by RA 10631, sets penalties after conviction:

- Animal dies: 1 year, 6 months and 1 day to 2 years in prison, and/or a fine up to P100,000
- Animal survives but is severely injured and can't survive without human help: 1 year and 1 day to 1 year and 6 months, and/or up to P50,000
- Other cruelty or neglect: 6 months to 1 year, and/or up to P30,000

Penalties go up to 2 years and 1 day to 3 years and/or up to P250,000 if the offense involves a syndicate, a business, a public officer, or 3 or more animals.

Q: What are my legal responsibilities as a dog owner in the Philippines?
A: Section 5 of RA 9482 lists the duties of pet owners:

- Have your dog vaccinated against rabies regularly and keep a registration card with its vaccination records
- Register your dog with the LGU
- Don't let your dog roam public places without a leash
- Give your dog proper grooming, food and shelter
- Report any bite within 24 hours and have the dog observed by a vet
- Help the bite victim right away and pay for their medical costs

Breaking these rules can lead to fines under Section 11.

Q: My dog keeps shaking his head and scratching his ears. What's wrong?
A: This is a common sign of an ear infection. Other signs are red ears, a bad smell, dark or yellowish discharge, and pain when you touch the ear. Allergies are often behind it, and dogs with floppy or hairy ears get them more often.

See your vet within 24 hours. The vet needs to look at the ear canal and eardrum and find the cause before choosing a treatment. Some ear medicines can cause hearing loss if the eardrum is torn, so don't use leftover or store-bought drops on your own.

Go now if he is in severe pain. Go today if the ear flap suddenly swells up. Left untreated, ear infections can damage the eardrum and cause lasting hearing loss.

Q: What vaccines does my kitten need?
A: Most kittens get these core vaccines:
- FVRCP (cat flu and panleukopenia), usually starting at 6 to 8 weeks and repeated every 3 to 4 weeks until about 16 weeks
- Rabies, given from around 12 weeks, which is required in the Philippines

Your vet may also suggest FeLV if your kitten will go outdoors or live with other cats. Keep the vaccine card, and add each shot in FurFriends so you get reminders for boosters.

Q: I just got a new kitten. What should I do first?
A: Take your kitten to a vet as soon as you can. Ask where you got her about any vaccines, deworming and food she has had.

- Vet visits: kittens usually see the vet every 3 to 4 weeks until about 6 months old, for shots and parasite treatment.
- Vaccines: the core kitten shots start at about 6 to 8 weeks and are repeated every 3 to 4 weeks until 16 to 20 weeks old.
- Deworming: worms are very common in kittens, so many vets deworm them routinely.
- Testing: a kitten with an unknown history should be tested for FeLV and FIV. Keep her apart from your other cats until the vet has checked her.
- Feeding: use kitten food, given several times a day.
- Litter box: one per cat, plus one extra, kept clean.

Q: My female cat hisses and pins down my kitten before licking her and cuddling her? I got a kitten a few weeks ago. At first my older female was unhappy with it of course, but no severe fighting, just a …
A: Cats hiss to intimidate another into not attacking, and pinning a cat stops any attack physically plus establishes dominance.

It’s possible your older female is still a bit nervous around the kitten; it’s another predator in “her” territory, after all, plus kittens tend to be rather energetic and “attack” their siblings and mothers as a form of play. So, she is making it clear to the kitten this is grooming time, not playtime. Once the kitten calms down and/or develops a better sense of when she is willing to play, the hissing and pinning will probably stop.

Q: Does my indoor cat need vaccines?
A: Yes. The American Association of Feline Practitioners recommends core vaccines even for cats that never go outside. Core vaccines for cats cover:
- Panleukopenia (feline distemper)
- Herpesvirus
- Calicivirus
(these three come together as FVRCP)
- Rabies, where the disease is present or the law requires it

Feline leukemia (FeLV) vaccine is advised for kittens under 1 year. For adults it depends on risk, such as going outdoors or living with cats that do.

Good news for indoor cats: global guidelines say low-risk indoor adults usually need core boosters only every 3 years or longer.

Your vet will choose the vaccines and timing that fit your cat.

- Panleukopenia (feline distemper)
- Herpesvirus
- Calicivirus

- Rabies, where the disease is present or the law requires it

Feline leukemia (FeLV) vaccine is advised for kittens under 1 year. For adults it depends on risk, such as going outdoors or living with cats that do.

Good news for indoor cats: global guidelines say low-risk indoor adults usually need core boosters only every 3 years or longer.

Your vet will choose the vaccines and timing that fit your cat.

Q: Why is my cat peeing outside the litter box?
A: First, have your vet rule out a medical problem. Peeing outside the box can be a sign of a bladder problem.

Go to the vet now if your cat strains in the box with little or no pee coming out, cries while peeing, or is vomiting or very tired. A blocked bladder can kill, and male cats are most at risk.

- Scoop daily, and change all the litter weekly

Q: My cat isn't eating. How long is too long?
A: Don't wait it out. A cat that stops eating can develop a serious liver problem called hepatic lipidosis (fatty liver). It can be fatal if not treated quickly. Overweight cats are at higher risk.

What to do:
- If your cat hasn't eaten properly for 24 hours, take her to the vet now.

messages.content:
Is it safe to take a small (such as a Robo or Chinese) hamster in airplane, or can they "explode"?

I am planning to fly from USA to Hong Kong and wanted to take my small Chinese hamster with me. My understanding is that a hamster would probably have to ride in the cargo hold with other animals (dogs, etc.).

But I was told by a friend that very small animals like the Chinese or Roborovski hamsters are unable to deal with the cabin pressure (or lack thereof) in airplanes. What that friend told me made it look like as if the hamster might explode.

This sounds like an urban myth to me but is it correct? Is it safe to take hamsters on an airplane, or should I instead try to find someone to take care of it here while I am abroad?

Explosion is obviously an urban legend.

I never heard of such a thing before. But Roborovski hamsters are adapted to similar pressures as humans and other mammals so there is no reason to assume that slightly lower pressure in airplanes might cause anything more than a discomfort to hamsters.

Hamsters have a very high rate of metabolism so you need to put some food in its enclosure during a long flight. Hamsters also have a very low tolerance to drafts and low temperatures so if you need to carry them in the luggage compartment, you need to include some bedding, like paper tissues.

The problem with carrying hamsters is that most airways assume that all hamsters are rodents which are capable of gnawing their way from their compartments and damage the plane. Therefore, however small the hamster is, most airways will reject carrying the hamster so make sure that you can carry them on your journey.

Q: How often should I feed my puppy?
A: Puppies do best with small meals more often while young, then fewer meals as they grow. A common schedule:
- 6 to 12 weeks old: 4 meals a day of puppy food
- 3 to 6 months: 3 meals a day
- 6 to 12 months: 2 meals a day
- Over 12 months: 1 or 2 meals a day of adult food

Use a food made for growing puppies or for all life stages. Adjust the amount based on how your puppy grows, and have your vet check weight and body condition at each visit. Large and giant breeds need careful portions to protect their bones and joints. Keep treats under 10% of daily calories.

Feeding at the same times each day also helps potty training, since puppies often need to go soon after eating.

Q: Is it legal to sell or eat dog meat in the Philippines?
A: No. RA 9482 bans the trade of dog meat. LGUs must enforce this ban (Section 7).

Under Section 11, anyone caught trading dog meat faces a fine of at least P5,000 per dog and 1 to 4 years in prison. The same penalty applies to using electrocution to put dogs to sleep. Foreigners who break these rules are deported after serving their sentence.

Killing dogs for food is also not among the allowed reasons for killing animals under the Animal Welfare Act (RA 8485, Section 6).

Snake bite. Venom spreads faster when your pet moves. Keep them still and get to a vet. Signs can be delayed.
Signs: A sudden yelp, swelling, puncture marks; Bleeding that won't stop; Drooling, wide pupils, trembling; Weakness, wobbliness, trouble breathing, collapse

2. Keep your pet calm and still, and carry them if you can.
3. Take off the collar if the bite is on the head or neck, because it may swell.
4. Go to the vet now. Call ahead so they can check for antivenom.
Don't: Cutting the wound, sucking out venom, tourniquets or ice. Waiting for signs to appear.

Q: How often should I feed my adult dog or cat, and how much?
A: Adult dogs: most do well on 1 or 2 meals a day. The ASPCA suggests two meals, about 8 to 12 hours apart.

Q: I saw little white things like rice in my cat's poop. What is it?
A: Those are most likely tapeworm segments. They look like grains of rice or sesame seeds and may be stuck to the fur near the tail or in the poop. Cats usually get tapeworms by swallowing fleas while grooming or by eating mice or rats.

Other worm signs include:
- Vomiting or diarrhea
- A dull coat or potbelly, mostly in kittens
- Weight loss

See a vet today if you notice black, tarry poop, pale gums or weakness. Heavy hookworm or roundworm loads can cause serious blood loss, especially in kittens.

Bring a fresh stool sample to your vet. Treat for fleas too, or the tapeworms will come back.

What should I do to make my cat active?

As my cat is growing up, she is becoming so lazy. She just eats and sleeps. She does not even play with her toys anymore. She is 3 year old. Please help me. What should I do to make her active?

It's perfectly normal for cats to lose their playfulness as they age. Human adults don't spend their afternoon running in the garden the same way a child does either.

While there can be medical/ulterior reasons for a cat's behavior to change, including playfulness; your question doesn't give me any reason to assume that this is the case. 3 years sounds about the right age to no longer be playful the way a kitten is.

If the change in behavior was incredibly sudden, you can take her to a vet to make sure.

Other than that, try to provide toys and playtimes that you know she used to like (or buy new ones - depends on the cat's personality), but in the end it's the cat's choice whether she still wants to play or not.

messages.content:
How do can you tell if your cat is hurting?

I have 2 cats around the same age as each other, but sometimes their play gets a bit too rough, and my sisters cat (the elder one) will hurt the younger, and he will get cuts that bleed. Is my cat really hurting, or is it just a shallow cut, and what should i do about it.

Cats hide pain. It's instinctive. The cat that shows pain, in the wild, is the cat the predators attack first. Being that cat is not a good survival strategy. In fact, if a cat is showing outward signs of pain, it can be an indication it has given up, or that the pain is extremely serious- in either case, get to the vet.

If the cat is not showing pain, it is really hard to know whether it actually is feeling pain. Treat the wound like you would for a child that came in from playing in the yard crying because he fell and skinned his elbow. If the cat will let you, that is. Do your best to determine the severity by spreading the fur and seeing the length and depth of the cut. Apply direct pressure with a (non-adhesive) gauze pad until the bleeding is completely stopped.

As always, when in doubt- vet.

Q: How do I get rid of fleas in my house?
A: Most of the flea problem lives in your home, not on your pet. Eggs fall off into carpets, bedding and corners, and flea cocoons can wait there for months.

What helps:
- Treat every dog and cat in the home, not just the itchy one, using products your vet recommends
- Vacuum often
- Wash pet bedding and blankets regularly
- If you use a home spray, keep pets out of the room and follow the label
- Never put a house or yard product directly on a pet

Fleas can live indoors all year, so experts advise year-round flea prevention. It can take weeks to months of steady treatment to fully clear an infestation.

Q: How often does my adult dog need booster shots?
A: It depends on the vaccine:
- Distemper, parvovirus and adenovirus: after the puppy series and an early booster (at about 6 months or 1 year old), modern vaccines protect for years. Global guidelines advise boosting no more often than every 3 years.
- Leptospirosis: protection is shorter, so it is usually given every year.
- Rabies: some vaccines last 1 year and some 3 years, but in the Philippines the rules of the Anti-Rabies Act (RA 9482) require a yearly anti-rabies shot.

Your vet will make a booster plan based on your dog's age, health, lifestyle and the products used.

Q: When does my puppy start his shots, and why so many?
A: Puppies usually get their first core vaccine at 6 to 8 weeks old. Shots are then repeated every 2 to 4 weeks until the puppy is at least 16 weeks old.

Why a series? Antibodies from the mother's milk protect a young puppy, but they also block vaccines from working. These antibodies fade at a different age in each puppy, so repeat shots make sure one of them "takes". The dose given at 16 weeks or later is the most important.

Global guidelines also advise another core dose at around 6 months old instead of waiting until 1 year, to catch puppies that did not respond earlier.

Your vet will set the exact schedule for your puppy.

Why does my dog wipe his paws on the grass after he poops?

After he does his business, my dog sometimes wipes his (usually rear) paws on the grass. I heard this was to spread his scent in the area, but I figured the result of doing his business did enough of the "scenting". He does this more often when unleashed in our yard than when leashed on a walk.

Why does he scrape the grass with his paws?

The behavior in wolves is known as "scrape behavior"; it is also present in their domesticated relatives.

According to Canine Behavior: Insights and Answers (Bonnie V. Beaver) the activity is commonly seen to be a visual marking, the scrapes, as well as a means of spreading scent to mark territory (as noted, dogs have scent glands in their paws). This activity happens most often in new areas, in the presence of other dogs, and in the early mornings. (Chapter 8, page 251).

It is possible to train your dog out of this behavior if you so desire. Basically, it involves distracting him immediately after his activity with something like a treat in order to get him out of the habit.

Q: My dog or cat has diarrhea. When do I need a vet?
A: Mild diarrhea in an adult pet that is still bright and eating can sometimes be watched at home for a short time.

Home care:
- Always keep fresh water out. Diarrhea can quickly cause dehydration.
- Ask your vet about a short rest for the stomach, or small meals of a bland or gut-friendly diet.
- When the stool firms up, switch back to the usual food slowly over about a week.

See your vet if it lasts more than 24 hours.

Go now if there is:
- Blood in the stool, or black, tarry stool
- Vomiting, weakness, fever, belly pain or no appetite
- Diarrhea in a puppy. It can be an early sign of parvo, which can be deadly.
- Straining with nothing coming out

Q: My cat isn't eating. How long is too long?
A: Don't wait it out. A cat that stops eating can develop a serious liver problem called hepatic lipidosis (fatty liver). It can be fatal if not treated quickly. Overweight cats are at higher risk.

What to do:
- If your cat hasn't eaten properly for 24 hours, take her to the vet now.
- Go right away if her gums, ears, skin or the whites of her eyes look yellow, or if she is very weak.
- Tell the vet when she last ate and if anything changed at home.

Most cats with fatty liver have another illness that caused the poor appetite, so the vet will look for that too. Fatty liver needs prompt treatment, so don't wait to see if she starts eating again.

messages.content:
How to ensure that while in a rough play session with my cat, the cat never gets distracted to any other human and starts to play rough with them?

I thoroughly enjoy rough play with my cat, and I encourage her to play rough with me. But everybody else in my home dislikes it.

It often happens that while I am in a rough play session with my cat, and another human passes nearby, she jumps to that human and starts playing rough, only to get severely scolded.

But when she is not deeply engaged in a play session she perfectly knows that she is allowed to play rough only with me and nobody else.

So is there any way to ensure that, even when the cat is deeply engaged in a play session with me, she does not forget that she is forbidden to play rough with anybody else?

Cats will learn the behavior of humans they often interact with - but they learn through trial and error. Not every cat will learn as fast, some may need a lot of repetition before they get the hint.

As long as you are always open for rough plays and the others always tell her off (or refuse to engage her), it will become apparent who does/doesn't allow for rough plays.

You can intervene here too. When you see the cat move on to someone else, catch their attention to redirect them to you. They may fail to do so initially, but the added reminder may speed up the process of them learning to only play rough with you.

Very young cats may simply be too excitable, to a point where they're not really able to adapt their playstyle to the human they're interacting with. That's not really misbehavior on their part, but rather an inability to assess the situation.

Dog too scared to come inside after incident

I'm new to this site.

I have a question: my baby (my dog) got her tail caught in the screen door and she has been injuried, resulting in a wound. Now she is scared to come inside or to come near me and I don't know how to help her.

How should I resolve this issue?

Best suggestion I've got:

Re-introduce yourself as you would to a Dog you've never seen before and that isn't sure it trusts you.Go outside, sit down, and give her a chance to come to you, with lots of space to retreat so she doesn't feel threatened. When she eventually does so, don't grab at her; make clear that you're happy to see her, possibly offer her a treat or two. Let her convince herself that you didn't mean to hurt her and she's still "your baby".

Then see if she can be persuaded to follow you back inside.

If she's willing to accept you as Mommy again, it'll be a lot easier to examine the wound, clean it, and if it's at all serious take her to the vet.

So, almost daily, my cat looks at me as if he's been starving for 25 days straight (but it's actually been hours at most), looking at me with huge eyes, making a pathetic "meow" sound to really make me feel sorry for him and give him fresh, high-quality food which he appears very excited about.

Then he eats two bites and goes away.

This happens again and again. You can never tell when he's just "begging for fun" or truly is hungry.

Why would a cat beg for food like this when he's clearly not hungry?

Please don't respond with "cats are just jerks" because that doesn't explain anything. I don't think my cat is "evil". He must have a reason for this.

Is s/he eating enough through the day? If not, there could be a problem in his/her mouth or gullet that makes it painful to eat. If s/he isn't eating well, then this is a medical emergency and you should book a vets' appointment ASAP

messages.content:
Why do dogs lick faces?

Why do dogs lick people and other dogs in their faces?

Domesticated dogs inherited this trait primarily from wolves, and more specifically, wolf pups. Wolf pups will lick the faces of their mother to try and induce her to vomit some of her last meal. For a weaning pup this is far easier for them to digest and eat than meat and bones right from a carcass.

Source

Part of the selective breeding that went into creating the domesticated dog species thousands of years ago involved breeding of more timid wolves and wolves that exhibited more puppy like behavior. Most adult wolves would have an untenable and difficult relationship with humans so a more fitting companion to a human would be a wolf that is less aggressive and more willing to follow the human pack.

Other wolf puppy behaviors that dogs carried is play. Adult wolves rarely play while wolf pups play consistently as a means of learning.

Q: How often should I deworm my puppy?
A: Puppies pick up worms easily, so they're dewormed more often than adults. A common schedule is:
- Every 2 weeks from about 2 weeks old until 12 weeks
- Then monthly until 6 months old
- Then every 3 months for adults

Your vet will choose the right product and dose for your puppy's weight, so ask them before giving anything. Keep the yard clean and treat fleas too, since fleas can spread tapeworm.

Q: I just got a new puppy. What should I do first?
A: Book a vet visit soon. Your puppy will need a series of shots and deworming.

- Vaccines: puppies get shots every 2 to 3 weeks until they are about 4 months old. Your vet will set the exact schedule.
- Until the shots are done, keep your puppy away from dogs that may not be vaccinated.
- Deworming: worms are common in puppies. Your vet may deworm and check stool samples every 2 to 4 weeks until two tests in a row are clear.
- Feeding: puppies 6 to 12 weeks old usually eat 4 small meals a day of puppy food.
- Potty training: start early. Take the puppy out often and praise them when they go outside.
- Socializing: let them meet people and other animals gently, especially at 2 to 4 months old.

Q: When do we need cat nets on window?

Sometimes I see windows with a cat net installed on it. How are they used? When should I consider using a cat net?
A: Any fall over 10 feet/4 meters could be dangerous to a cat. (Websearch "feline high-rise syndrome" for statistics). Cats may be OK above that, or may be at risk below that, but that's the point at which I would start worrying. (A past cat almost stuck her landing from 15', but banged her jaw on the ground and broke it.)

As with kids, the risk depends in part on how careful the cat is or isn't, but sudden wind gusts or a misstep are always a risk.

Insect screens aren't adequate to protect kids, but can do a decent job of protecting most cats, and are probably more useful and more attractive than netting...?

Q: Why does my cat knock over her water dish? I just adopted a cute little 1 year old and one of the first things I noticed when I brought her home is that she liked to knock over her water …
A: Cats in the wild prefer running water. Still water can have leaves and scum on it, so cats learn to clear the surface with a paw. Those where this instinct is strong can make a big mess.

A good way is to replace a water dish with a recirculating fountain to create a permanent stream. This will also encourage your cat to drink, which can help fight kidney disease in later life.

Q: Why does my cat prefer to stand on her back legs to drink water? My cat has her designated water bowl, but for some reason, she largely prefers to drink from a 30 cm (12 in) tall water buckets around …
A: Yes, this kind of behavior is normal for cats and dogs, but it has nothing to with standing on their hind legs.

See, the water in the bucket simply tastes different. It may have a different source (rain water instead of tap water) and a different chemistry due to standing outside for days compared to comming fresh out of a water pipe. It's actually common for pets to prefer "old" water over fresh tap water.

Another reason for this behavior could be the container itself. Whether your cats water bowl is made of plastic or metal, it can influence the smell and taste of the water.

Q: My cat is shedding so much! What to do?

My cat sheds so much, so I can't even pet her! Then there's cat hair everywhere! Can I do a homemade cleaner, or something like that?
A: If you brush or comb the cat (which many cats enjoy, if done gently), that will gather a lot of the loose fur, and leave her looking and feeling silkier too. Of course you and the immediate surroundings are going to get rather furred in the process, though doing this often caN limit how much is scattered at a time.

But a furry pet sheds fur. Some breeds shed less, or less obviously, but realistically if you can't cope with this then keeping a pet may not be appropriate for your lifestyle.

Q: How should I decide between a collar and a harness for a dog? Of all of the dogs that have been part of my family, we have only used collars for leashing. We've never had any negative experiences with them, …
A: A harness just puts the pressure of the leash around the strongest part of your dog's body. So, while the harness would technically be more comfortable for the dog, it will be less comfortable for you. A harness will help your dog control you better, rather than the control you're looking for.

The long-term solution is to train your dog not to pull on the leash. The ASPCA has lots of good guidance on that. Leash pulling is not necessarily a permanent behavior, regardless of whether you're using a collar or harness. It's possible to train it away, and that's the best solution.

A: Pets and the elderly are almost always a good combination, but a kitten may not be the best choice. Kittens tend to have more energy then their elderly companions, this can be problematic. Q: Lily pollen got on my cat's fur and she drank water from the flower vase. Is she in danger?
A: Yes, treat this as an emergency. For cats, every part of true lilies and daylilies is poisonous, including the pollen and the vase water. Even a small amount licked off the fur can cause deadly kidney failure. Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now.

Early treatment makes a big difference. Waiting 18 hours or more often leads to kidney damage that can't be reversed.

Before you go:
- Wipe the pollen off her fur with a damp cloth so she can't lick more.
- Bring the flower or a photo so the vet can identify it.
- Only make her vomit if a vet tells you to.

She may look fine at first. Early signs include drooling, vomiting, low energy and not eating. Keep lilies out of homes with cats.

Q: My dog got hit by a motorcycle but he's walking and seems okay. Does he still need a vet?
A: Yes. Please take him to a vet now, even if he looks fine. Some injuries don't show their full effects for a day or two, and pale gums, fast breathing or weakness can be signs of shock or internal bleeding.

To get him there safely:
- Be careful, because a hurt dog may bite. Use a cloth muzzle only if he is breathing normally and has no chest injury.
- If he can't walk well, slide him onto a firm, flat surface like a board or folded blanket, and keep his head, neck and back as still as possible.
- Keep him calm and quiet, and have someone else drive.

Call your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic as you leave so they're ready for him.

Q: What's the penalty for animal cruelty in the Philippines?
A: Section 9 of the Animal Welfare Act, as amended by RA 10631, sets penalties after conviction:

- Animal dies: 1 year, 6 months and 1 day to 2 years in prison, and/or a fine up to P100,000
- Animal survives but is severely injured and can't survive without human help: 1 year and 1 day to 1 year and 6 months, and/or up to P50,000
- Other cruelty or neglect: 6 months to 1 year, and/or up to P30,000

Penalties go up to 2 years and 1 day to 3 years and/or up to P250,000 if the offense involves a syndicate, a business, a public officer, or 3 or more animals.

Vets use a 9-point body condition score (BCS) from WSAVA. You can do a quick check at home:
- Ribs: Run your hands along the sides. At a healthy weight you can feel the ribs under a thin layer of fat. If you can't feel them without pressing, there is too much fat.
- Waist: Look down from above. You should see a waist behind the ribs.
- Belly: From the side, a dog's belly should tuck up. A cat at a healthy weight has only a small fat pad on the belly.

Signs of overweight are ribs that are hard to feel, no waist, a rounded belly, and fat over the lower back (and in dogs, the base of the tail).

Ideal is 4 to 5 out of 9 for dogs and 5 out of 9 for cats. Ask your vet to score your pet and plan safe weight loss.

Q: My dog or cat has bad breath. What causes it?
A: A healthy pet's breath should not smell bad. The most common cause is dental disease. Plaque and tartar build up on the teeth and inflame the gums, and the bacteria make the smell.

Bad breath can also point to other illness:
- Sweet or fruity smell: possible diabetes
- Urine-like smell: possible kidney disease
- Foul smell with vomiting, poor appetite or yellow gums: possible liver problems

What to do:
- Have your vet check bad breath that doesn't go away. A proper cleaning is done under anesthesia.
- Go sooner if you also see red or swollen gums, more drinking and peeing, weight loss, or poor appetite.

Q: My old pet has really bad breath. Is that dental disease?
A: Often, yes. Gum disease is very common in older pets, especially small dogs. Signs include:
- Bad breath that doesn't go away
- Red or swollen gums
- Trouble picking up, chewing or swallowing food

Bad breath can also point to other illness. A sweet smell may mean diabetes, and a urine-like smell may mean kidney disease.

See your vet for a mouth check. Proper cleaning below the gumline needs anesthesia. Vets check older pets carefully first, and treating mouth pain often makes them much happier.

At home, brush your pet's teeth with pet toothpaste, never human toothpaste. See a vet soon if your pet stops eating or has a lump in the mouth.

Q: What are my legal responsibilities as a dog owner in the Philippines?
A: Section 5 of RA 9482 lists the duties of pet owners:

- Have your dog vaccinated against rabies regularly and keep a registration card with its vaccination records
- Register your dog with the LGU
- Don't let your dog roam public places without a leash
- Give your dog proper grooming, food and shelter
- Report any bite within 24 hours and have the dog observed by a vet
- Help the bite victim right away and pay for their medical costs

Breaking these rules can lead to fines under Section 11.

Q: How often should I feed my puppy?
A: Puppies do best with small meals more often while young, then fewer meals as they grow. A common schedule:
- 6 to 12 weeks old: 4 meals a day of puppy food
- 3 to 6 months: 3 meals a day
- 6 to 12 months: 2 meals a day
- Over 12 months: 1 or 2 meals a day of adult food

Use a food made for growing puppies or for all life stages. Adjust the amount based on how your puppy grows, and have your vet check weight and body condition at each visit. Large and giant breeds need careful portions to protect their bones and joints. Keep treats under 10% of daily calories.

Feeding at the same times each day also helps potty training, since puppies often need to go soon after eating.

Q: My dog or cat has diarrhea. When do I need a vet?
A: Mild diarrhea in an adult pet that is still bright and eating can sometimes be watched at home for a short time.

Home care:
- Always keep fresh water out. Diarrhea can quickly cause dehydration.
- Ask your vet about a short rest for the stomach, or small meals of a bland or gut-friendly diet.
- When the stool firms up, switch back to the usual food slowly over about a week.

See your vet if it lasts more than 24 hours.

Go now if there is:
- Blood in the stool, or black, tarry stool
- Vomiting, weakness, fever, belly pain or no appetite
- Diarrhea in a puppy. It can be an early sign of parvo, which can be deadly.
- Straining with nothing coming out

Q: How do I brush my dog's or cat's teeth?
A: Use a toothpaste made for pets. Never use human toothpaste. It isn't meant to be swallowed and can upset the stomach, and some contain xylitol, which is toxic to dogs.

Steps:
- Start slowly. Rub a finger or soft cloth along the outside of a few teeth, near the gums.
- Let your pet lick a little pet toothpaste from your finger.
- Once they accept that, put toothpaste on the cloth, then move to a finger brush or small, soft toothbrush.
- Brush the outer surfaces at the gumline. Start with the big back teeth and the long fang teeth, where plaque builds up fastest. Aim for about 30 seconds per side.

Brush daily if you can, and at least three times a week. Keep sessions short and calm, and praise your pet.

What to do now:
1. Stop them rubbing it. Use a cone collar or hold their paws.
2. Chemicals: flush the eye with sterile saline or clean, lukewarm water for 10â€“15 minutes.
3. Eye out of its socket: keep it moist with a clean cloth soaked in saline and go straight away.

sources.label: FurFriends first-aid guide: Toad poisoning
sources.text:
Toad poisoning. Cane toads, the large brown toads that come out after rain, release a poison when a dog or cat bites or licks them.
Signs: Sudden heavy drooling or foaming at the mouth; Pawing at the mouth, shaking the head; Bright red gums; Vomiting, wobbliness, a racing heartbeat, seizures
What to do now:
1. Rinse the mouth straight away. Point the head down and run a gentle stream of water across the gums and tongue from the side, so it flows out of the mouth. Keep going for 10 minutes.
2. Wipe the gums and tongue with a damp cloth to remove the sticky poison.
3. Go to the vet now, especially if there's anything more than drooling.
Don't: Spraying water down the throat. It can go into the lungs. Making them vomit.
Go to a vet now.

Q: My cat is sneezing and has runny eyes. Is it cat flu?
A: It may be an upper respiratory infection, often called cat flu. Viruses like feline herpesvirus and calicivirus are common causes, and they spread easily between cats. Signs include sneezing, runny eyes or nose, mouth sores, tiredness and poor appetite.

What helps:
- Gently wipe her nose clean. A blocked nose can stop her smelling food, so she may eat less.
- Make sure she keeps eating and drinking.

See your vet within 24 hours if the sneezing doesn't stop. Go now if she:
- Has trouble breathing, or her gums look bluish
- Hasn't eaten properly for 24 hours
- Is a kitten. Young cats are more likely to get seriously ill.

Vaccines can make these infections milder.

I think there is a possibility your cat may have made a similar mistake.

Suggestions:
- To rule out health issues, take the cat to the vet. You should take new pets to the vet right away anyways.
- Clean the bag thoroughly with cleaners designed to remove the smell. This should help prevent repeat occurrences.
- Keep anything litterbox-like out of reach. Boxes and bags with objects in them, especially.
- Consider getting additional boxes. If a more ideal place is nearby, the cat will probably use those instead.

Remember also it's only been a week. The cat is still probably settling in, and it may not have habituated itself to the box yet.

Q: When should I spay or neuter my dog or cat?
A: The best age depends on your pet, so ask your vet. General guidance:

Cats: Many groups advise spaying or neutering before about 5 months old. Some vets do it around 6 months. Healthy kittens can be fixed as young as 8 weeks.

Dogs: The traditional age is about 6 to 9 months, and some groups advise before 5 months. Giant-breed males kept as house pets are often neutered after they stop growing, at about 12 to 15 months.

Benefits include:
- No heat cycles and no unplanned litters
- Lower risk of womb infections and breast tumors in females
- No testicular cancer in males, and less roaming and urine marking

Pets can gain weight after surgery, so watch their food portions.

Eye injuries. Eyes get worse fast. Flat-faced breeds like Shih Tzus and Pugs are prone to eye injuries, and an eye can even pop out.
Signs: Squinting, an eye held shut, pawing at it; Redness, tearing, cloudiness; Something stuck in the eye; An eye bulging out of its socket
What to do now:
1. Stop them rubbing it. Use a cone collar or hold their paws.
2. Chemicals: flush the eye with sterile saline or clean, lukewarm water for 10â€“15 minutes.
3. Eye out of its socket: keep it moist with a clean cloth soaked in saline and go straight away.
4. Go to the vet the same day for any eye injury.
Don't: Removing something stuck in the eye. Pushing a bulging eye back in. Human eye drops or ointments.
Go to a vet now.

Q: My Shih Tzu got into a fight and one eye looks like it's bulging out of the socket.
A: This is an emergency. Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now. The longer the eye stays exposed, the more it dries out and gets damaged, which lowers the chance of saving his sight. Flat-faced breeds like Shih Tzus and Pugs are more prone to this.

On the way:
- Don't try to push the eye back in.
- Keep it moist if you can, for example with a clean cloth dampened with saline. Ask the clinic how when you call.
- Stop him from pawing or rubbing at it.
- Keep him calm and still.

For other eye injuries, also see a vet right away. Flush chemicals out with lots of water first, and never pull out an object stuck in the eye.

Q: My cat is vomiting. Is it just hairballs?
A: Many cats bring up a hairball once every week or two, and that alone is usually not a worry. A hairball is a wet, tube-shaped wad of swallowed hair.

See your vet soon if she:
- Vomits more than once a week
- Seems tired or weak, or eats less
- Has blood in the vomit
- Drinks or pees more or less than usual, or also has diarrhea

Go now if she keeps retching or vomiting with nothing coming up, refuses food for more than a day, or is very weak. A hairball or a swallowed object like string can block the gut, and that can be fatal without surgery.

To help prevent hairballs, comb her coat daily, especially when she sheds. Don't give laxatives or hairball products unless your vet says so.

Can't pee (blocked bladder). A blocked bladder, most common in male cats, can be fatal within a day or two. It's often mistaken for constipation.
Signs: Straining in the litter box with little or no pee; Going back to the box again and again; Crying while trying to pee, or peeing outside the box; Licking the genitals; vomiting, hiding, low energy
What to do now:
1. Go to the vet now. Tell them when you last saw your pet pee normally.
2. Carry them gently in a carrier.
Don't: Pressing on the belly or bladder. Waiting until the next day.
Go to a vet now.

Q: My old pet has really bad breath. Is that dental disease?
A: Often, yes. Gum disease is very common in older pets, especially small dogs. Signs include:
- Bad breath that doesn't go away
- Red or swollen gums
- Trouble picking up, chewing or swallowing food

Bad breath can also point to other illness. A sweet smell may mean diabetes, and a urine-like smell may mean kidney disease.

See your vet for a mouth check. Proper cleaning below the gumline needs anesthesia. Vets check older pets carefully first, and treating mouth pain often makes them much happier.

At home, brush your pet's teeth with pet toothpaste, never human toothpaste. See a vet soon if your pet stops eating or has a lump in the mouth.

Q: My dog or cat has bad breath. What causes it?
A: A healthy pet's breath should not smell bad. The most common cause is dental disease. Plaque and tartar build up on the teeth and inflame the gums, and the bacteria make the smell.

Bad breath can also point to other illness:
- Sweet or fruity smell: possible diabetes
- Urine-like smell: possible kidney disease
- Foul smell with vomiting, poor appetite or yellow gums: possible liver problems

What to do:
- Have your vet check bad breath that doesn't go away. A proper cleaning is done under anesthesia.
- Go sooner if you also see red or swollen gums, more drinking and peeing, weight loss, or poor appetite.
- At home, brush the teeth with pet toothpaste, ideally daily.

First time owning a cat

This is the first time I have a cat in my life. She is almost 10 months. She came home yesterday and she was wandering around the house, which has a litter box, food, and water.

This morning, I found my cat hiding under the bed and she hasn't come out since then. She isn't drinking nor eating. She isn't even thinking about coming out.

How do I make this cat eat or drink? Would treats help it out?

There are many things you can try to solve your problem. The easiest of which is as follows:

Find a small room in your house, where you go often, that has a door. Such as a bedroom. Take all the things your new kitten needs into that room, and close the door. Keep the cat in there, and let it slowly get used to just that part of your house. Once your cat seems comfortable there, slowly introduce it to other places in your house, and expand its territory. Treats may help with this. Make sure your cat is happy with her food and litter. If this behaviour continues, it is time to consult a vet.

Good luck!

Q: How can I tell if my pet's problem is a real emergency or can wait?
A: An emergency is any sudden, serious problem. If you're unsure, call your vet or the nearest 24-hour veterinary clinic now. They can tell you whether to come in.

Go immediately if your pet:
- Has trouble breathing, breathes with the mouth open (cats), or has blue or very pale gums
- Is bleeding heavily
- Collapses, is unresponsive, or has a seizure
- Ate something poisonous
- Was hit by a vehicle or fell, even if they seem fine
- Is straining to pee with nothing coming out (especially male cats)
- Has a swollen belly and keeps retching (dogs)
- Suddenly acts very differently from normal

Save your vet's number and the nearest 24-hour clinic in your phone today, and know the route.

Q: A stray dog bit my dog. Should I worry about rabies?
A: Rabies spreads mainly through bites and scratches. Once signs appear, it is almost always fatal, so act quickly.

For your dog:
- Wear gloves and wash the wound with soap and water
- Call your vet today, even if your dog is vaccinated. Your vet will check the wound and advise what to do next

For people: if you or a family member is bitten or scratched, wash the wound right away with soap and water and see a doctor urgently. Treatment after exposure works very well when started early.

Worldwide, dogs cause most human rabies deaths. Keeping your pets' rabies vaccines up to date protects them and your family.

- A previously vaccinated dog that can be identified should be revaccinated immediately and confined for at least 90 days
- A dog bitten by a suspected rabid or unknown animal should be confined under a vet's supervision for 6 months
- An unvaccinated dog bitten by a confirmed rabid animal must be put to sleep right away

Wear gloves if you need to handle wounds, and avoid contact with your dog's saliva. Your city or municipal veterinary office can guide you.

Q: How often should adult dogs and cats be dewormed?
A: Parasite experts (CAPC) recommend year-round protection for adult pets. Many monthly preventives cover worms together with heartworm, fleas or ticks.

If your pet isn't on a year-round preventive:
- Deworm about four times a year
- Have a stool (fecal) test 2 to 4 times a year

Even on prevention, healthy adults should have their poop checked at least twice a year. Pets that hunt, roam, travel or mix with many animals may need it more often.

Ask your vet for a product that suits your pet's weight and age, and which worms are common where you live.

Q: How do I get rid of fleas in my house?
A: Most of the flea problem lives in your home, not on your pet. Eggs fall off into carpets, bedding and corners, and flea cocoons can wait there for months.

What helps:
- Treat every dog and cat in the home, not just the itchy one, using products your vet recommends
- Vacuum often
- Wash pet bedding and blankets regularly
- If you use a home spray, keep pets out of the room and follow the label
- Never put a house or yard product directly on a pet

Fleas can live indoors all year, so experts advise year-round flea prevention. It can take weeks to months of steady treatment to fully clear an infestation.

Q: How much water should my pet drink, and how do I spot dehydration?
A: Keep fresh, clean water out at all times, in places your pet can easily reach. Cats that eat wet food often drink less, because the food is mostly water. Cats on dry food need to drink more.

Signs of dehydration:
- Dry or sticky gums
- Skin that stays "tented" when you gently lift it at the back of the neck, instead of snapping back
- Sunken eyes, weakness, low energy or poor appetite

Vomiting and diarrhea can cause dehydration fast. Call your vet today if you think your pet is dehydrated. Go now if they haven't eaten or drunk anything for 24 hours, or are very weak.

Drinking much more than usual also needs a vet visit within a day. It can be a sign of kidney disease, diabetes or other illness.

Q: My dog is losing hair and very itchy. Is it mange?
A: Mange is caused by tiny mites. Dogs get two main types:

Sarcoptic mange (scabies):
- Sudden, intense itching
- Bumps and crusts, often on the belly, chest, ears, elbows and legs
- Very contagious to other dogs, and can cause itchy skin in people

Demodectic mange (demodex):
- Bald, red, scaly patches, often with little itching
- Common in young dogs; mild cases may clear on their own
- The widespread form needs vet treatment

Your vet will usually do a skin scraping to check. Treat all pets that have contact with each other at the same time, and clean bedding and grooming tools. Follow your vet's treatment plan, which can take a while.

Q: How do I trim my dog's or cat's nails safely?
A: Go slowly and keep it positive with treats and praise.

Dogs:
- Trim when the nails touch the ground or click on the floor. For many dogs this is about monthly.
- Cut small bits at a time. On light nails, stop a little short of the pink quick. On dark nails, trim just the very tip.
- Don't forget the dewclaws.

Cats:
- Gently press the toe pad so the claw comes out.
- Snip only the sharp white tip. Avoid the pink part, which has nerves and blood vessels.
- Trim every 2 to 3 weeks. At first, do just one or two claws per session.

If a nail bleeds, press styptic powder or cornstarch on the tip and make sure it stops. If your pet fights or gets upset, stop. Your vet can help.

messages.content: What do I do? My cat shows blue or pale gums and collapse.

This sounds like it could be choking. Something stuck in the mouth or throat. If your pet is still breathing and coughing, go to the vet. Only step in if they can't breathe.

What to do now:
- Stay calm and hold them gently but firmly. A choking pet may bite.
- Open the mouth and look. If you can see the object and get a grip on it, remove it carefully with fingers or tweezers.
- If you can't remove it and they can't breathe: hold a cat or small dog with their back against your chest and give 5 firm thrusts inward and upward just below the ribs.
- For a large dog, put your arms around the belly from behind, make a fist just below the ribs and push firmly up and forward 5 times. If they're lying down, push from behind the ribs toward the head.
- Check the mouth again and repeat. If they collapse and stop breathing, start CPR.
- Go to the vet even if the object comes out. The throat may be injured.

Don't:
- Sweeping your fingers blindly. It can push the object deeper.
- Pulling on string, thread or tinsel hanging from the mouth or bottom. It can cut the intestines.

Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now.

Stings & allergic reactions. Bee, wasp, ant and centipede stings usually cause swelling that settles. A spreading reaction or trouble breathing is an emergency.
Signs: Mild: swelling and pain where they were stung, licking the spot; Go now: the face swells and keeps spreading, or hives all over the body; Go now: vomiting, diarrhea, pale gums, weakness or collapse; Go now: trouble breathing, a sting inside the mouth or throat, or many stings

1. Move away from the insects.
2. If you see a bee stinger, scrape it out sideways with a card. Don't squeeze it.
3. Hold a cold pack wrapped in cloth on the spot for 10 minutes.
4. Watch closely for the next 1â€“2 hours and call your vet for advice.
Don't: Giving human allergy or cold tablets without a vet's dose. Some contain decongestants that are toxic to pets.
Call your vet for advice.

Q: How do I keep my cat cool during hot days?
A: Cats handle heat better than many dogs, but hot, humid days can still be dangerous.
- Keep fresh water in several places, and add wet food for extra fluids
- Give them a shaded, airy spot, and use a fan or air-con in the hottest hours
- Brush long-haired cats often to remove loose fur
- Never leave a cat in a parked car

Open-mouth panting, drooling, wobbliness or collapse can mean heatstroke. Move them somewhere cool and go to a vet now.

Q: My dog is vomiting. Can I treat him at home?
A: One vomit in a dog that otherwise seems well is often not serious, and many cases settle within a day. But vomiting can also be a sign of poisoning, a blockage or other illness.

Go to the vet right away if he vomits and also has:
- Blood in the vomit
- Diarrhea, belly pain or fever
- Low energy, no appetite or signs of dehydration
- A chance he swallowed something toxic or an object

See your vet today if vomiting goes on for more than 24 hours, even if he seems fine.

For a mild case, your vet may suggest resting the stomach for a short time, then small, frequent meals of a bland food. Keep fresh water available. Don't give human medicines unless your vet tells you to.

2. Keep your dog as calm and still as you can on the way.
Don't: Waiting to see if it passes. Giving food, water or home remedies. Trying to make them vomit.
Go to a vet now.

Q: What papers do I need to bring my dog or cat to another island or province?
A: You need a local shipping permit from the Bureau of Animal Industry (BAI), applied for online at nvqsd.bai.gov.ph. Under the BAI Citizen's Charter, dogs and cats need:

- A veterinary health certificate from a licensed vet, showing rabies vaccine details (brand, batch/lot number, date given, next due date)
- A rabies vaccination certificate signed by the vet with their PRC number
- The pet should be about 3 to 4 months old or older
- The rabies shot should be at least 14 days and not more than 1 year old (annual boosters can ship right away)

The permit is free; processing takes up to 3 working days. Rules may change, so confirm with BAI before your trip.

sources.text:
Pet Travel Safety — Weeks before your trip
- Book a direct flight when possible to decrease the chances of your pet being separated from you during extreme weather or layovers. - Check your pet's vaccinations to make sure they are up to date. Get a health certificate from your veterinarian dated within 10 days of your departure. For international travel, additional planning and healthcare requirements may be needed. Research the requirements for pets for your destination country as well as for the United States. When returning to the United States from abroad, your dog must meet all US entry requirements upon return. - For animals stowed in the plane's cargo area, purchase a US Department of Agriculture-approved shipping crate. messages.content: What papers do I need to bring my dog or cat to another island or province?

You need a local shipping permit from the Bureau of Animal Industry (BAI), applied for online at nvqsd.bai.gov.ph. Under the BAI Citizen's Charter, dogs and cats need:

- A veterinary health certificate from a licensed vet, showing rabies vaccine details (brand, batch/lot number, date given, next due date)
- A rabies vaccination certificate signed by the vet with their PRC number
- The pet should be about 3 to 4 months old or older
- The rabies shot should be at least 14 days and not more than 1 year old (annual boosters can ship right away)

The permit is free; processing takes up to 3 working days. Rules may change, so confirm with BAI before your trip.

Q: My pet seems sleepy after her shots. Normal or not?
A: Mild reactions are common and should be short-lived:
- Soreness or a small swelling where the shot was given
- Tiredness or less appetite
- Mild fever
- Vomiting once

Allergic reactions are less common but can be serious. Severe ones usually start within minutes to an hour, but other reactions can appear hours later. Go to a vet now if you see:
- Swelling of the face, lips or eyes
- Hives (raised bumps on the skin)
- Repeated vomiting or diarrhea
- Trouble breathing
- Weakness or collapse

Call your vet if mild signs do not improve or you are unsure. Always tell your vet about any past reaction before the next vaccine.

Q: Is it true that cats themselves are not smelly?

Q: My cat ate some leftover adobo cooked with lots of garlic and onion. Is that bad?
A: It can be. Onions, garlic and chives can upset the stomach and damage red blood cells, which can lead to anemia. Cats are more sensitive to them than dogs, so dishes cooked with them are risky for cats.

Call your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now and take her in, especially if she ate a fair amount or you're not sure how much.

Watch for vomiting, drooling, low energy, weakness and pale gums.

Before you go:
- Tell the vet what dish it was and roughly how much she ate.
- Only make her vomit if a vet tells you to.

On the way, keep her calm in her carrier. Avoid sharing seasoned human food with pets.

Q: Why is my cat peeing outside the litter box?
A: First, have your vet rule out a medical problem. Peeing outside the box can be a sign of a bladder problem.

Go to the vet now if your cat strains in the box with little or no pee coming out, cries while peeing, or is vomiting or very tired. A blocked bladder can kill, and male cats are most at risk.

If the vet finds nothing wrong, check the box:
- One box per cat, plus one extra
- Scoop daily, and change all the litter weekly
- Most cats like unscented, clumping, fine litter
- Put boxes in quiet spots, away from food bowls and busy areas

Stress, like a move or a new pet, can also cause it. Clean accidents with an enzyme cleaner for pet odors. Never punish your cat.

Q: Is there free anti-rabies vaccine for dogs from the government?
A: Often, yes. Section 6 of RA 9482 tells the Department of Agriculture to lead free anti-rabies vaccination of dogs, with priority for high-risk, low-income areas. LGUs must fund vaccines and run registration and vaccination (Section 7).

Q: Is anti-rabies treatment for people free?
A: Under Section 6 of RA 9482, the DOH must provide post-exposure treatment for bite victims at minimum cost, and free pre-exposure shots for high-risk workers. Free routine shots are also given to schoolchildren aged 5 to 14 in high-risk areas (Section 4).

Q: My old pet has really bad breath. Is that dental disease?
A: Often, yes. Gum disease is very common in older pets, especially small dogs. Signs include:
- Bad breath that doesn't go away
- Red or swollen gums
- Trouble picking up, chewing or swallowing food

Bad breath can also point to other illness. A sweet smell may mean diabetes, and a urine-like smell may mean kidney disease.

See your vet for a mouth check. Proper cleaning below the gumline needs anesthesia. Vets check older pets carefully first, and treating mouth pain often makes them much happier.

At home, brush your pet's teeth with pet toothpaste, never human toothpaste. See a vet soon if your pet stops eating or has a lump in the mouth.

Q: My dog or cat has bad breath. What causes it?
A: A healthy pet's breath should not smell bad. The most common cause is dental disease. Plaque and tartar build up on the teeth and inflame the gums, and the bacteria make the smell.

Bad breath can also point to other illness:
- Sweet or fruity smell: possible diabetes
- Urine-like smell: possible kidney disease
- Foul smell with vomiting, poor appetite or yellow gums: possible liver problems

What to do:
- Have your vet check bad breath that doesn't go away. A proper cleaning is done under anesthesia.
- Go sooner if you also see red or swollen gums, more drinking and peeing, weight loss, or poor appetite.
- At home, brush the teeth with pet toothpaste, ideally daily.

Q: My cat is vomiting. Is it just hairballs?
A: Many cats bring up a hairball once every week or two, and that alone is usually not a worry. A hairball is a wet, tube-shaped wad of swallowed hair.

See your vet soon if she:
- Vomits more than once a week
- Seems tired or weak, or eats less
- Has blood in the vomit
- Drinks or pees more or less than usual, or also has diarrhea

Go now if she keeps retching or vomiting with nothing coming up, refuses food for more than a day, or is very weak. A hairball or a swallowed object like string can block the gut, and that can be fatal without surgery.

To help prevent hairballs, comb her coat daily, especially when she sheds. Don't give laxatives or hairball products unless your vet says so.

Q: What are the causes of a cat jumping off a roof?

Currently my cat is in serious condition and I was wondering: what happens if a cat fell from a high height, aka a roof?
A: Lots of things can make a cat fall/jump of a roof.
- Getting scared.
- Hunting attempts, for example trying to catch a bird.
- Overestimating his/her abilities.
- Getting distracted.

Cats can get hurt if the fall is too short, because they haven't enough time to righten themselves.

A cat can get hurt if it is overweight and it falls from great height.

Wanting to get down but landing wrong can cause injuries, this is most common in kittens and very young cats.

Additional information: often cats that fall from tall buildings have a greater survival rate and less injuries than cats falling from lower buildings.

messages.content: How can I tell if my dog or cat is overweight?

Vets use a 9-point body condition score (BCS) from WSAVA. You can do a quick check at home:
- Ribs: Run your hands along the sides. At a healthy weight you can feel the ribs under a thin layer of fat. If you can't feel them without pressing, there is too much fat.
- Waist: Look down from above. You should see a waist behind the ribs.
- Belly: From the side, a dog's belly should tuck up. A cat at a healthy weight has only a small fat pad on the belly.

Signs of overweight are ribs that are hard to feel, no waist, a rounded belly, and fat over the lower back (and in dogs, the base of the tail).

Ideal is 4 to 5 out of 9 for dogs and 5 out of 9 for cats. Ask your vet to score your pet and plan safe weight loss.

Q: My dog eats grass. Is that normal?
A: Yes, it is very common, and most grass-eating dogs are not sick. Studies show fewer than 1 in 4 dogs vomit after eating grass. Dogs may eat grass for fiber, out of boredom or to get attention, or simply from instinct.

Q: My dog isn't eating. When should I worry?
A: A dog that stops eating is often unwell, so take it seriously and involve your vet early.

What to check:
- Does he seem hungry but struggle to pick up, chew or swallow food? That points to pain in the mouth, teeth or jaw.
- Has anything changed lately, like a move, a new food or a new medicine?
- Are there other signs, like vomiting, diarrhea, pain or low energy?

When to go:
- Skipped meals but otherwise acting normal: see your vet today, within 24 hours.
- Go now if he hasn't eaten or drunk anything for 24 hours, or if he is also vomiting, very weak or in a lot of pain.
- If he has diabetes and refuses even one meal, call your vet right away.

Q: My cat is breathing with her mouth open and sitting hunched up. Is that normal?
A: No. In cats, open-mouth breathing is a sign of serious trouble and means she may not be getting enough oxygen. Fast or hard breathing, sitting or crouching in a stiff upright position, and bluish gums are also warning signs.

This is an emergency. Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour veterinary clinic now.

On the way:
- Keep her as calm and still as possible.
- Put her in a carrier or box with good air holes, and cover it lightly with a cloth to help her feel safe.
- Don't hold her tightly or press on her chest.
- Call the clinic ahead so the team can get ready for her.

Cats need time to adjust and settle if you move house. They could get into serious danger trying to return to their previous home. To prevent this, keep cats indoors for at least two weeks after moving. Ensure your cat’s behaviour has settled before letting them outside.

messages.content: My dog has vomiting or diarrhea. Help, what do I do?

This sounds like it could be heatstroke. Overheating can damage organs within minutes. Flat-faced and thick-coated breeds are most at risk.

What to do now:
- Move them out of the sun right away, into shade or an air-conditioned room.
- Wet the coat with cool tap water, especially the belly, armpits, groin and paws, then fan them so the water evaporates.
- Offer small sips of cool water if they're alert. Don't force them to drink.
- Keep cooling for 10â€“15 minutes, then go to the vet with the car's air-con on, even if they seem better. Damage can show up hours later.
- If you have a rectal thermometer, stop active cooling at about 39.5 Â°C so they don't get too cold.

Don't:
- Ice or ice-cold water. It narrows blood vessels and slows cooling.
- Leaving a wet towel draped over them. It traps heat. Wet the coat and keep air moving instead.
- Waiting to see if they recover on their own.

Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now.

Q: Is it legal to sell or eat dog meat in the Philippines?
A: No. RA 9482 bans the trade of dog meat. LGUs must enforce this ban (Section 7).

Under Section 11, anyone caught trading dog meat faces a fine of at least P5,000 per dog and 1 to 4 years in prison. The same penalty applies to using electrocution to put dogs to sleep. Foreigners who break these rules are deported after serving their sentence.

Killing dogs for food is also not among the allowed reasons for killing animals under the Animal Welfare Act (RA 8485, Section 6).

Q: My cat is sneezing and has runny eyes. Is it cat flu?
A: It may be an upper respiratory infection, often called cat flu. Viruses like feline herpesvirus and calicivirus are common causes, and they spread easily between cats. Signs include sneezing, runny eyes or nose, mouth sores, tiredness and poor appetite.

What helps:
- Gently wipe her nose clean. A blocked nose can stop her smelling food, so she may eat less.
- Make sure she keeps eating and drinking.

See your vet within 24 hours if the sneezing doesn't stop. Go now if she:
- Has trouble breathing, or her gums look bluish
- Hasn't eaten properly for 24 hours
- Is a kitten. Young cats are more likely to get seriously ill.

Vaccines can make these infections milder.

Q: How do I potty train my puppy?
A: Patience, a routine and rewards work best.

- Take your puppy out at least every two hours, and right after waking up, eating and playing.
- Feed meals at the same times each day.
- Use the same outdoor spot each time, and say a cue word like "potty" while they go.
- Praise or give a treat right after they finish.
- Watch for sniffing, circling or scratching at the door, then go out right away.
- When you can't watch, use a crate or a small gated area.
- A puppy can often hold it about one hour per month of age. A 3-month-old may need a break about every 3 hours.

Never punish accidents. Calmly take the puppy to the outdoor spot, reward them if they finish there, and clean the mess well.

sources.label: FurFriends first-aid guide: Hit by a vehicle or fall
sources.text:
Hit by a vehicle or fall. Internal bleeding and chest injuries may not show at first. Pets that fall from balconies or windows need a vet check too.
Signs: Limping, not putting weight on a leg; Fast breathing, pale gums; Swelling belly, bleeding from the nose or mouth; Seems fine but was hit or fell. Still go.
What to do now:
1. Make sure you're safe from traffic first.
2. Approach slowly and speak softly. Hurt animals bite, so use a towel or muzzle unless they're vomiting or struggling to breathe.
3. Move them as little as possible. Slide a large dog onto a board or blanket to use as a stretcher, keeping the back and neck straight. Put small pets in a box or carrier.
4. Press on any bleeding, keep them calm, and go to the vet now.
Don't: Giving any painkiller. Trying to straighten or splint a leg. Giving food or water.
Go to a vet now.

messages.content: Limping, not putting weight on a leg, seems fine but was hit or fell. Still go.. My dog is like this right now, what should I do?

This sounds like it could be hit by a vehicle or fall. Internal bleeding and chest injuries may not show at first. Pets that fall from balconies or windows need a vet check too.

What to do now:
- Make sure you're safe from traffic first.
- Approach slowly and speak softly. Hurt animals bite, so use a towel or muzzle unless they're vomiting or struggling to breathe.
- Move them as little as possible. Slide a large dog onto a board or blanket to use as a stretcher, keeping the back and neck straight. Put small pets in a box or carrier.
- Press on any bleeding, keep them calm, and go to the vet now.

Don't:
- Giving any painkiller.
- Trying to straighten or splint a leg.
- Giving food or water.

Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now.

Q: What are my legal responsibilities as a dog owner in the Philippines?
A: Section 5 of RA 9482 lists the duties of pet owners:

- Have your dog vaccinated against rabies regularly and keep a registration card with its vaccination records
- Register your dog with the LGU
- Don't let your dog roam public places without a leash
- Give your dog proper grooming, food and shelter
- Report any bite within 24 hours and have the dog observed by a vet
- Help the bite victim right away and pay for their medical costs

Breaking these rules can lead to fines under Section 11.

Q: Is it legal to sell or eat dog meat in the Philippines?
A: No. RA 9482 bans the trade of dog meat. LGUs must enforce this ban (Section 7).

Under Section 11, anyone caught trading dog meat faces a fine of at least P5,000 per dog and 1 to 4 years in prison. The same penalty applies to using electrocution to put dogs to sleep. Foreigners who break these rules are deported after serving their sentence.

Killing dogs for food is also not among the allowed reasons for killing animals under the Animal Welfare Act (RA 8485, Section 6).

Q: My cat isn't eating. How long is too long?
A: Don't wait it out. A cat that stops eating can develop a serious liver problem called hepatic lipidosis (fatty liver). It can be fatal if not treated quickly. Overweight cats are at higher risk.

What to do:
- If your cat hasn't eaten properly for 24 hours, take her to the vet now.
- Go right away if her gums, ears, skin or the whites of her eyes look yellow, or if she is very weak.
- Tell the vet when she last ate and if anything changed at home.

Most cats with fatty liver have another illness that caused the poor appetite, so the vet will look for that too. Fatty liver needs prompt treatment, so don't wait to see if she starts eating again.
