Q: How much water should my pet drink, and how do I spot dehydration?
A: Keep fresh, clean water out at all times, in places your pet can easily reach. Cats that eat wet food often drink less, because the food is mostly water. Cats on dry food need to drink more.

Signs of dehydration:
- Dry or sticky gums
- Skin that stays "tented" when you gently lift it at the back of the neck, instead of snapping back
- Sunken eyes, weakness, low energy or poor appetite

Vomiting and diarrhea can cause dehydration fast. Call your vet today if you think your pet is dehydrated. Go now if they haven't eaten or drunk anything for 24 hours, or are very weak.

Drinking much more than usual also needs a vet visit within a day. It can be a sign of kidney disease, diabetes or other illness.

Q: My cat has round bald patches. Is it ringworm?
A: It might be. Despite its name, ringworm is not a worm. It is a fungal skin infection. Signs include:
- Round patches of hair loss
- Broken or stubbly hair
- Scaly, crusty or red skin
- Dandruff or extra grooming

Ringworm spreads to people and other pets, and children are at higher risk. Its spores can stay in a home for many months.

What to do:
- See your vet, since flea allergy and other problems can look similar
- Keep the cat in one easy-to-clean room during treatment
- Wash hands after handling her
- Clean and disinfect the home well

Treatment often takes six weeks or more.

Q: Can cats see equally well in both light and dark? I know that the cats can see in the dark, but I have been wondering: can cats see as well in the dark as they do in the light? Or …
A: Cats can't literally "see in the dark", although they can see better in dim light than people can, because their pupils can expand to let more light in. So like us, they need some light, the more the better up to a point. (Glaring lights can make it as difficult to see as no light at all.)

A cat's vision is different than ours in other ways. Their colour vision is limited, and they are nearsighted. However, they are very quick to spot movement!

Q: Do cats have a preference of being in the light or being in the dark? From time to time I have to put my very energetic cat in my bedroom for an hour or so while I'm cleaning, or working …
A: Cats are crepuscular, which means they prefer to be awake at dawn and dusk. As such they've evolved to prefer neither complete darkness or bright light.

That said, human sight is also suppose to be best at dawn and dusk as well. However, cats proportionally have more rods than cones in their eyes than we do. (Rods are what give us are ability to see in very low light and their placement in our eyes is why we can see better out of our peripheral vision in very low light.) Thus cats likely prefer a lower light levels than we do, and are able to see better in darker environments.

Q: My dog chewed up a whole pack of sugar-free gum.
A: Take him to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now, even if he looks fine. Many sugar-free gums contain xylitol (also called birch sugar), which can make a dog's blood sugar crash within 10 to 60 minutes. It can also harm the liver a day or two later, so he may need to stay for monitoring.

Watch for vomiting, weakness, wobbling, collapse and seizures.

Before you go:
- Bring the pack so the vet can check the ingredients.
- Only make him vomit if a vet tells you to.

On the way, keep him close, watch for weakness or shaking, and call the clinic ahead.

Xylitol is also in some peanut butters, toothpastes, mouthwashes and vitamins, so check labels and use only pet toothpaste.

Q: Can my dog have a treat with medicine that she can only take on any empty stomach

Can I give my dog medicine with a little treat even if it says take on any empty stomach?
A: One treat still counts as "empty stomach", so yes. Especially if the dog refuses to take the medicine alone but does take it together with the treat, the benefits outweigh the negative effect one single treat can have.

However, you also need to wait a sufficient time after the last meal for the stomach to empty itself. Usually such medicine is best administered in the morning before the dog has breakfast.

messages.content: Blue or pale gums, panic, struggling to breathe. My dog is like this right now, what should I do?

This sounds like it could be choking. Something stuck in the mouth or throat. If your pet is still breathing and coughing, go to the vet. Only step in if they can't breathe.

What to do now:
- Stay calm and hold them gently but firmly. A choking pet may bite.
- Open the mouth and look. If you can see the object and get a grip on it, remove it carefully with fingers or tweezers.
- If you can't remove it and they can't breathe: hold a cat or small dog with their back against your chest and give 5 firm thrusts inward and upward just below the ribs.
- For a large dog, put your arms around the belly from behind, make a fist just below the ribs and push firmly up and forward 5 times. If they're lying down, push from behind the ribs toward the head.
- Check the mouth again and repeat. If they collapse and stop breathing, start CPR.
- Go to the vet even if the object comes out. The throat may be injured.

Don't:
- Sweeping your fingers blindly. It can push the object deeper.
- Pulling on string, thread or tinsel hanging from the mouth or bottom. It can cut the intestines.

Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now.

Placating isolated kitten

I have a kitten (15 weeks) that has to be isolated while she's being treated for ringworm (for six weeks). She's from a shelter, and I don't know when she was separated from her mother or littermates.

The problem is that whenever there's nobody else in the room she makes a fuss and scratches at the door. Not just for a few minutes after being left there or whenever somebody passes by, but more or less all night.

How to keep her suitably socialised (considering her age and developmental requirements) without spreading the disease around?

An old rescue trick is to take a book/magazine/newspaper into the room and read to her. Since you're worried about contamination, just take something into the room and leave it there until after isolation is over. She'll get used to your voice and presence, and if she wants attention from you she'll come over.

If you plan to spend an hour or so with her each day, and make it at the same time, she should learn that she will get attention at this particular time and hopefully not pine for it at other times.

Q: I accidentally put my dog's flea spot-on on my cat.
A: This can be life-threatening, so treat it as an emergency. Many dog flea and tick products contain permethrin, which cats can't break down well. Call your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now and take her in, even if she seems fine.

Signs include drooling, restlessness, twitching or trembling, wobbliness, vomiting and seizures.

Before you go:
- Bring the product box.
- Ask the vet on the phone whether to wash the spot first. They may tell you to use mild dish soap and plenty of water, then dry her well.
- Stop her from licking the area.

On the way, keep her calm in her carrier. Only use flea products labelled for cats, and keep cats away from newly treated dogs until the product dries.

Q: pwede ba i-walk ang aso ko without a leash?
A: Not in public. Section 5 of RA 9482 says owners must keep their dogs under control and not let them roam public places without a leash. LGUs must also make sure dogs are leashed or kept inside the owner's property (Section 7).

The implementing rules add:
- The leash should be no longer than 1.5 meters
- The dog tag should be on the collar or harness
- Aggressive dogs should wear a muzzle in public

The law sets a fine of P500 per incident for not leashing a dog outside the house (Section 11). These amounts are as written in the 2007 law. Your city or municipality may have its own ordinance, so check with your city or municipal veterinary office.

Q: My cat is vomiting. Is it just hairballs?
A: Many cats bring up a hairball once every week or two, and that alone is usually not a worry. A hairball is a wet, tube-shaped wad of swallowed hair.

See your vet soon if she:
- Vomits more than once a week
- Seems tired or weak, or eats less
- Has blood in the vomit
- Drinks or pees more or less than usual, or also has diarrhea

Go now if she keeps retching or vomiting with nothing coming up, refuses food for more than a day, or is very weak. A hairball or a swallowed object like string can block the gut, and that can be fatal without surgery.

To help prevent hairballs, comb her coat daily, especially when she sheds. Don't give laxatives or hairball products unless your vet says so.

Q: My dog or cat has diarrhea. When do I need a vet?
A: Mild diarrhea in an adult pet that is still bright and eating can sometimes be watched at home for a short time.

Home care:
- Always keep fresh water out. Diarrhea can quickly cause dehydration.
- Ask your vet about a short rest for the stomach, or small meals of a bland or gut-friendly diet.
- When the stool firms up, switch back to the usual food slowly over about a week.

See your vet if it lasts more than 24 hours.

Go now if there is:
- Blood in the stool, or black, tarry stool
- Vomiting, weakness, fever, belly pain or no appetite
- Diarrhea in a puppy. It can be an early sign of parvo, which can be deadly.
- Straining with nothing coming out

Q: How often should I deworm my kitten?
A: Kittens often get roundworms from their mother's milk, so deworming starts early.

Parasite experts (CAPC) advise:
- Start at 2 weeks old
- Repeat every 2 weeks until your kitten starts a monthly year-round parasite preventive
- If a monthly preventive isn't used: every 2 weeks until 2 months old, then monthly until 6 months, then every 3 months
- Have the kitten's poop checked by the vet several times in the first year

Ask your vet for a product that suits your kitten's weight and age, and use only products made for cats.

Q: I just got a new kitten. What should I do first?
A: Take your kitten to a vet as soon as you can. Ask where you got her about any vaccines, deworming and food she has had.

- Vet visits: kittens usually see the vet every 3 to 4 weeks until about 6 months old, for shots and parasite treatment.
- Vaccines: the core kitten shots start at about 6 to 8 weeks and are repeated every 3 to 4 weeks until 16 to 20 weeks old.
- Deworming: worms are very common in kittens, so many vets deworm them routinely.
- Testing: a kitten with an unknown history should be tested for FeLV and FIV. Keep her apart from your other cats until the vet has checked her.
- Feeding: use kitten food, given several times a day.
- Litter box: one per cat, plus one extra, kept clean.

messages.content:
Do male cats mate with dolls or other things, like dogs?

It is well known that lone male dogs "use" (instead of a girl-dog) almost anything else: dolls, furniture, the legs of the people around, and even rabbits and chicken (when available).

However, I have no idea if male cats have a similar inclination. I welcome any information on this topic.

It's not quite the same nor remotely as common as with dogs, but yes, cats do sometimes hump at random things like inanimate objects.

It's more common with intact males or with males that were neutered later in life, but any cat including females might show the behavior.

However, as I said, it doesn't present quite the same as with dogs. With dogs, it can also be a play or dominance behavior, and so it seems to be much more common for dogs. With cats, if it comes up, it seems to often be a form of self-soothing, as they'll often start doing it as part of kneading on things like blankets, and they might tend to do it more if they're bored or stressed.

Q: Does my indoor cat need vaccines?
A: Yes. The American Association of Feline Practitioners recommends core vaccines even for cats that never go outside. Core vaccines for cats cover:
- Panleukopenia (feline distemper)
- Herpesvirus
- Calicivirus
(these three come together as FVRCP)
- Rabies, where the disease is present or the law requires it

Feline leukemia (FeLV) vaccine is advised for kittens under 1 year. For adults it depends on risk, such as going outdoors or living with cats that do.

Good news for indoor cats: global guidelines say low-risk indoor adults usually need core boosters only every 3 years or longer.

Your vet will choose the vaccines and timing that fit your cat.

Q: How much exercise does my old dog need?
A: Older dogs still need daily activity to keep their muscles, joints, weight and mind healthy. The type matters more than the amount:
- Choose gentle, low-impact exercise like shorter, more frequent leash walks or swimming
- Avoid lots of hard jumping and rough play
- Add brain games, new toys and simple training to keep the mind sharp

Make home easier:
- Non-slip rugs or yoga mats on smooth floors
- Ramps for the bed, sofa or car
- Block stairs or pools if eyesight or hearing is poor

If your dog limps, stops often or is stiff after walks, he may be in pain. Ask your vet for a check and an exercise plan.

messages.content: My dog: jaw chomping, drooling, losing control of pee or poo. What should I do?

This sounds like it could be seizures. Most seizures stop within 2 minutes. Keep your pet safe, time it, and call your vet.

What to do now:
- Stay calm and note the time it starts.
- Move furniture and objects away, keep them away from stairs and water, and put a towel under the head. Keep your hands away from the mouth.
- Dim the lights and keep things quiet. Film it if you can, since it helps the vet.
- Afterwards, keep them somewhere quiet and cool, and speak softly while they recover.
- Call your vet after any first seizure. Go now if it lasts over 5 minutes, they have another one, they don't wake up between seizures, or they may have eaten a poison.

Don't:
- Putting fingers or anything else in their mouth. Pets can't swallow their tongue.
- Holding them down.
- Giving food, water or medicine until they're fully alert.

Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now.

My Croatian Shepherd mix likes to go out in the balcony and sleep there during the day. Right now we have 28 degrees Fahrenheit (-2 Celsius).

If he's outside, can I assume, it's ok for him?

It's my first dog and I'm nervous about him getting a cold.

No dog should be left outside in extreme weather for prolonged periods of time. However, some time outside is not bad, especially if the dog is choosing to go out. Your dog, given it’s breed, has a pretty good cold weather coat. If it’s raining or snowing and their coat gets wet, don’t let them stay out as long.

Essentially, just monitor your dog when they are out, and be sure they always have the option to come back in when they want or need to (like a dog door). Consider providing some bedding outside for the dog.

A: The light reflecting cells in the dog's eye do send light to the light sensitive cells one extra time, giving the dog better night vision than we humans have.

But just as in humans, dogs can have eye problems and many of these problems can be treated by medication if they are diagnosed early; if you wait, the dog might be totally blind.

So please take your dog to the specialist as soon as you possibly can to get this diagnosed and treated. It is important for your dog's future.

messages.content:
Why is my German Shepherd scratching their mouth and ear?

My German Shepherd is scratching the upper part of his mouth and the inside of his left ear recently. I want to know, what would be the reason for this?

As people have mentioned in the comments it does sound like an ear infection and would warrant a vet visit.

Signs of an ear infection:
- Head shaking
- Head tilt
- Excessive scratching
- Hair loss or scabbing around the ears (from scratching)
- Foul odor
- Discharge from the ear

Causes
- Allergies
- Frequent swimming without drying the ears
- Inadequate ear cleaning (especially in floppy eared dogs)
- Polyps
- Ear mites

What to expect

During the exam the veterinarian will use an otoscope to look inside your dogs ear to check for:
- Inflamation
- Excess debris
- Appearance of the ear drum

After the otoscopic exam a sample of the debris from both ears will be taken to view under a microscope. The most common types of infection are:
- Bacterial
- Fungal

Each type of infection needs a specific medication though most veterinary ear medications treat both types.

Q: How do I potty train my puppy?
A: Patience, a routine and rewards work best.

- Take your puppy out at least every two hours, and right after waking up, eating and playing.
- Feed meals at the same times each day.
- Use the same outdoor spot each time, and say a cue word like "potty" while they go.
- Praise or give a treat right after they finish.
- Watch for sniffing, circling or scratching at the door, then go out right away.
- When you can't watch, use a crate or a small gated area.
- A puppy can often hold it about one hour per month of age. A 3-month-old may need a break about every 3 hours.

Never punish accidents. Calmly take the puppy to the outdoor spot, reward them if they finish there, and clean the mess well.

Q: When does my puppy start his shots, and why so many?
A: Puppies usually get their first core vaccine at 6 to 8 weeks old. Shots are then repeated every 2 to 4 weeks until the puppy is at least 16 weeks old.

Why a series? Antibodies from the mother's milk protect a young puppy, but they also block vaccines from working. These antibodies fade at a different age in each puppy, so repeat shots make sure one of them "takes". The dose given at 16 weeks or later is the most important.

Global guidelines also advise another core dose at around 6 months old instead of waiting until 1 year, to catch puppies that did not respond earlier.

Your vet will set the exact schedule for your puppy.

sources.label: FurFriends first-aid guide: Bloat (twisted stomach)
sources.text:
Bloat (twisted stomach). The stomach fills with gas and can twist. It can kill within hours and usually needs surgery. Most common in large, deep-chested dogs.
Signs: Swollen, tight belly; Retching or trying to vomit with nothing coming up; Restless, pacing, can't get comfortable; Drooling, pale gums, collapse
What to do now:
1. Go to the vet immediately. Call ahead so they can prepare.
2. Keep your dog as calm and still as you can on the way.
Don't: Waiting to see if it passes. Giving food, water or home remedies. Trying to make them vomit.
Go to a vet now.

Q: My German Shepherd ate a big meal and then ran around. Now he's restless and drooling. Can bloat wait until morning?
A: No. Bloat (GDV), where the stomach fills with gas and can twist, is a life-threatening emergency. Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour veterinary clinic now. Quick treatment greatly improves the chance of survival.

Signs to watch for:
- Restlessness and seeming uncomfortable
- Retching again and again with nothing coming up
- Lots of drooling
- A swollen, painful belly
- Fast breathing, pale gums, weakness

Large, deep-chested breeds like German Shepherds, Great Danes and Dobermans are at higher risk, especially when a big meal is followed by exercise.

On the way, keep him calm, don't give food or a lot of water, and call the clinic ahead so they can prepare.

Q: Do cats need clothes?

Do cats need dressing clothes when weather is cold?

If so, what is the temperature in which cats start to need clothes?
A: Cats generally have sense enough not to go outside/stay outside when it's dangerously cold unless they must. So unless you are forcing the cat outside, or your house is colder than most and you have a furless breed or much colder than most, this shouldn't be a problem.

Basically, most cats never need to wear clothes other than their fur. Remember, feral cats manage to survive in a wide range of climates.

Q: Why does my cat eat plants? I have caught my cat a couple of times chewing on household plants. Most of the plants now have chewed leaves. I have seen him do it outside but I suspect he might. Why …
A: Roughage, to aid digestion, help them pass/regurgitate hairballs, and sometimes just because they like the texture or it cleans their teeth (same reasons some cats like puncturing paper).

Q: Is it possible to overbrush a cat? I am taking care of an elderly Maine Coon who can't really groom himself well. He enjoys being brushed and he changes his lying position to indicate where he wants to get brushed. …
A: Actually, yes, it is possible to overbrush cats, though it also depends on what kind of brush you are using. The Furminator, for example, actually tends to pull out hair (which mind you doesn't hurt cats like it does humans), but it can actually thin out a cat's fur if used too much. If you use a more regular kind of brush that doesn't happen so much, and so it's probably fine to use on a regular basis. If you're really concerned, try to make sure you don't brush one area over and over, and keep an eye on your cat's fur.

Q: How do I get rid of fleas in my house?
A: Most of the flea problem lives in your home, not on your pet. Eggs fall off into carpets, bedding and corners, and flea cocoons can wait there for months.

What helps:
- Treat every dog and cat in the home, not just the itchy one, using products your vet recommends
- Vacuum often
- Wash pet bedding and blankets regularly
- If you use a home spray, keep pets out of the room and follow the label
- Never put a house or yard product directly on a pet

Fleas can live indoors all year, so experts advise year-round flea prevention. It can take weeks to months of steady treatment to fully clear an infestation.

Q: When should I spay or neuter my dog or cat?
A: The best age depends on your pet, so ask your vet. General guidance:

Cats: Many groups advise spaying or neutering before about 5 months old. Some vets do it around 6 months. Healthy kittens can be fixed as young as 8 weeks.

Dogs: The traditional age is about 6 to 9 months, and some groups advise before 5 months. Giant-breed males kept as house pets are often neutered after they stop growing, at about 12 to 15 months.

Benefits include:
- No heat cycles and no unplanned litters
- Lower risk of womb infections and breast tumors in females
- No testicular cancer in males, and less roaming and urine marking

Pets can gain weight after surgery, so watch their food portions.

Q: My dog was panting really hard after our walk in the heat and now he collapsed. What do I do?
A: This sounds like heatstroke, which is an emergency. Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour veterinary clinic now.

Before you leave and on the way:
- Move him out of the sun into shade or an air-conditioned space.
- Wet his body with cool (not ice-cold) water or wet towels, especially the belly, and use a fan or the car aircon.
- Don't dunk him in a tub of cold water.
- Offer small sips of water only once he is alert and starting to cool.

Other heatstroke signs are hot skin, drooling, vomiting, and wobbly walking. Keep cooling him on the drive, and let the vet check him even if he seems to improve.

Q: My dog suddenly collapsed and isn't responding to me.
A: This needs a vet immediately. Call your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic and leave right away.

Quick checks:
- Breathing: watch whether the chest rises and falls.
- Heartbeat: put your hand flat on the chest to feel for it.

If there's no breathing or heartbeat, ask the clinic on the phone to guide you through chest compressions. Keep going until your dog breathes on his own or the vet takes over.

On the way:
- Have someone else drive, especially if you're doing compressions.
- Lay him on a firm, flat surface and keep his head level and neck straight.
- Be careful when he wakes up, since a confused dog may bite.

Q: My puppy bites and nips a lot. How do I stop it?
A: Mouthing is normal for puppies. The goal is to teach them to be gentle.

- When teeth press hard, give a high-pitched yelp and let your hand go limp. Praise your puppy when they stop.
- If that doesn't work, ignore them for 10 to 20 seconds or walk away, then play again calmly.
- Keep a chew toy or tug toy handy and offer it when they go for your hands or feet.
- Play fetch or tug instead of rough games with your hands.
- Don't jerk your hands away. It invites more grabbing.
- Never hit, slap or shake your puppy. It can make biting worse and cause fear.

Get help from a certified animal behaviorist or veterinary behaviorist if bites come with a stiff body, growling or pulled-back lips, or hurt much more than play bites.

Q: What age do cats stop growing on average?

I've heard humans stop growing around age 18-24. What about cats? When do they stop growing in height?
A: There are a couple of growth periods for cats. The first takes about 4 months and takes them into the kitten stage. The second growth period of a kitten takes them from about 4 months to somewhere between 8 and 12 months to adult size depending on the size of the breed. Larger breeds will take longer to reach their adult size versus smaller breeds, but despite having adult size, they're still junior cats, they don't really become adult cats until their 3rd year.

I only mention the two growth stages (which are effectively continuous) because the dietary requirements change.

Q: Is there a disease where cats arch their backs and run weird, sideways? I think I saw this behavior in a funny cat youtube video where the cat arches its back and runs sideways in a weird way, and in …
A: Absolutely not a disease. Cats run like this when they are frightened, playing, or just trying to appear bigger than themselves. There are likely more reasons too. It's a reflexive action that can give you insight into their mood.

I suppose it's possible a cat can have a 'disease' similar to human Tourettes (a neurological disorder), but remember that cats use their body to communicate, and if they use communication it's more likely that you should listen to your cat and his / her needs than speculative youtube videos.

Q: Why does my cat sometimes run at me sideways? I've seen my cat charge at me from a distance while running sideways. He simply stops when he reaches me. I've read this is called "sidewinding" and some say it's to …
A: It is an attempt to look large and threatening and drive you off. In the wild, a cornered cat might do it, or a mother protecting kittens. Usually a cat will slink off and hide, though.

Q: Which vaccines are core for dogs?
A: Core vaccines are the ones every dog should get, wherever it lives. For dogs these protect against:
- Distemper
- Parvovirus
- Adenovirus (infectious hepatitis)

Rabies vaccine is also core anywhere the disease is present or the law requires it.

Global guidelines now say leptospirosis vaccine should be given to all dogs in places where the disease occurs, so in those areas it is treated as core too.

Other vaccines, like kennel cough (Bordetella and parainfluenza), are "non-core". Your vet suggests them based on your dog's lifestyle, such as boarding or contact with many dogs. Ask your vet which vaccines suit your dog.

sources.text:
Dogs — Get your dog vaccinated
Keep your dog up to date on routine vaccinations like rabies. Vaccines can help protect your dog from dangerous diseases and help them live a longer life. Tell your veterinarian about your dog's lifestyle, including whether it is often around other dogs or other animals. Ask about other vaccines you may need or want for your dog, like kennel cough.

Q: My 2 month old puppy bit me. He hasn't gotten any vaccines yet, is it dangerous? I was carrying him and talking to him and he suddenly bit me in my face. My 2 month old puppy hasn't gotten any …
A: No, it's not particularly dangerous. Rabies is the number 1 concern, but the probability your pug/dachshund mix has the disease is super low. Rabies is transmitted mainly by saliva/bites from infected animals such as dogs, raccoons, foxes, coyotes, etc.

There are other diseases that can be carried by your dog, but it's dependent on your location in the world.

If he punctured the skin, keep it clean to avoid infection.

In the meantime work on the biting behavior - socialize a ton and work on gentle play :) and start vaccines + parasite control.

Q: Golden Retriever puppy after vaccination My Golden Retriever breed puppy is 75 days old. Yesterday, he got his 2nd vaccination. However, after almost 36 hours, he behaves something different such as biting everything, peeing elsewhere, not listening our voice, and …
A: Any sudden changes after a medical treatment should be brought to the attention of a medical provider immediately. Call your vet, if they don't have an emergency service call your local emergency vet. Expect you will need to take the pet in for an exam.

Q: Is it legal to sell or eat dog meat in the Philippines?
A: No. RA 9482 bans the trade of dog meat. LGUs must enforce this ban (Section 7).

Under Section 11, anyone caught trading dog meat faces a fine of at least P5,000 per dog and 1 to 4 years in prison. The same penalty applies to using electrocution to put dogs to sleep. Foreigners who break these rules are deported after serving their sentence.

Killing dogs for food is also not among the allowed reasons for killing animals under the Animal Welfare Act (RA 8485, Section 6).

Q: I just got a new puppy. What should I do first?
A: Book a vet visit soon. Your puppy will need a series of shots and deworming.

- Vaccines: puppies get shots every 2 to 3 weeks until they are about 4 months old. Your vet will set the exact schedule.
- Until the shots are done, keep your puppy away from dogs that may not be vaccinated.
- Deworming: worms are common in puppies. Your vet may deworm and check stool samples every 2 to 4 weeks until two tests in a row are clear.
- Feeding: puppies 6 to 12 weeks old usually eat 4 small meals a day of puppy food.
- Potty training: start early. Take the puppy out often and praise them when they go outside.
- Socializing: let them meet people and other animals gently, especially at 2 to 4 months old.
